speechtext: 203. Estimates of the Sergeant-at-Arms, $715,836.

These are the estimates having to do with the office of the Sergeant-at-Arms and I believe they include provision for the security police. I should like to ask Mr. Speaker why it is that veterans of Canada cannot be obtained for this job. Veterans preference is supposed to apply in all of the civil service appointments. These men have, as part of their duties, the taking care of the memorial chamber, and yet apparently it has not been possible to keep the force up to strength with veterans. Can the Speaker tell us why that is so, why it is is not possible to get men who served in the forces of Canada to carry on this work? It does seem to me to be setting a very bad example. That is the one place about this building, and perhaps the whole civil service, where veterans should be employed. Perhaps the Speaker could explain just what the situation is.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as I understand the situation, veterans are employed for any of the positions that may be available on the House of Commons staff, and that, includes, of course, the positions on the protective staff. We have several veterans on our force at the moment. I have not made a close check of the position but I would imagine that we have more veterans on our

force than personnel that is non-veteran. To my knowledge, every time there has been a vacancy, if a veteran has been found for the job he has always been given preference. I can assure the hon. member and all members that it is always our aim to give preference to veterans and, whenever possible, to hire them. I know there was a case not very long ago where a promotional contest took place, and it might have been felt that a veteran should have had the promotion. But the civil service commission, when it organizes those promotional contests, deals only with the people who have reached the stage where they may be eligible for the contest itself, and it so happened that a non-veteran took the promotion. But when we hire people we always give preference to a veteran.
Of course, if the hon. member has a particular case in mind I would certainly be delighted to look into it but, as I understand it, the policy has always been to give preference to veterans and to hire veterans whenever possible.

Well, from the time that I first came here 21 years ago practically all of the men on the security force have been veterans. After the second world war, veterans of the second world war were added to the staff and after the Korean war some veterans of the Korean war were added, but now the practice seems to be to engage civilians. If Mr. Speaker will check the situation I think he will find that that is so. These men are guiding thousands of visitors around this building, showing thousands of visitors both from Canada and the United States through the memorial chamber and, of course, over the years hundreds of thousands. Surely, if there is one place in Canada where veterans should be employed it is on that particular job. I hope that Mr. Speaker will look into this situation and see what can be done to bring about the result that we have veterans of Canada serving in these jobs.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I fully agree with the hon. member. I assure him I will look into it.

Mr. Chairman, it is possible that I should have brought this matter up on item 202. Perhaps I can have the indulgence of the Chair to mention it. Just the other evening there was a telecast from the House of Commons which I understand represented the sixth occasion when various parts of the House of Commons were filmed. I am informed that there are now about six half-hour films available-I do not know in

whose possession they are but since permission for taking the film was given by the Speaker he would probably know.
I have long felt it is regrettable that school children from remote parts of Canada cannot enjoy the privilege of visiting the parliament buildings, this chamber and the Senate chamber, to see how legislation is passed in this country and to see also the beautiful buildings in which our government performs its function.
I am told that these six films which are now available could be made into a one-hour film for a very minor cost, a matter of a few hundred dollars. I wonder if Mr. Speaker would consult with the proper authorities whoever they may be-whether it is the C.B.C. or the national film board-to see if arrangements could be made to have this film produced from the existing films and then distributed or made available to schools and our interested parties across Canada so that if all Canadians are not giver an opportunity of actually seeing these buildings in person they will at least have the opportunity of seeing them on film.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the hon. member refer to six films that might have been taken a few years ago by the national film board?
No, I think the last in the series was the one taken the other evening in the course of the live telecast from these buildings a portion of which, as I understand it, was filmed in this chamber.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: That would mean that either the C.B.C. or the national film board would have to take some extracts from these various films and make a mounted film. The suggestion was that it be distributed to schools?

I suggest it be made available to schools on request and be advertised to the educational authorities as being available. As I understand it, it is merely a matter of editing to produce a one-hour film from the various short films now in existence.

speechtext: Has the hon. member seen the six films?
No, but they have been telecast.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

Mr. Chairman, I have not made the suggestion without having had excellent advice to the effect that it is possible and that the films are appropriate.

speechtext: I will be very glad to look into it. While we are on the subject of television I might mention this. In the last two years I have been asked before the opening of the session whether it would be our desire to be televised, that is our part of the opening ceremony, together with the opening ceremony of the Senate, and since the house is always in recess when the request comes to me I have not taken the responsibility of saying yes. Mr. Chairman, I think it is common knowledge among members of this house and its employees that the existing system by which the rooms are designated, the numbering of the rooms, is extremely confusing and also causes a great deal of inconvenience to people who come to the house for the first time and are looking for the rooms of certain members or various offices they wish to visit. I know from my own experience many people have wandered over almost an entire floor before they could find the office they were looking for.
Perhaps the best example I can cite is that on the fifth floor facing the elevators there is a sign which indicates that you will find rooms 501 to 586 in one direction and that in the other direction you will find rooms 599 to 560. That type of thing indicates that you can find rooms 560 to 586 in both directions simultaneously. It not only indicates the confusion which exists, it indicates the problem for those of us who are not accustomed to going in two directions at the same time as is the government. I wrote to Mr. Speaker earlier this year pointing out this matter of room numbering generally and asking him whether something could be done and also making certain other suggestions. I am wondering what progress has been made in that direction.

DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE A-Department-
166. Departmental administration, including annual contribution of $200 to the conference of commissioners on uniformity of legislation in Canada, $513,658.
Is the minister going to make a statement on the first item?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member was in the chamber when my estimates were first called and I indicated that I had no statement to make on the first item. We then went on to deal with the items of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. In that connection I undertook to get for the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich the date of the order in council dealing with northern allowances for the mounted police. I find that that was passed on October 7, 1955. I would suggest, however, that this morning we might start with the estimates of Justice proper, as the commissioner is on his way into Ottawa and will be here later this morning, about an hour from now.

This is the first item of the Department of Justice estimates. As the minister says, we have been considering other items in this department prior to this. It is not my intention to take very much of the time of the committee this morning on this first item. Although it is usual to discuss in general the affairs of a department on the opening item, this department is in a somewhat different situation possibly from some other departments, and this is particularly so this year because there have been various commissions that have reported, and the minister, I know, has not had time to deal with those commission reports as yet. I think that perhaps some criticism could be levelled at the minister and at the department for having allowed matters to drift along too long without making reconstructions in the Department of Justice, particularly in so far as penal matters are concerned, to bring the administration more in keeping with modern trends and modern conditions; but this year the minister has, I think, given direct attention to those matters. He has had the Fauteux commission report. There has been the committee from this parliament on capital and corporal punishment, which has been sitting for a long while and which is finally making a report. There is also the matter of insanity as a defence and what part it is going to play in the administration of our criminal law.
All of those things are now, one might say, on the minister's desk, and I presume he will give them all careful consideration. We, at least, of the opposition are prepared to give him time for that purpose Therefore I am not going to spend any great time at all this morning in dealing with those matters, although it is open to any hon. member so to do. Perhaps it could be done more profitably in the next session of this parliament, when the minister will be in a position to advise the house, by statement and, I hope, by legislation, just how much of these reports he is proposing to enact. So we let these matters stand for the moment.
There are one or two matters that I think should be emphasized. The other day I noticed the announcement that the proposed women's jail, or penitentiary-call it what you will-at Collin's Bay has been suspended. I believe that tenders had been advertised for, but I am not sure whether contracts have been awarded, and the matter is now in abeyance pending a conference between
Supply-Justice
the minister's department and the provincial authorities on the administration of criminal law. I can see why that step probably should have been taken. As a matter of fact, as the minister well knows, very strong objection was taken by the Elizabeth Fry society and other associations to the principle of confining all the women in one central penitentiary in Canada. I believe that the practice heretofore has been to have them confined in Kingston penitentiary. For many years they were confined in part of a wing in which men were accommodated as well. Then, in about 1910 or some time after that, a block was added to the south block of Kingston penitentiary, where a certain number were accommodated; and latterly one was built outside the confines of the penitentiary itself. I am told that at times there are something over 100 women confined there, although the number is less than that now, and that half of them are probably drug addicts.
Information from the brief of the Elizabeth Fry society which I have seen points out-in fact it quotes the Minister of National Health and Welfare dealing with the drug addict- that in the matter of treatment we move women here, say, from the west coast and that they are confined in the penitentiary for two years or whatever it may be. Then they are given a ticket home. They get as far as Toronto. They sell the ticket and exchange it for drugs and away they go again.
There is also I think a legitimate criticism because it is difficult, if not impossible, for the families to visit the women that come from the east coast or from the west coast and are confined at some central point. Personally, I am very glad to see that the construction is not being proceeded with at the moment. I would hope that, when the minister has this conference with the provincial authorities, some system can be worked out whereby we can avoid the bringing of women to some central point and locking them up there, as has been the practice heretofore. I think it might be better if arrangements could be made with the provincial authorities so that they could be confined at some provincial institution. It is better for their own rehabilitation and I think it is better for the administration of justice as a whole.
Certainly, on the matter of probation, which is also before the minister, I hope definite action will be taken along that line in the near future. That is something which has been a black eye in so far as the administration of justice in this country is concerned. We have lagged behind other countries not only from the standpoint of rehabilitation, in my opinion, but also from the standpoint

Supply-Justice
of cost as well. In the press last week I noticed a statement by Mr. Coughlan who is, I believe, director of probation for the province of Ontario. Putting it merely on a financial basis, he says this:
To lock a person in the federal penitentiary costs the taxpayer $1,760 a year. To keep an eye on him through a probation officer costs $50.
According to the department figure, it costs $50 a year to have him properly supervised under a proper probation system. Of course, we know that there are cases and cases and that probation may apply to one and not to another. But certainly we should develop that system much further than it has been developed in the past. I also noticed in the press a report by Chief Justice Pickup the other day in which he was dealing with this matter and in which he pointed out the merit of probation and of suspended sentence, and recommended that they be extended much further than has been the case in the past.
This is going to be an interesting year, I think, in so far as this department is concerned. There should be many changes and innovations adopted or at least tried, considered and submitted to this parliament for action another year. When next year comes I am sure that we shall be alert. I will only say this to the minister. If some action has not been taken on these various matters, I think he can expect a careful scrutiny of his department and a critical one at that. We of the opposition feel that it is this year in which these various actions should be taken.
Without letting the minister off with no criticism of the department at all, may I say this. I notice something which I am sure the minister read as well. I am directing his attention now to a little article in the Canadian Bar Review of February of this year by Mr. Bora Laskin a noted legal authority. He discusses-and I think properly so-rather critically the action of the Department of Justice in dealing with the Anaconda American Brass Ltd. appeal. As you will recall, Mr. Chairman, that was an appeal taken by the Minister of National Revenue on a decision of the National Revenue Department wherein our court originally held that the department was not justified in taxing the appellant. The matter was taken to the Supreme Court of Canada and the Supreme Court of Canada held that the department was in error and that the taxpayer was right. Then, forsooth, the Minister of Justice-or at least it would be carried by the Department of Justice although I presume on the recommendation of the Minister of National Revenue or his officials-took the case to the privy council. You have the situation whereby

our Department of Justice boasted of the fact that we had thrown off the last vestiges of colonialism and we had established our own supreme court as the paramount court in the land, which has denied to everyone else the right of appeal to the privy council, but yet because there was just a little bit of time left in which, legally, this appeal could be entered, they took the appeal to the privy council, and then forsooth the department went before the privy council. I think that fact puts the Minister of Justice in a somewhat anomalous position when we have this mighty court,-and I am not saying this sarcastically because it is a good court-the court of which he boasts, the court which he described as being our final court and the court which other appellants would not be allowed to go beyond, nevertheless we have this appeal taken to the privy council. I think it would have been much better for the Minister of National Revenue to have dealt with this matter by statute, if necessary, and to have had a statutory change made in the law rather than to have appealed to the privy council and to have had our own supreme court reversed in this way.
There is only one other matter which I would ask the minister to deal with when he speaks. I think he promised a statement on this matter. I may say that it does not come under the first item. He has had the matter before him in dealing with the alleged brewery combine in Canada. He was asked for a report. I understood he said that he was waiting for a report from counsel. I understand that report has been received. I wonder if the minister will tell us at the appropriate time what action, if any, his department proposes to take with respect to the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take up any great amount of time but I think that I would be singularly lacking if I did not express my appreciation of the attitude taken by the official opposition and, I believe, by all the members of the opposition in relation to this question of securing proper and adequate penal laws for Canada. This is just another example of the nonpartisan attitude which all of the parties in this house-I think to their own very great credit-have displayed on this matter from the very beginning.
I must say that up until the present time the progress which we have made has been fairly satisfactory and creditable. The other day in Toronto Saturday Night there appeared an article by a police magistrate. I may say it was not written by a man who had the prejudices of a lawyer. It was written by Mr. Haig-Brown who in addition

to being a layman police magistrate is a distinguished writer and who brought to a criticism of these new laws the, shall I say, more unprejudiced viewpoint of a layman, speaking as to how they would affect the people of Canada. This is the way in which he sums up the effort which this house made in revising the Canadian Criminal Code. One of my reasons for quoting this article is that he puts his finger upon what I think is one of the most important features in dealing with a law of this kind in such a way as completely to meet the criticism which has just been made by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings who has just taken his seat. This is what Mr. Haig-Brown has to say after having seen the new code in operation for over a year now and having taken part, as a police magistrate, in its administration:
Even at this early stage, I believe it is clear that the new code is simpler, fairer and easier to administer than the old one. I have an uneasy feeling that it is in some respects over-cautious, even timid, in recognizing advances in public thinking and in the changing face of Canada. There is a great deal of room for leadership by the central government in improving both the penal and the court systems of the provinces. It would have been good to have seen, for instance, much sharper recognition of the probation system and of special institutions for younger offenders. The hopelessly antiquated costs system in the magistrates' courts should have been abolished and some sensible alternative established. And it should never be a matter of routine for a Canadian citizen to wait three months for his trial, as must a man I committed on December 2, 1955, for trial at the spring assizes of March, 1956.
If I find fault in these matters, I do so with the utmost respect for the skill and integrity of those charged with the enormous task of revision.
This next sentence I would strongly recommend for the consideration of my colleagues.
A nation's criminal code is no suitable toy for the rebellious or hotheaded, or even for idealists in advance of their times. It is a document founded on the wisdom of hundreds of generations, to be advanced only cautiously, through deep and painful thought and clear experience. To have simplified, clarified and broadened the nation's criminal law so extensively while dropping over 400 sections, without the least sign of failure or dislocation, must be reckoned a major Canadian achievement.
I should like to bear testimony, Mr. Chairman, that that is a Canadian achievement in which all parties in this house, and particularly those serving these special committees, are entitled to their full share. It is only by the non-partisan attitude that was displayed by those members, by this house, and on this present occasion by my hon. friend from Digby-Annapolis-Kings, that this result has been achieved. But I think we should take the same attitude towards these other matters in which we are sometimes criticized for being guilty of some delay. The whole question of what the provisions of the penal
Supply-Justice
law of Canada should be and as to the way in which that penal law should be administered is, I suggest, one which should be an integrated whole. When my hon. friend criticizes us in the Department of Justice for doing the proper thing a little bit late may I, and I shall do it as courteously as I can, repudiate that criticism.
I believe we have proceeded as rapidly as we could having regard to the fact that the subject matter is, as Mr. Haig-Brown suggests, a document founded on the wisdom of hundreds of generations, to be advanced only cautiously, through deep and painful thought and clear experience. I am confident that upon reflection my hon. friend will agree with me this is the proper attitude in which to approach a matter of this kind.
What is it that we have done? We came to the conclusion that there was no purpose in concerning ourselves with reforms which may be made to the code and penal laws of Canada until we had first put those laws in a clear and understandable form. Having regard to the fact that the Criminal Code of Canada had not had a consolidation or overall revision for over 60 years, we conceived that the first step in this deliberate process was to consolidate the code. In this way we would know what the existing law was and have it in clear form so it could be understood by all members of the house and those citizens of Canada who might be interested. Then, having secured that-and it took five years of hard work taking into account the number of years spent by the royal commission, then by committees of the house and the two chambers of the house-we addressed ourselves to the question of those respects in which that law might be reformed. Our intention was from the beginning to cover the whole field of criminal law, criminal law administration and penal reform in Canada.
Now, with that in view and having had the Criminal Code consolidated, we set aside for special consideration by a joint committee of the other place and this house, the subject of capital punishment, corporal punishment and lotteries. We just received a couple of weeks ago the report of that committee.
Then, simultaneously and not in any desultory or accidental manner but quite deliberately, we set up two commissions under Chief Justice McRuer of the high court of justice for the province of Ontario, to deal with two related questions, insanity as a defence to a charge involving criminal responsibility, and criminal sexual psychopaths. We expect that the two reports from those two commissions will become available this fall.

Supply-Justice
We also sent to the Fauteux committee the task of examining the whole field of penal reform in Canada, including on the one hand those important subjects of our own responsibility, remissions and tickets of leave, and upon the certain other aspects which, as my hon. friend from Digby-Annapolis-Kings correctly pointed out can only be introduced by the provinces.
This Fauteux report has now come to hand. Within 24 hours of the time it was received in our department from the queen's printer it was tabled in the House of Commons and at the same time letters went out to the attorneys general of the provinces sending them copies of the report and asking them to consider with their colleagues the position they might take in relation to the recommendations of this report in order that we might later get together and consider the manner in which it could be implemented.
This report has 21 recommendations which can be implemented only by the federal government; four which can be implemented by the provincial government; 16 which must be implemented by both the federal and provincial governments; and three which can be implemented by the courts. In those circumstances it seems to me, and I would ask the indulgence of my colleagues in the house to agree with me in this regard, that the only way that affords any real hope of getting a good law which can be well administered is to carry along with us the judgment of those whose responsibility it will be to administer this law after it is put on the statute books. The British North America Act, paragraph 14, section 92 reads this way, that amongst those matters for which the provincial authorities have exclusive jurisdiction are:
The administration of justice in the province, including the constitution, maintenance and organization of provincial courts, both of civil and of criminal jurisdiction and including procedure in civil matters in those courts.
So that, so far as the criminal law we pass here is concerned, the only way in which it can be effectively administered is by the provincial authorities. As we all know a law is, generally speaking, not very much better than its administration. Our authority here, under paragraph 27 of section 91, is addressed to the criminal law, except the constitution of courts of criminal jurisdiction, but including the procedure in criminal matters.
When we have, therefore, received all of these reports-we are expecting two from Chief Justice McRuer this fall and we already have the report of the joint committee of parliament and the Fauteux committee-we will have the whole field of criminal law and penal administration covered in those
[Mr. Garson.l
reports, other than that which has already been taken care of in the consolidation of the code. We will be in a position, in consultation with the provinces, to lay the whole of this, material before these provincial administrators in the hope of securing the invaluable assistance of the views of these people who have had practical experience in the administration of the criminal law. Without such practical advice 1 do not think that a group of theorists, no matter how able they may be, can produce a really good result.
I mention these things to repel the idea that we have just been drifting along and letting things take their course, and that the reason that we are dealing with these matters now instead of six, seven or eight years ago, is some fault of the Department of Justice. That is not so.
We started our program faced with this fact, that we could not expect to get much co-operation from the provincial governments in the matter of penal reform if we had not to the fullest extent that we could within our own authority put our own house in order by implementing those recommendations of the Archambault report which we could implement. We first implemented those recommendations. Then we set up the royal commission to consolidate the Criminal Code, and as soon as that task was finished we set up those other committees and other commissions. Now, we have all the reports and we are in a position, as a result of a campaign of over eight or nine years, to bring this whole matter to a completion in collaboration with the provincial governments whose advice to us in the matter of drafting the law in the first place is invaluable and whose assistance is completely indispensable in making the criminal code a law which in reality is capable of administration. We cannot get along without provincial cooperation. That is the reason we have adopted the action which we have taken. There has been no delay. The whole matter has moved forward to the present stage as a matter of deliberate planning. If, in the meanwhile, we have not implemented the recommendation of the joint committee with regard, for example, to appeal as of right in capital cases to the Supreme Court, it is because on this particular subject, along with all of these other matters, we think it should properly be discussed with the provincial authorities before we undertake to pass any laws in relation to it here without any prior consideration of it at all by those who will administer it.

Mr. Chairman, I have been very much interested in the remarks of the Minister of Justice. It is not my intention to

hold up this item too long, but there are a few aspects that I would very much like to touch on.
First of all, as far as the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons on capital and corporal punishment and lotteries is concerned, I want to agree completely with the minister that in all the years I have sat on committees I never saw one in which there was such an aspect of non-partisanship. Everybody endeavoured to tackle the problem according to the terms of reference. However, sir, we now have on file in this House of Commons the three reports of the joint committee on capital and corporal punishment and lotteries. We have also on file in this house the report of the Fauteux commission that regards parole and ticket of leave, and other aspects of penology. It is obvious that these reports are not going to be considered at this session. I think, sir, that is quite understandable because I agree completely with the minister when he says that there is in all reports not a conflict of jurisdiction but a necessity of co-operation in jurisdictions as far as the federal, the provincial and the judiciary are concerned.
It is my understanding, Mr. Chairman, that, in addition to what has already been said by the Minister of Justice in the past few minutes, it is his intention in the latter part of this year to call a conference at which all of these reports will be discussed and some agreement reached and upon the results legislation introduced at the next session both from the federal and the provincial level. I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, that it is impossible to have any speedier action than that. I will say I do not think the minister can do anything else except what he is doing in that regard. However, I do think at this time certain statements should be made.
It was a great privilege for me to be a member of the joint committee for 2J years; but under the committee rules of procedure in the House of Commons a minority report cannot be brought in. I want to make it very clear to the minister through you, Mr. Chairman, that although it was a very good committee and all discussions were on a non-partisan basis, I cannot agree with all the recommendations brought in. I make the very definite statement that in my opinion, some of the recommendations cannot be substantiated by the two years of evidence that came before the committee. That being so, I would like to make a suggestion to the Minister of Justice that while his department is giving consideration to the recommendations that have been made by the various committees and commissions that have now reported, at the same time his officials be told to see whether or not the
Supply-Justice
recommendations can be substantiated by the evidence that was given before the committee. I think that is very important, sir.
I am not going to take the time of the committee to go into any detail but I am going to make this statement as a member of the committee and one interested for a long time in capital punishment. The evidence that was received over two years will not back up the statement of the committee that capital punishment is a deterrent, because all of the evidence from countries that do not have capital punishment compared with those that have shows there is only the slightest variation. It is so insignificant that it should not even be considered as conclusive proof, not only in the countries that have capital punishment, but in the six states of the United States that have abolished it for many years.
The major influence on those who supported capital punishment was the protection of our police officers. Until 18 months ago there was no study undertaken about the position of police officers as between abolish-ionist and retention countries, but a study was made by Professor Thorsten Sellin and the information and findings filed with the committee. The only statistical information ever obtained proves that capital punishment is not a protection for police officers. That is all I am going to say about it, but it is why I hope that in the studies that are now going to be made before the conference is held, I understand sometime in November, they will consider the evidence as well as the recommendations.
I have something in addition to that, Mr. Chairman. Because under the Criminal Code there is still capital punishment in Canada, and there will be for some time, I would like to ask the minister through you, Mr. Chairman, and the Solicitor General and the remission branch to give very careful consideration to how executive clemency is exercised. I know, Mr. Chairman, that the minister, because the remission branch comes under his department and because he knew the committee wanted the fullest possible information, as to how executive clemency was exercised, made a full report that is now a matter of evidence before this house.
Sir, I completely fail to understand, although I have heard the explanation of the Minister of Justice and have re-read the evidence, how a decision is reached, on a logical basis, concerning whether or not executive clemency will be granted. I am not speaking just as a theorist nor am I speaking from emotionalism because I always try to study these matters before I make any statement or recommendation.

Supply-Justice
To me it is most difficult to understand, in view of the information contained in the report which is now a part of the proceedings of this house, how a young man who commits premeditated robbery and premeditated murder can get executive clemency when someone else, with a psychologically bad background, who in the heat of passion and drunkenness shoots his step father, who has told him he will not be permitted to marry his step daughter and is alleged to have raped her, is hanged.
I fail to understand why another person with a bad psychological background who is known as a brutal man and kicks a man to death in a fit of drunken brutality urged on by people around him hangs whereas others -I am not going to mention names at any time-who commit murder in the course of premeditated robbery are given a life sentence.
I am not going to say anything more on that matter except to tell the minister through you, Mr. Chairman, that after a thorough study of all the types of cases I have referred to I quite honestly cannot help but come to one conclusion. I do not like to say this but I am going to say it. I cannot help but wonder whether executive clemency is not based on the flip of a coin; heads you die and tails you live. On no other basis can I make any sense of the exercise or nonexercise of executive clemency as far as a number of capital cases are concerned especially several which occurred in western Canada in the past two years.
Mr. Chairman, I did not like to say that although I felt compelled to say it in order to ask that, until a decision be made by parliament at the next session or at a future session on the question of capital punishment, perhaps a second thought be given to the question of the exercise of executive clemency as to whether a man hangs or gets life imprisonment so that perhaps it will be placed on a more sensible basis as to who lives and who dies as long as we follow the principle that if an individual takes a human life society has the same right in relation to the offender's life.
There is only one other point I want to raise. As I read the report of the special joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons and the Fauteux report, there are certain aspects or recommendations that do not require legislation and do not entail statutory action on the part of the federal government or the provinces. There are some recommendations especially in the Fauteux report that can be put into effect by regulations under authority that already exists. I have not had an opportunity of

discussing this matter with the minister but I sincerely hope that beneficial recommendations upon which action can be taken without legislative authority will be considered and that he will not wait until the conference is held in November, or whenever it is planned to be held, and that he will not wait until there will be a meeting of the provincial parliaments or the federal house. I think that is a normal and a good request.
Mr. Chairman, in order that I will not be misunderstood I am going to close my remarks with this thought. Criminals cannot and must not be coddled; if they break the laws of society they must be required to pay a penalty. I am not a person who waxes emotional because a person is a criminal; I have just as much feeling toward those who are hurt as toward those who do the hurting, if not more. Experience in modern penology throughout the world has proven that some of the methods used in the past are not the best methods and that those methods, some of which are in use at the present time, are most offensive.
I personally appreciate the studies that have been made under the authority of the minister concerning the question of penology and I believe if Canada can catch up to modern penology we will save not only a number of lives but a great deal of the taxpayers' money.
Just as I changed my mind in the committee more than once, I hope the Minister of Justice will change his mind more than once when considering the report and in undertaking to do what can be done now in the way of following their recommendations; and in checking on his remission branch the reports of which we now depend, although we know the final authority does not come from the remission branch at all.
The minister has a great and a grave responsibility. I look forward at the next session, whether it is before or after an election, to commending the Minister of Justice on the action he takes now that he has the reports in his hands.

When the minister first returned to the house 1 asked him about the policy being followed this year in British Columbia by the mounted police in refusing to issue permits to prospectors, geologists and men engaged in that type of work for the carrying of revolvers. This question will be found at page 5981 of Hansard of July 16. On that particular day the minister replied that he had run across two or three cases where permits had been refused under such circumstances, but it seemed to him the police had exercised their powers properly.
The following day the minister made a much fuller reply, to be found on page 6053 of Hansard, in which he pointed out that section 90 of the Criminal Code permitted no one to carry a revolver without obtaining a permit. The minister then went on to deal with section 94 which authorizes the issuance of permits. In effect his answer was that it was not the responsibility of the mounted police to decide whether these men should get permits, but that in a province it was the sole responsibility of the provincial attorney general. He suggested rather naively that I should send my question on to Hon. Mr. Bonner who is the attorney general of the province of British Columbia. On checking section 94 which provides for the issuance of permits I find that it reads as follows:
(1) A permit in form 42 may be issued by
(a)	the commissioner or a person authorized in writing by him, or
(b)	the attorney general of a province or a person authorized in writing by him.
That part of the section clearly gives the commissioner of the mounted police or any
Supply-Justice
person authorized by him the right to issue a permit equivalent to the right given' to the attorney general. Each of them is given the same authority. I do not know where the minister gets his backing for the statement that in the province of British Columbia only the attorney general or someone authorized by him can issue a permit. Section 94 goes on to provide:
(4) A permit in form 42 shall be issued only where the person who issues is satisfied that the applicant for the permit requires the firearm to which it relates
(a)	to protect his life or property,
(b)	for use in connection with his profession or occupation.
The next clause (c) is not material to my submission. The first two clauses clearly give the power to issue permits to men' engaged in occupations of this kind. I am told by the British Columbia and Yukon chamber of mines of Vancouver, which is a thoroughly responsible organization which has carried on for many years, that for at least 25 years it has been the practice to issue permits to prospectors and men carrying on activities of that kind. The chamber of mines wrote to Mr. J. R. W. Bordeleau, superintendent, officer in change, C. I. B., Royal Canadian Mounted Police, Victoria. The letter is dated June 4 and reads in part:
The officials of this organization cannot understand the reason why your department has taken such drastic action. For at least 25 years, to my knowledge, prospectors and other such persons have been allowed to carry sidearms in British Columbia and the Yukon Territory.
The letter then goes on to set out the reasons why this has been done, as follows:
1.	In many instances, prospectors who are working in rugged, mountainous country, in isolated areas, must depend on sidearms both for protection and survival, including the shooting of small game for food. In many cases prospectors have used their sidearms for signalling for assistance.
2.	To most prospectors and geologists travelling over long distances, through rugged terrain, weight is a vitally important factor. Some prospectors carry rifles, but others working in particularly difficult areas, cannot afford to carry the extra weight and cumbersome equipment.
3.	Many modem prospectors and engineers, when in the field, carry in their hands other tools that are essential to their profession, such as a prospector's pick, geiger counter, compass, dip needle or magneto-meter for locating ore bodies- steel tapes for running survey lines, etc. In such instances, the sidearm must take the place of the rifle.
We all know that what is set forth in that letter is correct. The chamber received a reply from Superintendent Bordeleau dated June 7, 1956, reading as follows:
I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter dated June 4th, 1956 dealing with the issue of small arms permits to prospectors, mining engineers, geologists, etc.
The points raised in your letter have been carefully and sympathetically considered, but it is

Supply-Justice
pointed out that the issuance of such permits is not merely a matter of this office exercising discretion but rather of issuing such permits strictly in accordance with the provisions of the Criminal Code.
I suggest that the Criminal Code is wide enough, certainly the section I read, to cover these cases.
It is felt here that while there may be some justification for the arguments set forth in your letter, the law as it stands at present is not sufficiently elastic to allow the issuance of such permits to the category of individuals and for the purposes you mention.
We are at present in correspondence with our headquarters on the matter-
No suggestion that he is conferring with the attorney general.
-with the object of exploring the possibility of suitable amendments being made to the appropriate sections of the code which would, under appropriate conditions, permit the issuance of permits to the type of individual referred to.
It is hoped that in the near future we will be able to communicate with you again on this subject.
Not a word in that letter about the practice of issuing these permits for the last 25 years and not a word about a change having been made this year. I have here a copy of a letter written by a prospector at Ootsa Lake, British Columbia, to Mr. T. Elliott, manager of the British Columbia and Yukon chamber of mines under date of July 16 and reading:
I have talked to numerous prospectors here in the north, all of whom are on the warpath due to the stupidity of someone who evidently has no idea of what he is doing in prohibiting prospectors from carrying pistols while in the hills.
Has this dimwit an idea that prospectors ran around shooting people? Does he realize that with a prospector's pick in one hand, he must have the other free to climb?
He is unable to carry a rifle on that account. Whoever hatched up this stupid idea should be turned loose in a grizzly country and not allowed a gun.
We, the prospectors of B.C., ask that the chamber of mines take up this injustice with the proper authorities and have this law revoked. You can have this letter published if they will print it.
Sincerely yours,
Billy McNiell.
The Vancouver Sun sums up this situation very well in an editorial on June 25, 1956, entitled "Why Pick on Prospectors?":
We do not look for any drop in the crime rate as a result of the decision to deny B.C. prospectors the right to pack pistols. This has the sound of small-bore officialdom.
The average citizen, including the sportsman, has no complaint against Criminal Code restrictions upon the use of pistols and revolvers, the "concealed weapons" as our law classes them.
Prospectors and mining engineers, however, have a special need for hand-guns. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police, who themselves must often backpack through our wilderness, should be the first to realize it.
Unlike the fishermen, the farmer or the logger, the prospector usually travels alone and by foot.

And always he must travel light. Every additional pound in the packsack is a burden when a man is chopping his way through salal, or slogging it over the rockslides.
The pistol's a skookum tillicum-
That is a British Columbia word.
-to any prospector.
He knows grizzly bears don't attack men-well, not often that is. But there he is, miles away from another human and well, if that bear should be mean that prospector's bones will leach into this hillside before another human is likely to walk this way. Who wouldn't want to feel the comfort, however false a comfort it may be, of a revolver butt in his hands in these circumstances?
Let's remember too that a pistol is handy for popping off rattlesnakes. For example, there's the case of an Osoyoos prospector-
That is in the Okanagan district, as the minister knows, very near the United States boundary.
-who killed 39 rattlers within 100 yards of his claim.
Finally, and perhaps most important, the prospector who treks farthest into our wilderness must depend for much of his food supply upon game-which the law permits him to take under proper circumstances. What can take the place of a pistol for popping off fool hens for the frying pan? Not, we're sure, a three-foot long rifle strapped to that dismally heavy packboard.
We'd suggest a little fatigue drill for the bureaucrat who made this decision. Say, three runs up the side of Grouse mountain holding a pump shotgun above his head.
I have other letters from prospectors, but I shall not read them. I suggest to the minister that he accept equal responsibility for this situation with the Attorney General, as the Criminal Code intended that the commissioner of the mounted police should have the same powers as the Attorney General to issue these permits. There is no point in passing the buck to the Attorney General. The firearm permit is contained in form 42, which says:

Then there could be a limitation on the period for which the permit is good.
I urge upon the minister that he take steps without further delay to see that this situation is remedied. I am sure he will agree with me that it is unfair to make these men go into the hills without permitting them to carry a revolver should they wish to do so. I only regret that most of the present summer has gone by and that these men who are the pioneers of Canada in these modern days are facing this handicap that has been placed on them so unnecessarily.

I should like very briefly to support the plea of the member for Van-couver-Quadra on this matter because it is a matter of great importance to a number of persons in my constituency, particularly prospectors, trappers, timber cruisers and handicapped persons. The member has outlined the case very well, and there is no necessity for me to repeat his arguments. I support them completely and fully.
I might say, with respect to handicapped persons, that it is impossible for some of these people to enjoy going back into the hills or undertaking trapping, prospecting or cruising without being allowed to carry small arms. In my own case, I had been up to recent years given a permit year after year by the police to carry a revolver because I naturally could not climb a mountain with a revolver in one hand and nothing in the other. I think that applies to a number of people I know. I urge that consideration be given to these very sensible requests of these people who are making a contribution to our country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am very sorry indeed,
especially in relation to the two amiable members who have just spoken, that I cannot agree with what they are seeking. That does not mean that I am in the least measure unsympathetic toward the prospectors, because I am very fond of outdoor life myself. I have travelled a good deal through the bush, at least enough to appreciate the value that a revolver could be to these prospectors.
However, the difficulty here, as I endeavoured to explain before, is this. Where we have this parliament with the authority to pass the Criminal Code, the provincial authorities with the responsibility for its enforcement, and an agreement as we have with the province of British Columbia under which our police force is made available to the provincial attorney general in order to help carry out their responsibility for the enforcement of the Criminal Code, it would just be monstrous if in that province the Royal Canadian Mounted Police would be attempting to administer at one and the same time the revolver permit policy of the attorney general of British Columbia on the one hand and the revolver permit policy of the federal Department of Justice on the other. This would be a fit subject for a Gilbert and Sullivan opera, not for any situation in real life.
As a matter of fact, the only way in which the taxpayers of this country can have the very great advantage indeed of having one police force act for both the provincial government and the federal government in eight out of the ten provinces of Canada is that
Supply-Justice
we in Ottawa shall be meticulous in respecting the full jurisdiction of the provincial authorities.
If these prospectors' needs are as great as the hon. members have indicated they are, then I cannot for the life of me see why the attorney general of British Columbia, as the head of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in British Columbia in relation to all matters of the administration of criminal law in that province, cannot instruct the police force there, under these circumstances that have been outlined, to grant these permits. It would certainly be a bad state of affairs if, he having decided not to issue these permits, I should be attempting to instruct the same police force to disregard his viewpoint and to carry into effect our policy in respect of a matter which comes under his jurisdiction.
I was asked questions when I was last in Vancouver, about certain reports being made by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police at the request of the provincial government that I should make them public, since I had access to their confidence. I have no access at all to them in relation to the matters that come under the provincial authority. The only way in which we can have this worked satisfactorily-indeed, the only way in which we could administer criminal justice generally -is by the two levels of government respecting the respective authority of each.

The minister is responsible for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. This letter was written to the superintendent in Victoria over two months ago. All he had to do was pick up the telephone and phone the provincial attorney general to find out whether it was British Columbia government policy that these men should not be issued revolvers. All the Minister of Justice had to do on July 16, when I asked him that question, was to have the R.C.M.P. checked in Victoria to find out what the situation was. He cannot get up here today and say that a mounted policeman in British Columbia is one kind of mounted policeman and a mounted policeman in Ottawa is another kind. It is all the one force.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I never said that.
I have the floor.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am rising on a point of privilege. My hon. friend is attributing to me a statement that I did not make, that I said "A mounted policeman in British Columbia is one kind of mounted policeman, and a mounted policeman in Ottawa is another kind of mounted policeman." I never made any such statement at all, and I am sure that my hon. friend will agree that I did not.

Supply-Justice
What I said was that where there is a police agreement, as there is in the case of British Columbia between the government of British Columbia and the government of Canada, under which we agree in consideration of the payment of a large sum of money every year to make available the Royal Canadian Mounted Police force to the provincial attorney general to the end that he may be thereby assisted to carry out his responsibilities that police force when it is acting in that regard is acting under his control and not under mine. It would be a fine state of affairs if, in derogation of this agreement, I were instructing the mounted police to pay no attention to the attorney general of the province in the face of the fact that one of the terms of the agreement is that it shall carry out his wishes in the enforcement of justice in that province.

The minister is responsible for the efficiency of the mounted police force. It seems to me to be extreme inefficiency for them if they did not take this question up with the attorney general at once, as soon as the complaint was received from British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?
Just a minute. I am making these remarks.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: How does my hon. friend know that the police officer in question did not phone the attorney general and that he was not told by him that he did not want to have a permit issued?

If that was the case, we should be told so here in the house. That is what I want to know. I want to find out who is responsible for this ridiculous situation. If the mounted police know that the provincial attorney general is responsible, let us be told that here. Then we can go after the provincial attorney general. But the mounted police officer, when he replied to the letter of the British Columbia and Yukon chamber of mines, did not say he was writing to the provincial attorney general. He said he was writing to Ottawa. I would say it is the business of the mounted police, if they are directed efficiently, to clear this thing up with the attorney general and with the justice department. There is no justification for their doing nothing about it.
There is something to be said for the minister's argument that he does not want to interfere with the provincial attorney general.

But why did not the mounted police go ahead and investigate this thing and find out who was responsible for this change of policy? Do the mounted police today know who is responsible? Did that order go out from Ottawa or did it go out from the attorney general in Victoria? The mounted police must know that, and we should be told. All I am trying to do is to get to the bottom of the situation and to find out who made this fool change in policy.
That is the point.
Mr. Chairman-
Wait a minute. I am getting an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the officer in British Columbia to whom my hon. friend from Vancouver-Quadra has referred has not written to me as to what he should do in the matter. In any case in which the matter concerning which he was writing had to do with the question of the policy to be followed by the attorney general of the province, our reply to him would be that this was a matter of provincial policy in respect of which he should take the direction of the attorney general of the province. That is the only possible attitude that we could take. Suppose that, for example, in the province of Ontario where there is no police contract we did not follow the practice that we do follow, of only issuing these permits with respect to interprovincial matters and express officers and so on who are travelling across several provinces, and suppose that in spite of the fact that the attorney general of Ontario did not issue any permits, we started issuing a great many of them from Ottawa in derogation of his policy. Is that the way in which to promote good relations between the two levels of government? I do not think so, and I am sure my hon. friend does not think so either.
Did the minister say that Mr. Bordeleau did not write in to headquarters at Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. I am saying that he did not write to me.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be very brief. They have to do in general with the R.C.M.P.
The historic significance of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is well known to Canadians. No police force is held in greater esteem nor regarded with greater pride or deeper satisfaction by the people it serves. It is indeed one of the finest police forces in the world. No other police force is so closely identified with the pioneering origins and progress of a country as is the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. It has preserved the many fine traditions of its origins and it has succeeded in attracting and maintaining a high degree of respect as an honest, efficient and dedicated group of Canadian men who serve their country, silently and often at great personal sacrifice, with dedication and a spirit of service not often seen in any field of endeavour.
Indeed, the force was originally intended to become another mounted regiment. The name was to have been "North West Mounted Rifles". Legend has it that, when Sir John
Supply-Justice
A. Macdonald realized that such a name might arouse distrust among our American neighbours of 1880, he took pen in hand and struck out the word "Rifles" and, in its stead wrote "Police". The force was not to number more than 300 men, all mounted and efficiently equipped, with, in Sir John's own words, "as little gold lace and fuss and feathers as possible". Ordinary constables were to get $1 per day, subconstables 75 cents.
In the famous westward march of 1874, Lt. Col. George A. French, the then commissioner, and his men performed a singular feat of human courage. They marched 781 miles from Red River and, except during the first 18 miles, did not see a human habitation beyond a few isolated Indian wigwams.
Inextricably interwoven with the history of the prairies and the growth of Canada, the force has made an outstanding contribution to peace and order and respect for law in Canada. Our Canadian heritage would indeed be the poorer had Canada not had a police force which fitted so well and so colourfully into the hard early and formative years of our country.
It has been my privilege to have served in the force. One other member of our party has also seen service in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Any member or ex-member of the force is always quick to recognize and to acknowledge the tremendous influence which tradition and the maintenance of high ideals of service have in all aspects of life and service in the force.
The present commissioner is to be congratulated on his forward-looking achievements since becoming commissioner of the force. Throughout the years, however, some unpleasant aspects of the military life of 1880 have been held over and have become not only .cumbersome but detrimental to the recruiting of well-suited men and the keeping of these men in the service. If I were to put my finger on the most glaring example of how one holdover from the days of the great ride west prejudicially affects the force, I would have to deal with the anti-marriage regulations now in effect in the force. I am quick to agree that in 1880 the duties of the force were such as to require free wheeling and fast moving men, without kith or kin to consider. Isolation was often the keynote of service, and long, dangerous, lonely patrols were the essence of the work involved. These conditions, except in northern service, have long since vanished and our concept of freedom today does not tolerate any interference in the rights of men engaged in police work in regard to marriage.

Supply-Justice
Early in 1956 I read the following headlines in the newspapers: "Six R.C.M.P. Constables Fired for Marrying". The article goes on to show how the six couples had been secretly married for about a year. At social functions, the wives pretended to be girl friends. This was not a so-called "secret marriage ring" the article said. The members of the force had acted individually, but all had been married for some time. Why should they not be married, Mr. Chairman? May I point out the very detrimental aspects of this unnecessary, morally injurious and prejudicial regulation, for which there is no reason today.
Consider how this regulation limits the age of the recruit. It now requires, in most cases, five years' service and other qualifications before permission to marry may be granted. The ideal member is likely to be the young man who has completed his education and has had some experience in one or more fields of endeavour. By this time, the young man is in his early twenties and is looking for an opportunity to settle down, found a home and raise a family. I maintain this man is more often than not prevented and discouraged from joining the force merely because he cannot do so if he is married, and cannot get married for five years if he does. Often it is the bright young accountant or young lawyer, about age 28, who wants to make police work his life's endeavour. The F.B.I. in the United States has long limited recruiting almost exclusively to men of these professions. Here again he is prevented from joining because he is married or discouraged from joining because he has to postpone marriage for at least five years, which would make him 33 and that is too long to wait. Thus the R.C.M.P., by this morally wrong regulation, is depriving itself of the services of men most likely to be most suited and qualified. The force, by this unnecessary rule, limits recruits to very young men who, after joining, often soon find the occasion to get married.
Let me say this, Mr. Chairman. Under such influences as are found in life in the force, no such morally wrong anti-marriage regulations will stand for long in the way of love. Thus some members, like the six constables mentioned in the news item, live secretly wedded lives and must continue to do so if they wish to keep their jobs. I commend those men who would rather break a stupid anti-marriage rule in the force than live in the risk of breaking the laws of God in respect to morality in sex and marriage.
Will the Minister of Justice, who sits there with his glum expression, tell me what he has against marriage by members of the

force? Does he not agree and recognize that the family units are the very basis of our society? Does he not agree that no reason whatever exists to punish our men in the force by denying them the natural right to found a family and live a peaceful married life? Is there a member of this house who disagrees with me when I say that the Canadian people do not want this situation to exist? The Canadian people want the members of the force paid increased wages to permit them to lead comfortable married lives and be permitted to marry as and when they please, with aid and encouragement from the force itself. I appeal to your sense of the value of morals to appreciate how this senseless regulation is inclined to affect sex morality in the force. This government is morally responsible for placing these young men in the force in a position where they cannot, without living secretly wedded lives, exercise fundamental, inherent basic rights of the human race.
One of the detrimental results not always apparent by reason of this regulation, which in a police force is morally wrong, is the terrific turnover in the personnel of the force. Many well trained, experienced and valued men in the force, rather than live a secretly married life or wait for years on end to get married, leave the force. This often occurs at a time when their services in the force have become most valued and needed. This regulation defeats and discourages recruiting of men and the retention of their services in the mounted police. Remember this: a distinction is necessary, because I refer not to the voluntary vows of celibacy for life in various religious institutions, and which we all recognize to be a way of life voluntarily accepted in the vocation of religious life. I say this because I know some Liberal members will try to twist and turn the meaning of remarks. Let us remove the barnacles from the force. I request, on behalf of the people of Canada, that the members of the force be paid higher wages and be permitted to marry as and when they choose. Let this government place the force in a position to hire and keep policemen. I realize that in some cases involving police work in small towns a member of the force may be permitted, under certain circumstances, to marry after three years. However, be it three years or five or seven years, as it was formerly, it is the concept of this curtailment of liberty which is wrong and which should be righted in the light of morality and the betterment of the force.
Another holdover from the regimental status of the force in the 1880's is the system of promotion. Now, the army system of promotion in Canada is good, although there is

room for much improvement. However, it is not the same system as existed in the 1880's. The old army system of promotion of 1880, presently practised by the force, does not meet the requirements of the force nor does it give sufficient recognition to the valour and efficiency of its members. It is, on the whole, entirely unsatisfactory. In the army today a private may become a corporal overnight. But in the R.C.M.P. it usually requires eight or more years' service. A corporal in the army today can become a sergeant in a matter of months, but in the R.C.M.P. it usually requires 15 or more years. Indeed, the majority of the members spend their entire careers in the force as third, second or first class constables and retire as constables. It will be readily seen that the present system of promotion does not provide sufficient recognition and acknowledgement for ability, efficiency, outstanding service or seniority of service.
Furthermore, in the public mind, the rank of corporal in the force is synonomous with the rank of corporal in the army. I have every respect for the army rank of corporal but we all know that, in the force, apart from the use of the same terms, the similarity ends. A corporal in the R.C.M.P. has already been a third class constable; a second class constable; a first class constable; and in some cases a sub-constable. He has also seen an average of 10 years of service; has become proficient in many branches of police work and has become an expert in some. His training has been extensive and his conduct and application to duty have been outstanding over a long period of time. Then, again, the corporal in the R.C.M.P. is normally in charge of policing an area, a district, county or town. He has usually several men under his command. He is like the chief of police in a given area. His work, his responsibilities, his influence place him in a position of honour and responsibility in the community. I suggest, therefore, that the term corporal be abolished and replaced by a term which more suitably designates and describes the duties involved and the meaning of the promotion, such as chief officer.
The same reasoning should be applied to all other terms used to designate rank and authority in police work below the rank of inspector. I do not intend this remark to apply to subinspectors, inspectors, superintendents, deputy commissioners, assistant commissioners or commissioners. You will note that in these commissioned officer ranks, appropriate names of rank for police work have been adopted, and wisely so. Why not recognize the same principle in regard to ranks below those of commissioned officer ranks? I maintain that a new importance
Supply-Justice
would be given police work and a new and better recognition would come to members of the force if these two aspects of life in the force were altered along the lines I suggest. Recruiting would be helped. Better men, more educated men, would be encouraged to join the force, and fewer good men now in the force would be inclined to leave. This government and the people of Canada simply do not know and do not appreciate the real sacrifices imposed upon the men in the force by reason of these and other stupid regulations which have no reason for existing in 1956. They are holdovers from the regimental unit which the force was in 1880. The army of today would look silly with some of the regulations of 1880. Why punish the men in the mounted police by retaining those holdovers of 1880? Now, lest some Liberal again twists my remarks, let me say that the desired changes can be brought about without in any way detracting from the fine traditions associated with the force.
The force is out of date and out of step. Let the government give our men in the force a decent break and a fair deal.
Let me say a word on pensions. While in Edmundston the other day I was talking to a man who retired from the force some 10 years ago with the rank of sergeant. He mentioned to me that today a sergeant retired with about three times what he was getting. Does the government not think that it would be only fair to reconsider the pension scheme that has been applied to the force over the years and do something toward bringing up to date today the pensions that were given say 10 or 15 years ago. The men who retired on pensions some years ago are now living in almost pitiable conditions. The same thing applies here as applied to the men of the Canadian National Railways who are expected to live on $25 a month.
I am sure there is not one man in this house who disagrees with me. If we all agree that this is right, then it is only because the government lacks the courage to do something about it. Why not recognize that a man who has spent his life in the force is almost just as intimately connected with the administration of justice as a judge, or a lawyer in the employ of the government, and his training and ability, although on a different plane, are most important. Whereas a judge interprets the law and imposes sentence, the policeman enforces it and prevents its breach. If there is one singular aspect in connection with the mounted police today it is in the efforts they are making to prevent crime. Why not adopt the attitude that the members of the force should be considered in the same light as

Supply-Justice
other law enforcement officers employed by the Department of Justice who do not happen to be members of the force?
Today, in police work, as in all fields of law, specialization is the key and the order of the day. Gone are most of the old duties of the force, the patrolling of boundaries, the quieting of unrest on the reserves, the long prairie patrols. Those were great days in the history of the force of jobs well done, often under adverse and dangerous conditions. Great traditions were then embedded and have stood the force in good stead ever since. But today new duties and new specialties are required.
The F.B.I. in the United States has come up with a more realistic answer to the problem inherent today in police work. Canada, although a much smaller country, should not tarry in adopting, to a greater degree, the more modern and efficient methods used by the F.B.I. and Scotland Yard. This can be done without detracting from the traditions of the force in any respect. Police work today must be based on specialization and a keener atmosphere of service, and more encouragement must be provided. In this, the force falls short of the mark and more corrective methods are needed.
Pensions in the force are inadequate and should be raised. They should be made uniform and simple. The mumbo-jumbo that now exists in pension regulations should be more uniform and the force retain its marks of greatness. No one even suggests that the uniforms be changed or that the horses be abolished, or that the training be abolished, but do not let these things become so nostalgic as to prevent the force from becoming the modern police force which Canada now needs.

It is almost one o'clock. I have just one brief question. In view of the fact that the R.C.M.P. has the responsibility of enforcing the regulations of the Canada Shipping Act, and since apparently a great many new regulations are contemplated, particularly with respect to regulating small boats and craft on the great lakes, minor waters and other waters of Canada, has the minister contemplated making any additions to the force effectively to enforce the new regulations which are contemplated, particularly since we understand from the Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport that these regulations will be coming into force sometime this fall. I might say that we are very happy that this year the R.C.M.P. has made a special effort to enforce the existing regulations under the Canada Shipping Act. Those of us who come from the great lakes area of southern Ontario greatly appreciate the fact that they are enforcing the fire and life-saving regulations. Does the minister contemplate making any additions to the force in view of the great number of regulations that will be coming into effect?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We have this matter under consideration. There have been some additions to the force since we have taken on this new responsibility. I would not suggest that they are directly attributable to that. It may be that we shall have to add others. At the present time we have under consideration just what will be involved in the complete administration of those regulations, and we shall be governed by the conclusions that we reach on the basis of the attention we give to these matters.
