speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, I have been doing a little thinking and a little figuring concerning the Royal Canadian Mounted

Police force and I have come to the conclusion that they are the finest group of men that could be gathered together in one association. Many years ago they established a splendid tradition and this has been lived up to over the years.
Sometimes I think certain things could be done for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police force that would not only benefit the force but would encourage the individuals who comprise it. For instance the qualifications for enlistment in the R.C.M.P. are both rigid and strict and they are certainly enforced to the letter. When a young man wishes to join the force he must be possessed of a high I.Q.; in other words, he must not only be an intelligent fellow but he must be physically fit. I believe the standards for enrolment in the R.C.M.P. are higher than those which apply to any other police force in the commonwealth of nations.
I do not believe the force is presently being overrun with volunteers nor is it swamped with applicants, because from time to time advertisements such as the one I hold in my hand appear in the newspapers and these are designed to encourage volunteers. This advertisement reads in part:
The prime requisites of a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are intelligence, loyaity, integrity and courage. Service requirements frequently entail long hours, inconvenience and personal danger. Service benefits and advantages include a certain prestige, good comradeship, a measure of adventure and satisfaction through service to Canada.
There is no doubt that this force renders a great service to Canada and perhaps the service it renders is greater than that rendered by any other organization within the boundaries of our country. There is also no doubt that these men create, promote and maintain a feeling of mutual understanding and good will between the people of various races and religions who live in this country. They do a great deal more than just policing in the areas where they are stationed.
I am happy to say that the R.C.M.P. is the only branch of government service where the patronage system has not crept in and possibly this has been prevented because of the efforts of the top officials in the force.
The young men who join the R.C.M.P. are about the poorest paid civil servants, if you want to call them that, in any department of government. Their salaries start at $2,500 a year and I believe $50 a month is taken off for board, clothes and other things. These men do not put in an 8-hour day and a 5-day week, I might point out, and I know this of my own knowledge.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend permit me to interrupt just for a moment before
Supply-Justice
he commits himself as to any statement concerning what these men are paid? I suggest that the hon. member abstain from doing so because on page 3596 of Hansard for May 4, 1956 he will find that I recorded the whole pay list of the entire force and it is considerably better than the amount he suggested.

I realize that, but you did not take into account the $50 a month I referred to in the list you put in Hansard on May 4; you did not say anything about that. I am referring to take-home pay. Every labourer and employee is more concerned with take home pay than gross pay. You may give a man $5,000 a year but if you take off $2,000 the net remains $3,000. I believe the R.C.M.P. are underpaid from start to finish in every wage classification.
It is perhaps all right to underpay these men for the first two years during which they are in training because the course they undergo for the first two years is equivalent to the same number of years of university training. It certainly goes a long way toward making them better citizens and more capable policemen. These men did receive a slight raise at the time the rest of the civil service got a raise and I am not complaining about the salary they receive during the first two years of training, but after that period of time they should receive $4,000.
Because these men are of such a high calibre and because they are intelligent, capable, wholesome men they could command a salary of at least $4,000 in industry or elsewhere, and when one considers the long hours they put in and the dangers and hazards which accompany their position they should receive at least $4,000 a year the third year they are in the force.
As the hon. member for Restigouche-Mada-waska said, promotions in the force are very slow in coming. This is quite true and it has to be that way because there are only a certain number of officers in the force. I suggest the pay for these men should increase not only year by year, as it presently does, but that during the third year they are in the force their salary should jump to at least $4,000.
I can understand why young men join the force; they see the red serge and the colourful uniforms and they have read about the tradition and heroism of the force; but after the third or fourth year of service the glamour begins to fade unless there is a little increase in pay.
Perhaps the top officials in the force, whoever they are, may be receiving enough money but the young men who after two years of

Supply-Justice
training must work tor $2,600, $2,700 or $3,000 a year are not going to be content to stay in the force on the basis of the glamour and glory of serving with it.
I think the minister will agree that a number of young men are leaving the force. The minister is shaking his head but I can tell him that I know some who have left and I believe more will be leaving unless some improvement is made in the salary for service after two or three years. I think the government should take this into consideration and pay these men according to their worth and capacity.
These men do not put in an 8-hour day or a 5-day week. I know policemen who serve anywhere from 15 to 20 hours a day, day in and day out, for long periods at a time. People in the armed services are required to put in only a 5-day week and I see them hitchhiking home on Friday nights. Policemen seldom have a Sunday off and they never go to bed at night without hanging their uniforms on a chair within reach in order that they can jump into them quickly. These men are on call 24 hours a day 365 days a year except for a brief holiday period and it must be remembered that they have no say as to when they wish to take their holidays. Many of them probably have to take their holidays in the fall or winter. If the government intends to pay these men what they are worth in the third year of their service they should receive not less than $4,000 a year. I urge the government to take this matter into consideration immediately.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be very brief. I heartily support the remarks made by the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra and the hon. member for Kootenay West with regard to the issuance of revolver permits to prospectors. These hardy, courageous pioneers of Canada should not be denied personal protection on their hazardous journeys through the wilderness in the northern reaches of this country. I know that the prospectors of the Yukon have encountered the same difficulties in obtaining permits as those related by the hon. member to whom I have just referred as well as those who serve the British Columbia and Yukon chamber of mines. The prospectors are the backbone of our northern areas and should be assisted to the fullest extent possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at this point I think perhaps I might very briefly tell the house the result of my telephone call to Mr. Bonner, the attorney general of British Columbia, at the noon hour which was suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. I was not able to get Mr. Bonner because he is out of town, but I did get his

deputy and he confirms the fact that there is no doubt at all that this is a matter of provincial government policy. I have here a circular which we sent out to our own people which reads:
Whether or not permits should be granted to prospectors and geologists as suggested in the communication forwarded by the chamber of mines for British Columbia and the Yukon, is a matter which we feel should be decided by the issuing officer, bearing in mind the policy which the attorney general wishes followed.
That is the attorney general of the province. Then I may say that from time to time, as I am sure the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra who is a lawyer is aware, the commissioners on uniformity of criminal law administration meet and if there is any embarrassment in the present law in relation to the policy followed in British Columbia I have told the British Columbia authorities that we would be most happy to co-operate in any amendment that the uniformity commissioners might agree upon.
While I am on my feet I should like to clear up one or two points. I am sure the hon. member for Bestigouche-Madawaska will not think it an intentional discourtesy if I do not deal with his remarks upon the subject of marriage by members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The fact of the matter is that I dealt with this at length during the debate on my estimates on May 4 and there is no purpose in my going over the same ground today.
I should also like to point out that I must take strong issue with some of his other remarks. It is not true that there is a large turnover in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. That statement which he made is quite spectacular but it is not correct. The fact of the matter is, and this should be borne in mind by those members who sometimes throw out the suggestion that there is a large turnover in the force, that while the figure of wastage varies over the past five years it has fluctuated between 5J per cent per annum and 8 per cent per annum. That is one of the lowest wastage rates, if not the lowest, in the entire civil service.
Another thing which should be said, although I am sure it is not necessary in this chamber, is that the information prompted by the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska that the traditions which the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have retained, I think with the approval of all of us, in relation to their musical ride, their uniform, their conduct, their smartness and the like, should not apply also to old-fashioned methods of crime detection. His statement to this effect is completely without foundation. I have been through the crime

detection laboratory of the mounted police and I cannot imagine anything that would be a greater discouragement to an intending criminal than to see from it what small chance he has of escaping detection. The methods used there are as up to date as those used by any police force in the world. I think it is rather regrettable that the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska should suggest otherwise.

The minister did not indicate what report he had from Superintendent Bordeleau in Victoria. Also, what about the Yukon? The hon. member for the Yukon has said that this same policy is being followed by the mounted police in the Yukon and certainly the attorney general of British Columbia cannot be blamed for that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is quite true. As far as the Yukon is concerned, the point made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra is quite correct. I am the responsible minister there. I have not had any cases such as those raised by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, any specific concrete cases, but if there are any I would be glad to examine them when they are brought to my attention.
I should like to quote from a letter from J. R. W. Bordeleau, superintendent, officer in charge, Victoria, dated June 7, 1956, addressed to the commissioner, Royal Canadian Mounted Police in Ottawa. It reads:
Consequently, at the beginning of this year the policy formulated here, which was received with agreement by the deputy attorney general, was to the effect that an effort should be made towards limiting these permits to those cases which fell strictly within the exemptions provided by statute and as a consequence the recipients were greatly reduced in numbers.
There is no question as to what the policy is.

Who was present at the formulation of this policy? The letter refers to a meeting at which the policy was formulated and I should like to know who was present. It says that the deputy attorney general approved the policy, but who actually formulated it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am afraid I could not tell my hon. friend. He is a resident of British Columbia and perhaps he can say with greater certainty as to how the British Columbia government formulates its policy. I presume it might be the cabinet on the recommendation of the attorney general, or it might have been a purely intra-departmental policy, that is formulated within the department of the attorney general and not necessarily commanding the attention of other members of the government.
Supply-Justice

That letter reads as though some police officers, which of course would be mounted police officers, formulated this policy and then the deputy attorney general approved of it. If that is the case and if the minister thinks that this policy is wrong in so far as the Yukon is concerned, then I suggest that he see that a change is made in respect to the Yukon. I am sure there would not be the slightest doubt that the British Columbia government would be glad to follow suit because this letter admits that there has been a definite change in policy this year and that there has been a limitation in the issuance of these permits to carry revolvers. I do not think it can be argued that that policy is not unfair to prospectors, engineers and geologists. In fact, the minister has admitted that in so far as the Yukon is concerned. I would hope that he will do whatever he can to see that this whole situation is remedied quickly and at least throw his weight behind a movement to restore the issuing of permits to the position in which it has been for the last 25 years. How does the minister interpret these provisions:
A permit in form 42 shall be issued only where the person who issues is satisfied that the applicant for the permit requires the firearm to which It relates
(a)	to protect his life or property,
(b)	for use in connection with his profession or occupation.
What is the minister's opinion with regard to the right of a prospector or engineer or geologist to get a permit under that section?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think I could reproduce language that would be more clear than the wording of that statute which my hon. friend has just read as an abstract proposition for general application; but the problem arises when an application comes in from Mr. John Jones, who is a prospector in British Columbia or the Yukon. He says he wants a revolver permit. The facts are examined and a decision reached as to whether he has brought himself within the meaning of this section. If he has he is granted a permit, if he has not he does not get it. I do not think I can add anything. In view of this apparent misunderstanding, could the minister outline briefly what areas of police activity fall within the responsibility of the attorney general of the province and what areas remain under federal jurisdiction in a situation such as in British Columbia where there is contract with respect to the services of the R.C.M.P.?

speechtext: Does my hon. friend mean in general or in relation to this particular matter?
Not necessarily in relation to this particular matter. There must be some general areas under the agreements where the responsibility is in federal hands.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police are a federal force. Their responsibilities are to administer those statutes which are peculiarly federal in character such as the narcotics act, the Customs Act, antismuggling activities, the Excise Act and the other federal taxation statutes. As I indicated this morning, so far as the general body of the criminal law is concerned, while its enactment is within the jurisdiction of this parliament, its enforcement comes entirely under the heading of the administration of justice and enforcement of the law which are exclusively the responsibility of the provincial government. In those provinces such as Ontario and Quebec where they have provincial forces of their own you will find that it is that provincial force that enforces the general body of the criminal law, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police deal only with customs irregularities, antinarcotic work and things of that sort.
We have entered into an arrangement for reasons of economy in eight of the provinces of Canada under which the enforcement of the law, the administration of justice, all the police work necessary in those two connections, are handed over to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police under a police agreement. In consideration of the federal government thus making the services of the R.C.M.P. available for provincial administration of the law these provinces pay us

each year a large sum of money. In that way we have just one police force that serves all of the provincial purposes and the federal purposes in that one province at a great saving to the taxpayer.
But in order to have that work properly and effectively done it is of the utmost importance that we in the Department of Justice should not take advantage of the fact that our police force is working under the direction of the provincial attorney general to interfere in any way with the direction which he has over them which is analogous to that which he would have over his own police force if it were still in existence. He should have the same control over the mounted police in respect of all his sphere of responsibility as he would have if British Columbia still had a provincial police force.

I am interested in having this point cleared up because I should like to have a clear understanding with regard to certain incidents that have occurred in the province of British Columbia. Stories have appeared in the British Columbia press to the effect that the attorney general of that province has had Inspector Butler, I believe, of the criminal investigation branch carrying out certain investigations into the activities of a former minister of the British Columbia government. Is that something that the attorney general of British Columbia could properly assign such an inspector to do?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Under the police agreement the attorney general of British Columbia can properly direct any member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to do anything that he could direct the analogous provincial officer to do if British Columbia had its own force. I do not know enough about the particular case to which my hon. friend is referring to say whether it falls into that category. But I would assume that it did. Otherwise the police officer would not take on the task. In general, my hon. friend can clear up any doubt he has in his mind if he will put himself in the position of the provincial attorney general. If he were the attorney general, would he under such a contract continue under the responsibility to the people of that province to see that the law was properly enforced unless he had the same kind of control over the Royal Canadian Mounted Police under the police agreement that he would have had if he had continued with a provincial police force?

I can understand the minister's point in that connection quite readily. I simply wanted to be clear about the matter. From what the minister has said I understand that if an inspector of the R.C.M.P.

were to be requested to do something by the attorney general of a province which was not covered by the terms of the agreement the inspector would be in a situation where he could refer the matter to R.C.M.P. headquarters to determine whether or not it was a proper assignment. Is my inference in that connection correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would prefer to have my own language be considered in this connection. I am not suggesting that what my hon. friend says is incorrect. Even though there may be the odd occasion when it is embarrassing, I prefer to stand by my own language.
It is a delicate situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Under the terms of the police agreement, in consideration of the annual payment which we receive we undertake to defray all of the expenses that the police incur in connection with the legitimate work which they do under the terms of the agreement for the provincial government, and in that event we would pay that cost.

That is to say, the province pays the federal government so much a year by contract for the use of the R.C.M.P. The federal department is obliged to pay the expenses and salaries of the R.C.M.P. Perhaps the minister could place on record a statement showing where we stand with regard to these eight provinces. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I wonder whether my hon.
friend from Dauphin understands-and if he does not, it is my fault for not having explained it previously-the nature of the police contract. In essence, it is this. Let us take as an example the province of Manitoba with which he is familiar. You start out with two police forces in that province, namely the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the provincial police force. They say, "What is the sense of having two police forces here? Can we not enter into an agreement which would be economical for both of us and just have the one?" So in the case of Manitoba the provincial police force was disbanded and Manitoba entered into a contract for the services of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. After that contract is entered into we have paid to us by Manitoba roughly 40 per cent of our entire costs. We have to increase our staff to some extent in order to take care of both these tasks, although not to the extent that one might think because in many places the one force can do the job just as well as two forces could do it, without any increase in staff at all.
My hon. friend asked about debit and credit. The fact of the matter is that both governments are saving money, the province by paying a smaller amount of money to us

than they would have to pay in order to maintain its own police force and we, by virtue of the fact that we get this substantial subsidy from the province in order to continue maintaining a police force that we would have to maintain in any event.

As 1 understand it, there is no cost accounting kept to find out whether this arrangement is actually costing the federal government any money or not. It is simply assumed that about 40 per cent of the work will be done for the purposes of the provincial government and in that way you charge approximately 40 per cent of the costs to the province. Is that the arrangement? There is no cost accounting kept as to what it actually costs the federal department to administer the provincial law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think we have a record of the money that we have spent or, if we do not have it, we can secure it by taking it off the books if we set some clerks to work to the end of finding out, for example, police costs in the province of Manitoba over a period of a year. But there is no cost accounting set up with a view to debiting one concern or the other. The whole theory is that if you have two forces, and if you abolish one and have the remaining force do the work of two, it is a very good arrangement for a province to pay 40 per cent and it is a very good arrangement for us to get 40 per cent and to carry on in the way we had been doing previously.

Mr. Chairman, when we received the Fauteux report and the report of the joint committee, and shall in due course receive the two McRuer reports, we shall first of all have to consider carefully in the Department of Justice what the implementation of the recommendations of those various reports may cost in order that I may submit my report to my colleagues with a view to getting approval of that cost. And then, as I have already indicated, having regard to the fact that all of these matters have to be administered by the provinces, we shall have to get together with them and confer as to what should be and what should not be implemented. It will not be until all these things have been done that we shall have a policy in relation to which there could be

any item reflected in these present estimates. Therefore, the $22,000 has nothing to do with any changes.

I just want to say a few words on this item. Of course, most members of the house who have anything to do with the remission services know that they are doing a very good job with the equipment they have; but at this time what I am concerned about is not the fellow who is appealing to get out, but the position of the man who has done any time in any of our penitentiaries. I am concerned with the position he is in when he gets out. There is $30,000 earmarked for recognized prisoners' aid societies. I do not know what work they are doing. I know the John Howard organization is attempting to do something all the time. During the session of the house one runs into and receives letters from men who have served short sentences. The thing that strikes me is the fact that a man who does a year in a prison is treated in about the same way as a man who does 15 years when it comes to the matter of employment, once the stigma of a penitentiary term is hung on him. During this session three people who did a short term and were rooted out of jobs have written to me. One of them lost three jobs, when it was learned that he had served a short term in the penitentiary. The one who had lost three jobs had a position when he wrote to me, and he said to me he wondered what was going to happen next. He said, "As far as I am concerned, if I am thrown out of this job there is not anything left for me to do but to go back to the penitentiary". I believe it is that attitude on the part of employers particularly that causes so many of our repeaters to go back to the penitentiaries.
I think the magistrates have quite a responsibility. I do not think many of them realize, when they hand out a sentence of a year or 18 months to a kid who has taken a motor car for a joy ride, that they are sentencing that boy not to a year or 18 months but to life, because when the 18 months are over the theory is that the prisoner has paid his penalty to society and has washed the slate clean. But that is not so. The record follows the individual from job to job and, like the people who wrote to me during this session, they lose one job after another. One chap lost three jobs despite the fact he was doing his work satisfactorily, and he was waiting to lose the next one. The magistrates have to think of the future.
If a man commits a serious crime he has to be punished for it, but there are a whole lot of youngsters in this country, and it is going on from day to day, who commit

slight misdemeanours. Take the boy who takes a car. The magistrate thinks he is sentencing him to a year, but the boy is debarred from holding public office for the rest of his life. If he wants to go to the United States or to any other country he is classed as a convict and is not allowed to enter. His record follows him from job to job.
In addition to the matter of remission, there should be greater concern on the part of the public and on the part of those administering justice for the man who comes back and tries to rehabilitate himself. Despite the work of those recognized prisoners' aid societies, they are only touching the fringes. They aid those who happen to get into their hands, but by and large the men who try to help themselves run into these difficulties. Mind you, it is not only the employment agencies but also some of the employment offices.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Public opinion.

Exactly. It is because of lack of education. It seems that everyone sits back and acquiesces in this kind of thing. It is time that someone in this country started to educate the public that the theory is intended to work in practice, and that when a sentence is served the stigma is not supposed to follow the individual for the rest of his life. If you are trying to do a good job in rehabilitating, then these men should be helped rather than pushed into the discard and back to the penitentiary. I have seen this happen, since the war particularly. It was not very noticeable prior to 1946 and 1947. Since 1947 I have noticed a stronger trend in that direction than I have ever seen before in this country.
If more money is needed for these voluntary societies, that is fine; but I believe there should be some agency of the Department of Justice whose responsibility it would be to try to educate the public into giving the man who wants to rehabilitate himself a break.
Secondly, I believe that magistrates should be cautioned against hanging a life sentence onto a boy whom they think they are sentencing to only a year, because it is a life sentence. I know of the case of a boy who got into difficulty, and all hon. members could name case after case, where other corrective measures could have been taken. I just wanted to say that, sir, because I think it is becoming a very serious problem in this country.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I had it marked down as something I had

intended to discuss but the hon. member may have dealt with it better than I could have done.
In addition to what the hon. member has said, I should like to say to the minister that in the next year, after he has received those reports and is negotiating with the provincial attorneys general on this matter of administration, I should like to see more done in the field of probation before conviction. In many of these cases I believe the place to start is at the beginning. As the hon. member for Cape Breton South said, once a chap is convicted and sentenced and goes into a jail or a prison he really goes to a school of crime in a good many instances. I am sorry to have to say that. I believe the province is responsible for setting up probation service. After negotiations I should like to see the law changed considerably to see whether a new system cannot be devised so that these young people who get into trouble can be treated in some way so that a sentence would be the last resort.
While I am on my feet there is one other matter I would like to bring up. After reading the report I concluded that it contains many good recommendations and there is one I cannot resist speaking about because I have always felt that poverty should not be a cause of imprisonment.
Under our present law there are many cases where a man goes into court and is fined for a breach of criminal responsibility and if he cannot pay his fine he is sentenced to jail for a certain period of time. I do not think that is good law. In the first place it really spells out the fact that poverty may be a cause for being put in jail and I do not think Canadian law in this modern age should carry such an implication.
I have one other matter with which I would like to deal. In my own experience I have seen men sent to jail for some small crime. Perhaps he has committed several small crimes, none of them too serious. Sometimes when these men come out the sheriff or a police officer has a collection of warrants and the minute the men are released from prison they are arrested again and confronted with another charge and a further sentence.
I would like to recommend to the minister, through you, sir, that he take steps to see if our law can be changed. It seems to me in the cases I am thinking about a man should come out with a clean sheet and should not have to face at the door the sheriff or a police officer who has a warrant to arrest him. I think the provinces recommended setting up provincial prison reformatories and this may take care of some of the cases of this type such as we have had in the past.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make just one suggestion to the minister following what the hon. member for Cape Breton South has already said, with which I agree, and it concerns the method of check-up employed by the police.
I believe the present system is wrong. I know of one or two cases where the police have gone to check on a man who had been in prison and served his sentence and presumably paid his debt to society.
In one case the police went into the establishment where the man was working and in front of his employer they proceeded to check on the man and also discussed him with his employer. That being the first occasion on which the owner became aware of the fact that he had an ex-prisoner in his employ, the employee lost his job immediately.
He moved to another town and took another job. He had not been there for more than a few weeks and was doing very well. The owner of the establishment where the man was working liked him but here again, lo and behold, in came the police to check up on the man and exactly the same thing happened. This went on for a long time and the young man became almost desperate. Finally he wrote to one or two hon. members of this house.
I think instructions should be given to the police that at no time must they interview ex-prisoners in the presence of their employers or while they are working. This should be done after working hours or at the home of the men or by appointment. The present system works a hardship on these fellows who have paid their penalty to society and I believe the present system should be changed.

I had not intended to make any further remarks during the discussion of the estimates of this department but in view of the remarks made by some hon. members of the house and particularly those made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South it occurred to me that while I thoroughly sympathize with the views they expressed it would be unfortunate if a misapprehension were left amongst hon. members of this house generally.
The impression which I think could be left by these remarks is that first offenders are generally severely punished and chastized and receive prison sentences.
This may take place on some occasions but I have had some experience with the actual enforcement of criminal law in the past and I should think the hon. member for Cape Breton South would be very pleased to know that in cases of a first offence, particularly when young men are involved, the matter of

sentence is usually thoroughly discussed between the crown attorney and the police and the type of charge that is to be laid is given careful thought.
I do not know what takes place in other provinces but I know that is the way these matters are handled in Ontario. When the magistrate is about to pronounce sentence in practice he often consults the crown attorney, and I think properly so. In Ontario we have probation officers who before the sentence is handed out make an inquiry into the offender's background in order to ascertain what kind of home and family life he has had. Before passing out the sentence the magistrate refers to the report of the probation officer.
I thought these facts would be of interest to the hon. member for Cape Breton South and I felt it would be unfortunate if the impression were left in this house that it was the general practice in Canada to sentence first offenders to prison, because this is not so. As I say, I do not know what goes on in Nova Scotia or New Brunswick or some of the other provinces.
It is done in some cases in Ontario, too.

However, I have related the facts as they obtain in Ontario and probably in some other provinces. Concerning joyriding charges, as the hon. member for Cape Breton South knows, two types of charges can be laid. One is a charge that bears a mandatory minimum sentence of one year and there is also a lesser charge and it depends entirely on the circumstances in actual practice which charge is laid.
It is not the desire of any law enforcement officer to send people to jail for a first offence and, as I say, reports from probation officers are received before sentence is pronounced by the magistrate. The crown attorney is usually consulted as to the background of the offender. I think most magistrates-certainly those with whom I have been in contact in Ontario-carefully consider the circumstances before sending people to jail. As a matter of fact, in our part of the country the magistrates are usually criticized for not being severe enough. I think magistrates in general should not be criticized for that because I believe they do their best to try to keep people out of the schools of crime.

Mr. Chairman, after that lecture I feel obliged to say something. The question I would like to ask is this. What are we going to do with the fellow once he gets out?
The hon. member spoke of his personal experience in courts but it must be remembered that when he appears in court it is 67509-477
Supply-Justice
on behalf of a client and the client is protected by him. I was thinking of young men who do not have legal advice.
They are better off.

I am going to cite a case that took place in the hon. member's own province. This took place back in 1945. I was wired from a town in Ontario. Two kids had been picked up on this joyriding business the hon. member for Oxford referred to. These young men were tried, convicted and sentenced in about 20 minutes without counsel. When they got in touch with me they had already been sentenced to a year in Guelph reformatory. The hon. member for Oxford does not see that kind of occurrence because when he is in court he is representing someone and they are protected, but there are many cases in the magistrates courts across this country where sentences are doled out pretty quickly and are grossly unjust.
I am not going to argue with the hon. member for Oxford because I think the way to start preventing the process of making a convict out of a kid who walks into that kind of situation, as any of us could have done between 16 and 18 years of age, is by protecting him from becoming a repeater as the years go by.

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry to prolong this discussion further but another minute or two is surely not going to make that much difference. I am sorry that the hon. member for Cape Breton South appears to have misunderstood my intentions. I was not quarreling with the hon. member; in fact, I am very sympathetic toward his views. I was just attempting to point out to him that in certain parts of Canada justice is not as harsh as he may think.
Back in 1945 in Ontario I do not know what went on there because there was another administration just prior to that and I do not wish to go into that subject. While I have represented clients in court I have had the job in the past for some little time of acting as crown attorney. The probation officer system has been brought in in Ontario in the last few years, as the Minister of Justice knows. More than that, I think I can safely say that the policy of the administration of justice in Ontario at the present time, and I expect in other provinces as well, is that no magistrate would convict anyone of any serious offence without that person being represented by counsel. The various bar associations in Ontario, and I believe throughout the country, have members who are ready to represent people who have not counsel

Supply-Justice
when it is felt that they should be represented. I certainly know that in our own area a magistrate would not hear a case unless the person was represented by counsel. That possibly applies in other parts of Canada, although it may not, but that is the way it is in Ontario.

I wonder if the minister can bring us up to date on the Clifford Williams case, which he will recall was discussed earlier this session. I have had some correspondence on this matter representing quite a body of people in my district which raises three questions. First, why has no appeal been launched? Second, what sentences did Williams' accomplices get? Third, why is there such a disparity in sentences meted out in Canadian criminal courts?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am speaking from memory, but as I recall Clifford Williams was brought up on a number of charges of armed robbery when there was a rather severe epidemic of armed robberies in the district in which he was operating. It was suggested that he had used a toy pistol but there was evidence that members of the group with which he was associated had loaded revolvers with which this series of robberies were committed and that on one occasion one of his accomplices or associates had pistol-whipped a victim with his loaded revolver.
The magistrate sentenced Williams on a number of separate charges. The penalty for each case was not in itself so much, but instead of having the sentences run concurrently, which is sometimes the practice, the magistrate had these sentences run consecutively with the result that they added up to 28 years. That would have been an extremely severe penalty for any one of the offences, or for all of them put together for that matter.
It is true that in the remission branch of the Department of Justice we have a general rule that we do not release a prisoner until he has served half of his sentence. One of the main reasons for that is that in our view, and I think it is in accord with modern ideas of penology, one of the things which retard the rehabilitation of a prisoner is to have no hope. If he has some definite period like half of his sentence to which he can work to he has some incentive to try to rehabilitate himself while in prison and also if he is going to take any courses of education it indicates the period of time which he has in which to take them.
It does not follow from that that there are not cases in which the application of that rule would create hardship; and in Mr. Williams' case, as I have said on previous occasions and repeat now, it will be a question of his

rehabilitation as a person rather than the total of the consecutive sentences which will determine the date upon which we can release him.

I should like to recommend to the minister that along with the remission service the federal government should also operate a rehabilitation service. It is one of the cruellest things a person can witness to see a prisoner come out of jail without sympathetic assistance to help him along the road during the first few hard months. This rehabilitation service could work along with the provinces and prompt those provinces where they are not doing anything at the present time to put into effect a system whereby the prisoner would be followed from the moment a charge is laid until he is rehabilitated after his sentence has been served, either in whole or in part.
Another thing I might mention. In this day and age it is my opinion that the big chain stores like Eaton's, Simpsons and others go out of their way to encourage people to buy on credit. They offer every inducement to people to go into debt. In a good many cases there are people who do not know how to control their own finances; people who are not too well educated can easily get over their heads in debt. They may be ignorant of the processes of law and therefore land in jail in many cases because they have gone into debt. They do not know what it is all about and they hate to go to a lawyer. They just do not answer a summons.
It is a pleasure for me to associate myself with the four or five hon. members who have spoken in this connection. I hope the minister will be prompt in giving this matter every consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I should like to say just one word, otherwise a wrong impression might be left. In the administration of the ticket of leave act we provide after-care supervision for 70 per cent of all parolees in the Dominion of Canada. When one stops to think of the large number of these people who go into small villages and communities where it is impossible to provide after-care, he will appreciate how large that percentage is. Within six years the percentage has risen from 15 per cent to 70 per cent. I am not suggesting that my hon. friend's idea is not a good one, but I do say that as far as the federal government is concerned we have already gone a long way toward that end. The purpose of our present effort is to bring these matters to public notice throughout the whole Dominion of Canada.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.

Yukon territorial court-
171. Administration, including administration of justice-Yukon Territory, $79,020.

Mr. Chairman, on this item 171 I wish to bring very forcibly to the attention of the Minister of Justice, and through him to the attention of the government, a serious situation recently created in the Yukon Territory-a situation that cries out for correction at once and for a return to basic principles of justice and fair play. I refer to the directive issued by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources dated July 23 last. It is a directive in terms applying to all federal government employees as well as all members of the armed forces of Canada. It prohibits any such persons from acquiring any interest in territorial lands except for housing purposes, under the terms of the Yukon Quartz Mining Act, Yukon Placer Mining Act and the Territorial Lands Act.
To fully appreciate the intent and effect of this directive it is only necessary to point out that under the Territorial Lands Act the word "land" includes mines, minerals, easements, servitudes and all other interests in real property.
I cannot speak out too strongly, Mr. Chairman, against this outrageously undemocratic directive. It is entirely without precedent and will result in the creation of two distinct classes of citizenship in this country, namely, a class with no unusual restrictions on its activities, and another class of citizens ruthlessly deprived of rights and freedom of choice that ought to be a normal part of their Canadian citizenship.
There may be some justification on ethical grounds for the issuance of such an order covering a very small group of civil servants whose particular work might give them preferred access to information on mining claims. But, in my opinion, it is a travesty of justice to make the directive apply to all government civil servants and to all members of the armed forces.
I have just returned recently from a visit to the Yukon and I found feeling in the territory against this arbitrary action to be running high. It is widely regarded as applying discrimination of the very worst kind. The civil service federation of Canada, White-horse-Yukon council, as well as the Whitehorse branch, Yukon No. 2, of the Canadian Legion, are already on record strongly protesting this violation of basic democratic rights. I want to urge upon the Minister of Justice with all the emphasis at my command that he take up this matter with his colleagues of the cabinet and have this unwise, 67509-477J
Supply-Justice
unsavory and undemocratic directive rescinded without delay.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Combines Investigation Act-
173. Restrictive trade practices commission, $82,330.
I asked the minister this morning about the investigation in connection with the brewery case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In that case, Mr. Chairman, the report was received some considerable time ago, over a year as a matter of fact. My hon. friend has probably read the report of the restrictive trade practices commission. It was noteworthy for the fact that they said in one of the paragraphs that an attempt had been made to bring the industry under control and in another paragraph that it was not actually under control. Therefore, without any question, it does pose quite a substantially difficult point.
We were unfortunate in that the counsel to whom we sent this matter for an opinion was taken very seriously ill, had to undergo an operation and had to go to the south to recuperate. However, on August 1 we had an opinion from him, and since that time, with the house sitting as it has, I have not had any chance to give it the careful study that we would have to give it in order to reach an opinion of our own. However, it will be considered at the earliest opportunity.

Mr. Chairman, this is far from being the most popular item to say anything about and I rather gather that if you do say anything you are reputed right away to be a friend of big business. However, it seems to me that the commission is affecting the ordinary businessman more and more and it might be wise for a few words to be said on this item. Under section 19 of the amending act of 1952 it would appear to the ordinary reader that the terms of reference of the restrictive trade practices commission were to appraise the effect on the public interest of arrangements and practices disclosed in the evidence.
We are having volumes of reports, and it would appear that we have reached the stage where, as far as the commission is concerned, their conclusions deal simply with the question whether there has been a fixation of price and their findings have not gone any further to determine whether in fact the fixation of price is or is not in the public interest. I am reminded to a certain extent of my practice before the air transport board where the term "public interest" is used quite extensively. In the normal course there it is not simply a case of whether additional

Supply-Justice
companies are to be allowed into the field because there is a certain demand for the service. In the ordinary course the board goes beyond that to determine whether it might not be possible that the additional companies coming into the field might go bankrupt and whether this might have a detrimental result for the whole country.
Finally, I should like to say that in the United Kingdom the monopolies and restrictive practices commission in their investigations go beyond what has been the case here in Canada. They go beyond a mere finding that there has been a lessening of competition in order to determine whether on balance the public have been harmed, unaffected or have benefited by the specific lessening of competition which has been shown. I should like to point out to the minister that more and more we are hearing people say that this failure to take the next step in an investigation is having a very detrimental effect in many cases. Though we have started out in the right direction, it may be that the net result will be bad. It will do the public little good if we have a situation where, although we can say that there have been conversations and the fixing of prices it results in numerous small business people being put out of business. I suggest that the minister keep a very close watch on this particular aspect of the work of the commission so that if we go across the line where the public interest is not assisted we may consider making some amendments in the future.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
174. Office of investigation and research, $441,993.

I should like to raise some questions under this item with regard to the investigation that has been going on in British Columbia into the united fishermen and allied workers' union. The matter has been raised in the house on previous occasions by questions but I feel that the time has come when the minister should be prepared to make some statement as to the situation. I am not going to make a speech. I think the minister knows that I view with serious misgivings the activities that have been carried on in connection with this union. There are two questions I should like to put to the minister and I hope he will comment upon both of them. First of all, in view of section 4 of the act, which was designed to protect the trade union movement generally, why is this investigation being carried on? Second, if a combine did exist it is my understanding that it is something that has resulted from certain general activities, and I should like to know why the investigation was not inclusive not only of

the one party to the agreement but also of the other party. In other words, how could such an investigation be launched into the union and not into the fishing companies who were parties to the agreements that have existed in British Columbia arising out of the bargaining that has gone on between those parties?
There is one other matter I should like to have clarified. I should like to know the situation with respect to the application for an injunction against the investigation launched by the union. I have a report here which appeared in The Fisherman, the union publication, the issue of July 3 last, in which it is said:
It will be at least a month before the application of the united fishermen and allied workers' union for an injunction to halt federal investigators from searching and seizing union records will come before the courts.
The question that arises in my mind is, first of all, what has happened just recently in respect of that matter. The second question is this. When an application of that kind is before the courts, on which a decision makes for delay, does the investigation proceed as if that application for injunction had not been made? If that is the case it would appear-and according to the report here the moves for delay have been made by the crown -that in effect the delay could be construed as an effort to ensure that the investigation was going to be all completed before the application was heard. I think there are several points there which the minister could probably clear up while we are having discussion of this item.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in one way I am glad my hon. friend has raised this matter, because I have received a large number of letters from labour officials in various parts of Canada which indicate that they have an inadequate and incorrect impression of what were the facts involved. By correspondence I was glad to clear up the misunderstanding in their minds; but this present question will give me an opportunity to put the explanation on the record where it can be seen by everyone concerned.
In this particular matter, in May, 1956, as the result of a formal application received in November, 1955, the director under the Combines Investigation Act commenced an inquiry into the production, purchase and sale of fish and related products in the province of British Columbia. The application alleged, in effect, that the members of the united fishermen and allied workers' union were combining to fix and enhance the price of fish sold by them to the canners and to interfere with the activities of other fishermen

in a manner that amounted to a restraint of trade to the detriment of the public.
In relation to the question of a formal application, I think I should say that there are three ways in which proceedings can be commenced under the act. One is on a direction by the minister to the director, which we very seldom have to use. Another is on the initiative of the director himself. Then in those cases where a group of Canadian citizens feel that the department perhaps is not diligent enough in the enforcement of the act, six Canadian citizens may make a formal application requesting that the matter be investigated. That privilege is rarely used, but it was used in this particular case.
When we receive this application the act provides that the director-and I now quote from the act-
. . . shall . . . cause an inquiry to be made into all such matters as he considers necessary to inquire into with the view of determining the facts.
Once an inquiry has been commenced, it continues until-
. . . the director is of the opinion that the matter being inquired into does not justify further inquiry . . .
-or until it culminates in a written report from the restrictive trade practices commission to the minister.
The director, having come to the conclusion that the application raised an issue to be inquired into, sent representatives to examine the files of various associations of fishermen, including the union, an association of boat owners and an association of packers. That is the other party, I suppose, that my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni has in mind in this matter. As the result of information obtained upon some of these premises, the director subsequently obtained authority from the commission to examine the files of the packing companies. That is what my hon. friend has in mind, is it not?

Yes. One of the questions that has been raised, as the minister probably knows, is as to why the two aspects of this investigation were not launched simultaneously. I have heard it alleged that it was only as the result of an afterthought that the fishing companies were investigated.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No. I do not suggest that
there was an afterthought. As a matter of fact, if an illegal agreement existed it would exist in relation to all these people. They are the alleged parties to an alleged agreement. Section 4 of the Combines Investigation Act, the one in question, provides as follows:
Supply-Justice
Nothing in this act shall be construed to apply to combinations of workmen or employees for their own reasonable protection as such workmen or employees.
Obviously, Mr. Chairman, there can be no abridgement by the combines branch or anyone else of the protection conferred by section 4 upon trade unions, and I do not think any person would wish to abridge this protection. If the activities in question are found to come within section 4, then that is obviously an end of the matter. The director took the view that in order to obtain the facts upon which to form an opinion as to whether or not section 4 did apply, he would have to see the files of the organizations I have mentioned. The purpose of any steps that have been taken to date, therefore, has been simply to ascertain the facts in the manner which the act provides.
Should the director, upon gathering the facts, be of the opinion that section 4 does not apply, that of course does not settle the matter. What happens in such a case is that if the director believes there is a contravention of the anti-combines legislation, he prepares a statement of evidence and presents it to the restrictive trade practices commission and to any parties against whom allegations are made in the statement. The commission, which is an independent body, then sets a time and place for argument, and at this stage any party against whom an allegation has been made has full opportunity to state his case and to show that section 4 does apply, or that the activities in question are in some other respect not within the application of the act. Even should the commission decide that section 4 does not apply, their conclusion is not binding because the only final authority on the subject is the court.
The union, a few days after the director commenced to examine its files, brought an action against the director in the supreme court of British Columbia, asking for a declaration that section 4 does apply to the activities into which the director is inquiring and asking for an injunction to restrain the inquiry. Some weeks ago the director undertook to hold the inquiry in abeyance, so far as the union is concerned, until the court had given judgment in these proceedings, provided they were not delayed and that proceedings should take place in a normal way.
While, as I have said, if the activities in question are covered by section 4 they are not subject to the Combines Investigation Act and that is an end of the matter, I would not, however, like to see any group take the stand that the director should not even *commence an inquiry into a situation where

Supply-Justice
a trade union was involved. Such an attitude would, in my view, greatly weaken the general public support which the act receives.
No such action has been taken by a union in the past. It was not taken, for example, in my own city of Winnipeg when the activities of a Winnipeg local of a Canadian union were inquired into in connection with the investigation into bread prices in Winnipeg several years ago. It goes without saying, of course, that when an inquiry has been started it is open to a union to show, either in the course of the inquiry itself or in the kind of proceedings that are now taking place in the court, that section 4 applies to the activities in question.
My own hope would be that organized labour in Canada, which has always been a strong supporter of the anti-combines legislation, would adopt the attitude that their files were always open to examination under the Combines Investigation Act, reserving, of course, the full right which they have to argue, when the facts have been made known, that any particular activities are within the embrace of section 4. If there are any activities that are being engaged in by trade unions today that are not within the embrace of section 4, then it seems to me that it is in everybody's interest, including the unions', to know that such is the case.
As to the manner of this inquiry, I understand that it was carried on in the same way as are practically all other inquiries under the Combines Investigation Act. The director under the act is responsible for commencing investigations. I can instruct him to commence an inquiry but I cannot instruct him to terminate one, nor can I tell him how to carry it on. That was the will of parliament, namely that the director should have a certain independence of action; and obviously if he is to carry out the purposes of the act he must be allowed a certain amount of discretion as to how to proceed. Should it appear that he is going about abusing that discretion, that, of course, is another matter which would involve the government in direct responsibility as to whether he were a proper official. There is, however, in my view nothing upon the record so far that would warrant the view that the powers of the director are being abused.

I am not going to comment or discuss this matter any further at this time. I want to thank the minister for having made a fairly complete statement on this, and I know it will be studied by the many trade union bodies.

Did the minister consider any other property before purchasing the Ben Franklin farm? Did they have any other property under consideration?

In these supplementary estimates the purchase of this Joyceville property is in two items. One is $48,097 and the other is $73,250. According to Hansard of June 27 the price paid for one property was $123,000. Why does that amount not appear on the supplementary estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A portion of that was paid out of an item in the main estimates.

The minister has informed us that they had other property in view in that immediate area. I know the area quiet well, and I wonder why they purchased this property of 427 acres. There are only about 175 acres of tillable land in the property, and they could have purchased property to the south or to the north with at least 80 per cent or 90 per cent tillable land. The balance of this property is only slash and swamp. Has the government made any offer for this other property, or how far have the negotiations proceeded in connection with this particular property?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, we have made an offer but so far it has not been accepted.
I should like to ask the minister what offer has been made.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In fairness to the taxpayers and the government I do not think I should reveal the offer. We are trying to drive a bargain. If we fail, having regard to the fact that this second piece of property to which my hon. friend is referring is contiguous to the main part of our property, we will have to get it. This would mean we would have to expropriate it, and the whole question of what it is worth would have to be decided by the courts. I do not think we should commit ourselves to any statement on its value, even in parliament.

It has been the considered opinion of many of the residents, not only of this particular district but throughout Kingston-the minister is well aware of it- that the object in building the penitentiary there is to relieve overcrowding in Portsmouth penitentiary and to bring out the shortterm prisoners, or what I should like to call the trusties, to this penitentiary. I also believe that the city is desirous of obtaining the penitentiary farm at Kingston to use the land for building purposes, for industry, and so on. The idea of this new penitentiary farm is to take the trusties to it.
As I said before, it is the considered opinion of many well-informed people in Frontenac and in Kingston that it would perhaps be much better if a penitentiary of this nature, which has a farming connection, were so placed that the trusties could not so easily escape. As we all know, not a year goes by without many men escaping and remaining at large for quite some time. It would have been better if the penitentiary had been built on one of the islands adjacent to Kingston. There are the islands of Amherst, Wolfe and Howe. Many of the farms on the islands contain from 90 per cent to 100 per cent

Supply-Justice
tillable land. It would be very much more awkward for the prisoners to escape from those islands than from a penitentiary on the mainland. I might say that many of the residents of that community know of these circumstances, and when it is mentioned to them they smile; some of them laugh out loud and others swear.
This particular piece of property, Mr. Chairman, has an assessed value-and I might say this assessed value is the new equalized assessment that was made by an experienced assessor within the last two years-of $20,125. For this property the department is paying $123,000. Perhaps $123,000 could have been tolerated had the property been expropriated, but I might inform the committee that the gentleman who owns this property is selling it in pieces and, according to the assessment, $123,000 is far in excess of the selling price of any other portion of the property.
As I said before, there are only 175 acres of tillable land. There are 250 acres of slash and swamp which is of no use whatsoever. Another portion of the land consisting of 205 acres of tillable land was sold at just about the same time for $25,000. Perhaps the buildings are not quite as good, but I should like to say to the committee that while there are exceptionally good buildings on the land that has been purchased by the department, still, as many hon. members here know, especially those whose constituencies are adjacent to Kingston, the Kingston penitentiary specializes in a dairy herd. They have an exceptionally large and good dairy herd, one of the best in Canada.
While the buildings on this particular place are exceptionally good, they are built for beef cattle and certainly are not buildings that are required for a dairy herd. They are not appropriate for the carrying on of that kind of dairy business. It will cost many hundreds, yes, thousands of dollars, to remodel the barns to take care of this dairy herd and the dairy equipment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If it will reassure my hon. friend, may I tell him that it is our plan to move our beef herd to these particular premises and our dairy herd out to the farm at Collin's Bay.

There is another point; the Canadian Bank of Commerce is one of the creditors of this estate to the extent of $200,000. I might say, Mr. Chairman, that the Hon. Mr. Campbell, who is a senator, is a very good friend of the owner of this particular farm; not only that, but Senator Campbell is a director of the Canadian Bank of Commerce. If the price paid for this farm had been in the same proportion as the price at which the department is trying

to purchase the adjacent farm there would not have been enough assets to satisfy the Canadian Bank of Commerce.
I might say here, Mr. Chairman, one other thing. I know about how much the department has offered for the Franklin farm. If $123,000 is not too much for the property they have purchased, the price offered for this other farm which belongs to Mrs. Franklin is not half enough. If the price offered Mrs. Franklin is enough for her farm, the price of the Ben Franklin farm is exorbitant.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, when one takes all these facts into consideration; when one knows there is other property, much better property, which could have been purchased for less money; and when one knows that Senator Campbell is a director of the Canadian Bank of Commerce and that the Canadian Bank of Commerce is a creditor of this particular estate, it seems rather suspicious that this deal should have been put across. I leave it at that, Mr. Chairman. I know what the people around Joyceville think. As I said before, they smile and laugh out loud; some of the creditors swear. I leave it to members of the House of Commons as to what they think. I am not a lawyer, just a common chap, but I know the situation. The other residents know it as well and, as I said before, it looks rather suspicious.

Mr. Chairman, since I represent the -constituency in which this land has been chosen for a new penitentiary I might say that I can truthfully speak on behalf of the residents of all of the constituency, the district of Kingston and the township of Pittsburgh. It is my considered opinion that they are most happy about it.
As far as moving to an island is concerned, since I have some experience of islands in that district, may I say it would be very unfair to ask the guards, or those in charge of administration, to live on an island and increase their cost and expenses because we might have to -consider, as we have done before in this house, an increase in salary for guards, which was granted by the minister's department and was highly appreciated by the guards. The guards have a very exacting job; therefore in this instance I think the penitentiary branch has shown very good judgment in having the penitentiary on the mainland. We should also think of available emergency services for both guards and convicts. When we had a riot a couple of years ago the armed forces were available to help, to step in and stop any riot which occurred and assist in the protection of the people of Canada as a whole.

I was rather surprised by the statement made by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, to the effect that the people in the district were very dissatisfied, though I am sure he said it in all earnestness.

Mr. Chairman, on a question of privilege, I did not say they were dissatisfied. I said they know the situation and they just smile. I did not say they were dissatisfied or anything of the kind; they just smile at the circumstances.

Perhaps I took the smile on the hon. member's face as being a little deceptive concerning the attitude.
I must say one of the best examples of public relations I have ever seen occurred two weeks ago in the township of Pittsburgh, when every member of the council including the clerk attended on the commissioner of penitentiaries and discussed future plans for the development of the penitentiary in that area. It was gratifying to know that the council took sufficient interest in township affairs and in the development of the township and the district surrounding the area where it is anticipated that the penitentiary would be constructed to go and see the commissioner of penitentiaries and discuss their common problems with him. It is my considered opinion this is an advantage both to the township and to the Department of Justice.
When we talk about trusties being allowed to work on farms, it may be that some residents feel concerned or alarmed about escapees from the penitentiary. I have lived close to penitentiaries during a great deal of my lifetime; I have had quite a bit to do with people who live in penitentiaries, and I believe common sense dictates that when anyone escapes from these institutions the established pattern is that they get as far away from the penitentiary as they possibly can, and they do so as quickly as they can. They do not stay around the district at all.
Right from the horse's mouth.

Across from Collin's Bay penitentiary there is one of the largest subdivisions in that district. Over 200 homes have been constructed in 14 months. This subdivision is situated, as I said, right across the road from the penitentiary, and the people who occupy these homes show no concern for escapees. This may be another case of an alarmist predicting that the people in the district would be concerned about this. I confess I have not heard any expression of concern about it. The only alarm I have encountered is that many people from Seely's Bay, which is in my hon. friend's riding,
Supply-Justice
have come to me asking if I could do something on their behalf to see if they could get a job in the penitentiary there.
Tell us about the land deal.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Kingston has just spoken about the council meeting that was called to formulate plans. I am quite certain that if the land had been purchased north or south in that municipality or in any other district within the municipality the council there would also have met to formulate plans, just as they did in this particular case.
Sit down.
We will say when we sit down, not you. Come out from behind the curtain.
Come on out and let us have a look at you.

The hon. member for Kingston and I have a certain amount in common. We were both born on farms and spent our early boyhood years there. The only difference between us is that I am a Conservative and he is a Liberal, and he has followed a more lucrative path than I have.
I wish to state here, Mr. Chairman, that I did not say the residents of the area are afraid of prisoners escaping. I was referring to the fact that prisoners may escape, and I mentioned the difficulty in apprehending them. However, I shall leave the matter at this point so the people in the house can draw their own conclusions.
Is the minister not going to say anything in connection with the price for this property? Would he tell us if this firm is the same firm that was involved in the other transaction?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: For the reasons I have already stated and with all deference to my hon. friend, I do not think it is desirable to ask that we, on the eve of what may be an action in the exchequer court to determine the value of the additional property we are attempting to secure, should have to commit ourselves to the submission of any of these valuations. I am quite prepared to defend this whole transaction expressly upon the point of value when this matter is completed, but until it is completed I do not think we should be asked to do it.

Mr. Chairman, about ten days ago I filed a motion for the production of papers. I was wondering if the minister could tell me when I could expect that request to be complied with.
