DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES Field services-
Protection branch-
140. Operation and maintenance, $3,288,650.

Mr. Chairman, when we last had the estimates of the Department of Fisheries under discussion on June 8, I was in the midst of addressing a question to the minister in respect to the retirement of patrolmen who are hired by the department on a seasonal basis. I had made some mention of a few reports I received of some of the earlier activities of the patrolmen before they were taken over by the department, and the minister questioned whether these activities were a recommendation for the job. I suggested that perhaps the experience they had might have prepared them to render more efficient service to the department.
The concern I have about this matter is that it has been represented to me in some cases at least that the compulsory retirement of some of these patrolmen at the age of 65 would have a bad effect upon the efficiency of the department because of the difficulty of replacing them with people with adequate experience. I was about to point out that my observation is that in many cases older fishermen who feel they no longer want to engage in full-time fishing activities are willing to enter into this work with the department.
I did ask a question related to this matter, of the Secretary of State when the estimates of the civil service commission were before the committee, in an attempt to determine whether compulsory retirement is a matter of decision within the Department of Fisheries or whether it is a matter of the implementation of a broad government policy through the civil service commission, and the Secretary of State indicated to me that it is a matter lying within the decision of the Department of Fisheries. That being the case I hope the minister will give it some consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the matter of retirement at 65 years of age is of course the .general practice in government service, but there is always the possibility of extensions. These patrolmen on the west coast are

seasonal employees, and the type of work they do is rather rugged, being mostly in isolated inlets and coastal areas. Another important consideration is physical vigour. It is quite true that when most men reach 65 years of age they simply cannot undertake the type of work that can be done by younger men. We do keep men on over 65 years of age if they are in good physical shape and if we cannot get suitable men of younger age. We do not want our Department of Fisheries staffed entirely with old men. It has been said by the opposition that the cabinet is old, but we certainly do not want to have the Department of Fisheries patrolmen made up of men over 65 years of age. Where there is a good case we do extend employment beyond the age of 65 years.

I am glad to hear the minister say that. Actually when I raised the matter some time ago what was worrying me was that this was being done because of some directive passed in Ottawa, and was more or less beyond the power of the minister to control.
There is another related matter I should like to bring up. I have been impressed generally with the fine morale of the people in the Department of Fisheries, and I would not like to see anything done which would cause a lowering of that morale. I have had some problems brought to my attention which have arisen in the minds of some of the patrolmen in relation to the implementation of the five-day week. The reaction I get from some quarters is that some of the patrolmen would be quite willing to work more or less around the clock during the season in which they are engaged, particularly in territories where the application of the five-day week might be difficult to carry out. I need not explain to the minister that I am in favour of the five-day week, but some of these men feel that it is to their disadvantage to maintain inspection over the week ends.
I think we realize that patrolmen, particularly when working in isolated inlets along the coast of British Columbia, are hard to replace over the week end. I am wondering whether the minister has had this particular problem in view. Here again I am wondering whether there is freedom of action within the department to adjust the situation to the realities that exist, or whether this is carried out under some directive of the civil service commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
The application of the five-day week to the protection officers and the crews of our protection boats has worked out quite satisfactorily by the use of relief

crews. The problem raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is one affecting his riding, your riding, Mr. Chairman, and my own riding. In all these ridings there are patrolmen operating in isolated inlets where it is sometimes difficult to relieve them.
These men are hired on a seasonal basis. It is quite true that they are very busy at times, but there are also slack periods when the fishing season is closed during week ends generally in British Columbia. We have found generally that the value of conservation is so well thought of that we do not have much of a problem in carrying out patrols during closed seasons.
We have worked out a system of compensatory leave which is granted at the end of the fishing season to make up for the extra time worked. Some of these patrolmen are hired with their boats. We pay a charter fee for the boat as well as a salary to the man. These men want compensatory leave for their boats as well, and that is just a little beyond my power to grasp at the moment. We have not yet agreed to pay charter rates for compensatory leave for the boats after the end of the season.

I heard something of what the minister is talking about and I shall not pursue the matter, because I do not claim to know more about the department than does the minister. There is one other matter I should like to mention. The minister referred to the increasing appreciation of the value of conservation on the part of commercial fishermen in British Columbia, and I agree with what he has said. But there is increasing concern over the depredations of the fisheries by sports fishermen, particularly by yachts and cruisers which come north from United States ports. I think most people in British Columbia recognize the value of the tourist fishing industry, but it has been brought to my attention that in many cases these large sports vessels, which I understand are allowed by regulations to come into our waters, take advantage of our latitude in this matter. Some of our United States friends have made the statement to Canadians that they thought we were suckers for allowing them to get away with what they do.
As an example, it was brought to my attention that a United States boat took 99 spawn-ers in Muchalat arm at the mouth of the Gold river. That boat travelled by sea, I suppose from a Puget sound port, directly to the fishing grounds and returned the same way and did not spend a dollar of tourist money in British Columbia during the few days fishing.
Supply-Fisheries
This is a problem to which we should give attention. I understand that some additional restrictions have been put into force as to the number of fish that can be caught, which I believe is a move in the right direction. This is a problem which we expect the Department of Fisheries to keep very well in hand.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
There is the happiest of relationships between the sports fishermen and the commercial salmon industry in British Columbia. The sports fishermen caught somewhere between 200,000 and 250,000, a quite considerable number of fish. The commercial fishermen are very glad to have such a large active group as the sports fishermen to help them in their efforts against the encroachment of power into these fine fishing streams.
My hon. friend referred to the yachts and cruisers which come up and go back without spending one dollar. This is something which is aggravating to the ordinary sports fisherman in British Columbia, but I would be most hesitant to introduce a licence fee for sports fishing in British Columbia, because that is about the only area in Canada where a Canadian citizen can fish without having to pay even a $1 licence fee. Since there is no licence fee for Canadians it would be rather difficult to impose a licence fee on United States fishermen.
I know that in various provinces across the country there is a considerable difference in the sports fishing licence fee for Canadian residents and for foreigners. However, that matter is under study right now. We hope to come up with some new policy during next winter but, as the hon. member has pointed out, we have taken the first steps already in restricting the catch in the most famous of the fishing areas, Rivers inlet and Phillips arm. The question is under continuous review.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
141. Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and equipment, $285,950.

I do not want to be the only member jumping up here, but there is one point I should like to mention to the minister on this item. As I understand it, this item has to do with the provision, among other things, of accommodation for some of the fisheries officers. I make this suggestion for his consideration. Where housing accommodation is being provided for officers of the department I suggest that consideration might be given to including the provision of one or two basic items such as kitchen stoves and the heating system. It has come to my attention that in different communities they have

Supply-Fisheries
different types of fuel and the type most easily available should be used. Sometimes a man is moved to another area. In such a case he may make arrangements with the incoming man to take over that equipment, but in some cases that is not feasible because the man coming in may have his own.
It seems to me that it would be a reasonable arrangement if we were to provide the necessary money to equip the houses with the basic items which would go along with the house, and which are heavy and difficult to move. I know that the place I rented in Ottawa last winter was equipped with a range and a refrigerator, and when landlords are willing to do that sort of thing it does not seem to me unreasonable for us to make provision of that sort in isolated places.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: We do not do that at the present time in these fisheries officers homes which we build in isolated areas where there is no other housing accommodation. We do pay the removal expenses on the furniture of our officers when they are moved. Most of our officers in these places have a fairly long tenure there, and once they get in one of these nice homes they are very reluctant to move. We do pay the removal expenses on their furniture if they are posted away from one of these government houses.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Fisheries research board of Canada-
149. Headquarters administration, $135,070.

This is the first item on the fisheries research board, and there are two matters I wish to draw to the minister's attention in connection with the board. I am sure we all appreciate the studies and work which have been done by the board. Some most interesting research work has been carried on, and I believe the expenditure is one which is thoroughly justified.
I spoke to the minister this morning, and I should like to ask him now concerning one report issued by the research board; then there is another one I wish to ask him about later. First of all I should like to refer to the one dealing with the green crab. If anyone wants to read a thriller or a detective story or crime mystery novel on the Hitchcock style I think he should read this little booklet on the predations of the green crab. In short, apparently this is a new infestation which has been working up the Atlantic coast. Many years ago it was found in southern waters, and apparently due to the slight change of temperature and the fact that our waters have become warmer during the last few years this crab has been moving up our coast. Five years ago it was off the

coast of Maine and now it is at my own back door. It is moving altogether too fast to suit me, because it is in Minas basin and I can throw a stick out and hit them in the water.
Apparently it is an infestation which is going to cause very serious damage, particularly to the clam fishery. In this booklet, which I presume all members have received, there is an illustration of a little wooden trap with wire mesh siding. The trap is 24 inches long, 18 inches wide and 12 inches high. Yet two of these traps set out for a period of 20 days caught 14,965 crabs; just 35 short of
15,000	in 20 days. The only reason they did not catch more is that the officers in charge could not empty them fast enough. Every time they went out the traps were completely filled again.
According to the report, what is left of the clam fishery, limited as it is by infestations, restrictions and so on, will be completely destroyed by the green crab unless the department or the research board evolve some method of dealing with them. Apparently when this report was published a few weeks or a few months ago they had no hope of being able to do that because there was no way in which they could be controlled without the use of poison which would remove many other species as well. Since it is a matter of substantial importance to the clam fishermen, and since it also illustrates the very useful work which the board is doing, perhaps the minister could give us a word or two on it at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
I must thank the hon. member first of all for his very well justified praise of the fisheries research board of Canada. It is one of the very top flight research boards in the world, one reason being, of course, that we are one of those nations which have a national department of fisheries and national control over fisheries. They have done splendid work in many fields.
When I was in Russia last summer I saw how large their fishery establishment was. They have a larger fishery than we have, but I am sure that the quality of their work is no better than here at home. That is why I am so keen to have two of the top Russian scientists here this fall to visit our research stations.
As far as the green crab is concerned, that is something new to Canada. As the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings has said, that particular publication of the fisheries research board reads more like a mystery thriller than their usual publications with their very long words and obscure phrases. I think it was in 1951 that the

green crab was first noticed in the bay of Fundy. It has moved up from Chesapeake bay, up the Maine coast-
In 1954 it was only as far as Passamaquoddy.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
That is even later than I
thought. The scientists relate its appearance to the general warming of the waters of the north Atlantic. It is found all over the world in warmer waters, and I understand that nowhere in the world has any satisfactory way been found to check it. It is impossible to poison the sea. We find it very difficult even to poison lakes to kill coarse fish or lampreys but it is impossible, of course to poison the sea.
The main method of attack is to try to discover some other animal which will kill them or some disease or virus with which we can affect them. The particular damage this crab does is to shellfish. Although it is only a small crab, it has very powerful claws and can crush small clams, oysters and mussels. One shellfish which it does not attack is the barnacle, and that is one where we would welcome some parasite in order to destroy it.
Our scientists are working on the problem. They are trying to find some other animal which will kill this crab or some disease which will wipe it out. One ray of hope comes from another branch of fisheries science, oceanography, because the indications now are that the waters are beginning to get a little colder. There may be one of those long cyclical retreats, in which case the crab will retire down the coast.

There is one other publica-cation I want to draw to the minister's attention, particularly in view of the discussion we had a year ago when I suggested that the fishing regulations which had closed all the rivers along the Northumberland strait should perhaps be relaxed by the department. At that time the minister appealed to my spirit of conservation. He suggested that we were all very interested in preserving the salmon fisheries, that these restrictions were necessary, and that at the moment at least he could not consider any relaxation of them.
I should like to draw the minister's attention to another very interesting report which has been prepared by the research board. He will find it on page 13, No. 139, progress reports of the Atlantic coast stations, for November, 1955. This deals specifically with the problem of salmon fishing on the eastern coast. It points out that there we have had, ever since 1874, records of catches taken. Records are prepared showing the catches from year to year, the parent run from year
Supply-Fisheries
to year and the fact that there we have a six-year term between the parent spawning and the offspring return. Having compared all the records of the catches since 1874 the board now comes up with this summary, and here I am quoting from page 14 of the progress report:
It can plainly be seen that no relationship whatsoever is evident between the sizes of catches from parents and their offspring. This conclusion has been tested mathematically and shown to be a safe one.
I suggest that if that deduction is correct -and I am sure it is one that the minister would not question, coming as it does from his officials-I think the time has come for him to reconsider these regulations, because what they were dealing with were regulations relating to sports fishing in the rivers, not to fishing in the sea. It is said here that in the rivers in the years in which the biggest catches have been taken they have the biggest return, whereas as to years in which there was a very small catch, six years later there may have been none return. At least that is the summary. I simply am bringing the matter to the minister's attention now, not in the regular manner. I wish he would read that report, then apply it to the discussion we had a year ago, and see whether he could not consider some relaxation of these regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
I have not only read that report but I have read much else on the Atlantic salmon, because I think it is the thorniest problem which the department has to face. It is a very valuable resource, both commercially and especially as far as sports and tourist attractions are concerned. There is no doubt that over recent years, on the whole the catch of Atlantic salmon has declined.
We have gone into the main reasons previously. One is the great increase in the number of fishermen and the opening up of these streams right to the headwaters with roads in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland; the five-day week which gives everybody a couple of days instead of just an afternoon or evening to fish; and holidays with pay. The second factor is the increasing industrialization in New Brunswick. At times we hear from the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska about how far behind New Brunswick has fallen, but we see the other side of the story. This industrial use of water for industry, for hydroelectric dams; the pollution of water because of industry; this spruce budworm spraying, which is another effect of industrialization, all these things take their toll of Atlantic salmon.

Supply-Fisheries
In the report which the hon. member mentioned I think he has taken that remark a little bit out of context. There is no direct and immediate relationship between the number of fish removed from a stream on the Atlantic coast and the returning catch. The Atlantic salmon spends three years in a stream. Much more important than the actual catch are other factors such as the presence of food in the stream, the type of winter, the availability of spawning beds because of variations of high water and low water, depending on the climate. But it is certainly a factor, and one which we can control.
I am quite heartened by the very good work which has been done by the Atlantic salmon co-ordinating committee, which is composed of our deputy minister of fisheries and the four deputy ministers concerned with fisheries in the provinces. We have brought in uniform regulations. We have cut down on the fishing season in the hope of restoring the salmon fisheries on the Atlantic -coast. We are sure we can do it. We have good reason for that. Most of our reason is based on the fact that we have done this on a much bigger scale on the west coast. We are certainly getting public appreciation and cooperation.
One of the reasons I think it is important to prosecute this company which for the third time sprayed one of our hatcheries is to draw to their attention the fact that we regard this resource as an extremely valuable one, and to serve notice on them that they must be more careful in the future than they have been in the past.
But I think I can give a fairly progressive report1-not an optimistic one-and say that I believe we have turned the corner in connection with restoring the Atlantic salmon resources for both commercial fishermen and sports fishermen.
I certainly do not intend to get into any argument at this time as to the relative value of the commercial fishery and the sports fishery. Our job is to restore the fish so there will be an adequate catch for both these fisheries.

I simply drew the minister's attention to the matter. I am not quarrelling with what he said, but apparently the restriction of catches is not the most effective way in which this objective is to be accomplished. I think the last sentence in the report bears out that statement:
Therefore if we want to increase our salmon stocks we must look for more promising ways than merely placing further restrictions on fishing.
That is, of course, what the minister himself said a few moments ago in dealing with the

problem. I am suggesting that less emphasis should be placed on the restriction of sports fishing and that more emphasis should be placed on increasing the number of fish.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: We are trying to approach the problem from every angle.

I should like to ask one question with reference to this budworm spraying. I am not referring to the unfortunate occurrence to which reference has been made, but I want to ask the minister whether a report is now or will be available with regard to the general effect on salmon growth of budworm spraying. Some conflicting statements have been made. Various pseudo experts have said that it may not affect the salmon, while other officials come along and say it will. Now that we have the cycle of growth nearly complete, I am just wondering whether the minister can say something about the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
I shall be very happy to make a few comments on that matter, Mr. Chairman. About two or three years ago I brought the top scientists of our department to a meeting of the Atlantic salmon association, which is perhaps the major association of the Atlantic salmon fishermen sports, and we discussed the whole problem.
To begin with, the spraying for the spruce budworm is just as essential for the continuance of the salmon fishery as it is for the continuance of the pulp and paper industry in New Brunswick. For this reason. If the spruce budworm is allowed to spread and destroy the forests, then there is no cover for insect life on which the small salmon and trout feed. The rivers are ruined because there is no hold-back of the moisture from rain. Then by this run-off the gravel beds on which they spawn are washed away. We certainly realize that this spraying for spruce budworm must be done. But we should like to see it done in a way which would damage the fishery as little as possible.
As far as the effects of the spraying are concerned, we have quite dramatic evidence after three years' study. On the Miramichi river the actual spraying concentration, as I recall it, was a very light one. But if it is as effective on the spruce budworm on the trees as it is in the streams-not on the salmon, but on the life in the streams on which the salmon feed; the fry, the smolt, and the parr-it will serve the purpose intended. In the first three years of their life in the upper Miramichi the young salmon need insect life for food. The spraying almost completely wiped out the insect life in the stream itself. It has a consequent effect actually on the small salmon. That was shown in the hatcheries where their feed

was not affected. Other places were affected by quite heavy concentrations.
We have no hostility to the spraying. We know it must be done. What we tried to work out, when they showed us their spraying plans, was to keep them if possible away from the fringes of streams and especially to avoid all our hatchery areas. On the whole it has worked out fairly well. We know that in the years ahead, when the six-year return comes, there is going to be very poor fishing in parts of the Miramichi because of that loss. The thing we must do is step up our hatchery program in order to restore the natural balance, because we hope by that time the necessity for spraying will be gone and that insect life in the streams will be back to normal. Then we can build up the streams. Last year we put over 10 million salmon fry into the streams down there. I think we can step up that program in the years ahead provided, of course, the planes do not come across our hatcheries and spray them again.

I should like to join with the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings and the Minister of Fisheries in expressing appreciation of the work that is being done by the fisheries research board. I have in my hand a little clipping which came to my attention. It is taken from the issue of the Campbell River Courier which reached me this morning. I thought the minister might refer this matter to the fisheries research board for studies. The headline reads "Blackfish doing Rock and Roll?" The story states:
A roving blackfish or killer-whale caused plenty of excitement Saturday as it put on acrobatic display in the discovery passage waters off Big Rock.
Mrs. Boyd Wilson, Big Rock store, reported the creature was rearing and tossing in the water and appeared to have some sort of parasite, like a gigantic lamprey, attached and causing the eccentric thrashing about.
Mrs. Walter McClean also saw the creature and said that it was rearing and leaping right out of the water, poising on its strong tail, and then would hit the water with a resounding thud. The "jitter-bugging and waltzing" continued until it was abreast of the police station, then course was changed towards the Indian village. It was last seen heading south.
What was the mystery of the monster of the deep?
Perhaps I could send this across to the minister to turn over to the fisheries research board for appropriate study. In a more serious vein, Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister what the situation is in regard to the blackfish as a salmon predator on our coasts. I have had one report given to me that there were 25 salmon found inside one young blackfish which was caught in a seine net. I was wondering how serious a predator the blackfish is.
Supply-Fisheries

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: The word "blackfish" at home is used rather loosely to describe either a porpoise or a killer whale. I do not think the porpoises are a very great threat to the salmon. If they do get caught in the seines or in the gill nets they do a fair amount of damage. The killer whales are probably the most dangerous fish, and they will even attack great whales or sea lions. Most fishermen watch them pretty carefully and keep away from them. I think people often get more alarmed by the playful thrashing of these porpoises than there is really any need for.

Item agreed to.
152. To provide for federal share of administrative expenses of the great lakes fisheries research committee established jointly with the province of Ontario: and to provide for a program designed to eliminate lampreys in the Great Lakes, $485,000.

I wonder if the minister can tell us just how that matter stands now. speechtext: We prepared this item before the commission actually had been set up. I should like to ask the
minister the percentage of the value of fish produced in Canada under provincial control?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: All commercial fisheries as a whole, in round figures, have a market value of about $200 million, of which probably 10 per cent is from the great lakes and prairie areas. About 5 per cent would be from the great lakes.

Has any request been made to the minister to have fishing operations on lake Erie brought under the jurisdiction of the federal fisheries department?

Supply-Fisheries

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
We have had no official request. As I have pointed out before, under our constitution fisheries are the responsibility of the federal government. But over the years some provinces by agreement, have been given the authority to handle sports fishing. I think that is an arrangement which has worked out very well. They are closer to the sports fishing than we are, and they can tie it in with their game operations as well as with their tourist trade. Seven of the 10 provinces handle sport fishing.
In Ontario they also handle the commercial fishing on the great lakes. This is one substantial commercial fishery which is not operated by the federal Department of Fisheries. At various times we do receive letters from great lakes fishermen asking that we regain administration of commercial fisheries. We have taken no action on that. If the province of Ontario chose to relinquish control of commercial fisheries we would, of course, have to exercise our constitutional responsibility. The great lakes fishermen are one of the relatively small groups of commercial fishermen not under the direct jurisdiction of the federal Department of Fisheries.
I might say that we pass on the sports fishing regulations in Canada. They come here from the various provinces, are reviewed by us, and then are subject to the approval of the governor in council here in Ottawa. But the practical management of sports fishing in itself in seven of the 10 provinces is in the hands of the provincial administration.
If the fish operators were under federal control, can the minister say whether they would have the advantage of vessel insurance and unemployment insurance?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
So far as vessel insurance is concerned it has been a move that has been welcomed by the fishermen on both coasts. We in the federal Department of Fisheries administer that through our officers; certain officers are assigned to that work, but they are not full-time on it. Since we have no officers of that description in the great lakes area it has been impossible for us to bring in vessel insurance there. We give coverage at 1 per cent for vessels up to $7,500.
So far as unemployment insurance is concerned, we hope to bring in this plan of coverage by April 1 of next year. It will, of course, come under my colleague the Minister of Labour, and he has unemployment insurance officials right across the country. He is going to have to depend upon the federal Department of Fisheries for

information as to the total catch which would qualify a fisherman to be regarded as a fulltime fisherman. We have not such records for the great lakes. Those records will have to be obtained from the lands and forests department of Ontario. I am sure it is my colleague's intention that when the unemployment insurance comes in it will be applicable in the central areas as well as on the coasts.
I notice that a part of this item is for lamprey control. What amount has been spent on lamprey control by the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: We are putting up all the money for lamprey control. On the research program we share the cost with the government of Ontario; we are each putting up $15,000 toward administration. There is about $460,000 being spent on the extermination of the lamprey this year. This coming year, for the first time, we will have a budget presented to us by this international commission, but in the last two years we have been carrying on under the department this work of lamprey control.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
159. To provide for the extension of educational work in co-operative producing and selling among fishermen, $80,000.

This item provides $80,000 for the extension of educational work in co-operative producing and selling. It appears to be a fairly modest amount if this work is to be done right across Canada. Does this apply to the fishermen right across Canada, or is this a vote for a particular area? For example, does this apply to the fishermen of the prairie provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
We have given this assistance to the areas we administer and to the universities which have specialized in such work. Last year St. Francis Xavier University down in Antigonish, Nova Scotia, which is a small university-but I do not think any university in the world has done a finer job in the field of co-operation than has this university- received $46,000. Then the fisheries school at Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere, Quebec, received $24,000. We have a small course in co-operation at the University of British Columbia, and the amount available to them is $10,000. That has not been fully spent in recent years.
At the University of British Columbia we are trying a new approach. I think the education and co-operation have been pretty well done across the country, but we are one of the few fishing countries of importance that do not have professional schools for fishermen. In the last two years at the University

of British Columbia we have run schools for practising commercial fishermen, which have been very successful with the high-liners of the west coast. A good cross-section of fishermen attended the course during the past winter, and my hope would be that we could extend that type of education to other fishing centres on the east coast and in the central provinces.

The specific question I wanted to ask was whether anything was being done under this item in the prairie provinces. I was thinking particularly of my own province of Manitoba, where there are quite a large number of fishermen. I realize this is a very small amount of money to be spent across Canada, but I am wondering how the benefit of this type of education-incidentally, I approve thoroughly of it and would like to see the item enlarged-is brought to the actual level of the fishermen. So far there has been excellent research work and educational work done in this respect in the universities, but at what point does it get to the actual fisherman who is doing the fishing? What machinery or what facilities are there for bringing it to the fishing community and setting up actual study groups in order to bring this into effect?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: Perhaps I used the wrong words when I said "at the university". At these three universities the work is done by the extension service of the universities and is taken actually to the fishing areas. In recent years Manitoba members have asked that this work be extended to the prairie provinces. We have been in touch with the University of Manitoba and suggested that we would be sympathetic to setting up a similar course at the University of Manitoba if they put forward a syllabus similar to the one at the University of British Columbia, at Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere and at St. Francis Xavier. So far we have had no response at all from them along these lines.

One word in extension of what the minister has said, particularly with respect of St. Francis Xavier University. I have been associated as solicitor with the cooperative union, and also with the maritime united fishermen, a co-operative undertaking of which this was the genesis. I do not know of any money which has been spent more effectively or on which there has been a greater return than the money made available to the extension department of St. Francis Xavier. The work they have done has been for the fishing communities all over the maritime provinces. Dr. Coady and others who have been associated with that work have made a contribution which is absolutely
Supply-Fisheries
incalculable, and goes far and away beyond the amount of money spent.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: I heartily agree.

One more question on the same item. Is there any liaison between the department of Indian affairs, which I realize comes under another minister, and this department in this type of work among Indians on Indian reserves? In the province of Manitoba, as the minister probably knows, a great many of our Indian reserves are situated on lakes, so the chief occupation, the chief source of income, I would think, would be from fishing. Some effort has been made, I know, outside the aegis of the government entirely, to bring about this idea of the co-operative handling of processed fish among the Indians; but I am wondering whether the Indian department, in co-operation with this department, does any actual work among the Indians in that respect?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
We do in British Columbia, in the Yukon and in the Northwest Territories, where we actually administer the commercial fishing. We do not in the three prairie provinces, so I cannot speak of whatever co-operation there may be between the Indian affairs department and the department of the provincial government which administers their fishing. Great Slave lake, which is one of our most profitable fisheries, for trout and whitefish, is an example of where the interest of the Indians has been very closely protected, and an endeavour made to help them to engage in the commercial fishery.
In British Columbia I do not think we have to teach the Indians very much about fishing, because they are amongst our most successful fishermen. They have their own organization, the native brotherhood, which deals directly with the Department of Fisheries.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
161. To provide for assistance In the construction of vessels of the dragger and/or long liner type, subject to such terms and conditions as may be approved by the governor in council, $200,000.

This item deals with assistance to draggers and long liners, and again brings in the perennial problem of those trawlers fishing beyond our territorial waters. We know they are licensed, of course, to operate outside the 10 or 12-mile limit, and it has been a problem for many years on which I am not going to elaborate now. But it is a satisfactory point, I think, at which to remind the minister of the request I made to him when the estimates were before this committee previously and he told me that he thought he would be able to produce the

Supply-Fisheries
Curtis report on territorial waters and file it for the benefit of members.
I would also like to have him comment on the situation as it now exists, in view of the rather interesting statement made by the Prime Minister the other night when he told us of the approach our government is going to make to the United Nations gathering in San Francisco, I think later this year. I think the situation should be clarified quite a bit, and I should like the minister to do it now.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am just a little embarrassed, and I do not embarrass easily, about having made that commitment last year that I would be very happy to table a copy of the Curtis report. Dean Curtis, the head of the law faculty of the University of British Columbia, was engaged to prepare a report on territorial waters for the government, which would be the basis of our presentation at the general assembly of the United Nations this fall on this matter of territorial waters.
I read the report, and naturally assume that because part of the report involved fisheries, that portion of the report could be made public. The whole report, however, is a document of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and he has told me that while he sees no reason why the report should not be made public, though it is a departmental report, he prefers to hold it, since it is the basis of the case which Canada will put forward at the United Nations general assembly. I do not think it would be wise to state our case publicly, or expose our hand, before we take the rostrum.
Has that not been done fairly well now?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
As far as the statement made by the Prime Minister is concerned, the hon. member probably noticed that the fishing cabinet ministers, my colleagues from Newfoundland, from Nova Scotia, from New Brunswick, and myself were very pleased the evening the Prime Minister gave an indication of what the Canadian position would be.
Speaking from memory, I think he said that we would naturally respect a decision of the international court of justice such as in the Anglo-Norwegian case on the validity of base lines along the coast rather than following the sinuosities of the coastline. Then I think he said further that he felt that the interest, especially of fisheries, could be much better served if we had a 12-mile territorial zone rather than the present 3-mile territorial zone. That certainly is something which the fishing industry and the fishermen's organizations across the country have been advocating for some time.

Certainly, Mr. Chairman, I hope this is one which the minister will see that our government presents as forcibly and as rapidly as possible, so this matter can be settled while the minister is still in charge of this department.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: That will be for some time, I think.
He has a few more months to run, but let us get it done this fall.

speechtext: At the time we had to prepare last fall for our main estimates we had not yet completed an estimate of the cost of this Valleyfield experimental station which will be opened this fall. This is a new fisheries experimental station in Newfoundland in which we are going to try to improve the processing, the packaging and the merchandising of salt cod, which is an extraordinarily important item of commerce in the Atlantic provinces and in the Caribbean area, but which has fallen behind other types of food in its appeal as far as the public is concerned. Can the minister tell the committee what the present situation is with regard to the fishermen's wharf at False Creek in Vancouver? Dispatches I have here indicate that work has been stalled for about a month.

There is no more trouble?

stagedirection
speechtext: 324. Departmental administration, $1,596,132.
Does the minister propose to make a statement at this point, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, I did not propose to make a statement. The estimates of the department were rather thoroughly scrutinized and studied by the estimates committee. I did make a statement before that committee, and I did not intend making one at this stage.

Supply-Post Office
either non-delivery or slow delivery of mail. Having said that I must in fairness to the department point out that this figure has remained reasonably stationary over the past several years, and is an indication that the department is not losing ground in this respect and indeed may be gaining some ground, because their volume has increased.
Looking at the post office from the over-all point of view, one matter that disturbs some of us is their failure to compare their operation with the operations of other countries which have similar problems relating to postal service. On a number of occasions we asked the question as to how this situation compared statistically or actually with the experience in the United States, and without exception I believe we were told that the department had not obtained comparative figures and did not think they had any validity.
I would suggest to the department and to the committee that as so many of our problems in Canada and the United States are similar, and because a great deal of work has been done in Canada in collecting statistics in connection with postal operations, it would be a good thing if certain of those statistics were compared with the experience not only in the United States but in other countries, so we could measure the efficiency of our department as against that of other departments.
It is evident to many of us that this policy of having a sizeable profit each year for the Post Office Department, according to their own system of accounting, means that a profit is being made on services rendered the Canadian taxpayer. I do not think many people, certainly not myself, would recommend the operation of the post office at a loss, bookkeeping or otherwise, but we find that in three of the last four years there has been shown a profit of $6 million a year or over and a deficit in only one year of some $2,500,000. That would seem to indicate that we are burdening the taxpayer with postal charges which are in excess of what it is necessary to charge.
I make this point not only with respect to the future but I would harken back also to 1954, when we on this side staged quite a battle against increases in the postal rates. The statistics show that had the old rates been continued we would have been operating at something of a loss; but in 1955, the first full year we can examine, the new rates produced a surplus, as shown in the Postmaster General's annual report, of $7,700,000. I suggest that certain rates, whether for local, out of town or other classifications of mail, were probably raised disproportionately high.

There does seem to be a continuing desire among people to whom I have spoken that consideration be given to returning to the two a day mail service in at least the major centres of this country. That can be coupled with the desire of many smaller localities where there is no house delivery at the present time that they be furnished some measure of house delivery, even though not on a two a day basis but certainly a minimum service of once a day. In the committee we examined a proposition to introduce a two a day mail service on a five-day basis in all centres where deliveries are now provided and the department produced a statistical analysis showing that this would increase their costs by approximately $3 million at the present time, leading to an eventual increase of in the neighbourhood of $3,700,000, if my memory serves me right.
As was pointed out in the committee, that does not necessarily take into account all the factors. There is a suggestion that with a five-day week a man would remain on the same route throughout the year, and the efficiency of this department might be noticeably increased. In any event it is possible to say that the establishment of a two a day delivery service on a five-day week basis across the country would still leave the department with a substantial profit, and it is quite conceivable that something could be applied to the extension and betterment of delivery services in centres where none are now provided.
I must express my regret that the minister has not provided an opportunity for the committee to inspect the new electronic sorting equipment we inquired about at the time the departmental estimates were being considered. At that time this equipment had cost something over $700,000 to develop and research, but it was temporarily out of operation. They were awaiting a few parts from a manufacturer, at which point it would go back into operation again. The minister will perhaps remember that an undertaking was given at that time that as soon as it was in operation the committee would be invited to have a look at it.
That was almost three months ago, and what worries me is whether we have paid out an amount which is rapidly approaching $1 million for a machine which has not been brought to the point of operation during a period of three months so those of us who are interested could see it. I wonder if when this machine goes into operation and a few parts are again needed, it will be laid up for another period of three months.
I certainly support the idea of modernizing as many functions of the post office as can be

successfully undertaken without unfair effects upon the staff, but I am wondering whether this immense sum, which is increasing all the time, is going to result in a machine which will operate successfully. It might be pointed out that the time at which it was to go into operation has been delayed and delayed, and it would be interesting to know whether the minister still expects to make the target date, which I believe is the end of this year.
There is another matter which is perhaps peculiar to one area in this country and to which I express strong objection. The department has a policy

perhaps it is not fair to call it a policy-or a practice in Quebec of encouraging people to obtain letters of reference from their members of parliament when they wish to obtain temporary employment with the post office. Shortly after my election, which was in August, I began to get phone calls from people who wanted letters of introduction in order to get jobs with the post office. In my innocence I said, "Oh, you do not need them. Just go down and tell them you want to work, and if they have a job for you they will take you on." However, I received so many of these calls all in the same tenor that it became quite obvious that it was a practice in the main post office in Montreal to expect a person coming in to have a letter of recommendation from his member.
I am not complaining, Mr. Chairman, that this is patronage in the sense that there is discrimination as between one member and another. Some of the people to whom I gave letters of recommendation got jobs with the department. Of course there were not quite as many as in the case of some of the more fortunate members. I find it difficult to identify the riding of the top recommender, but one member recommended some 428 people who obtained employment. The figures range from there down to the hon. member for Mount Royal, who had 14, and myself with 12, if my memory serves me correctly, with intermediate numbers of 200, 275, 305. To sum up the situation, out of 6,947 people who obtained temporary employment with the post office last Christmas in Montreal 4,465, or approximately two-thirds, supported their applications with letters from members of parliament.
This is not the way to have the best possible government service. The best possible government service arises from allowing the departments freedom to choose their people without being influenced and without forcing applicants into obtaining recommendations from their members. When we pointed this [DOT]out to the minister in the committee he said
Supply-Post Office
this was not their policy. I would hardly expect that it is, but I do suggest to the minister that in at least this one area of Canada it is the established practice, and I say that it should be curbed in the interests of good service on the part of the post office and so they may be left free to obtain the best possible type of employee.
Turning to the question of the people who work in the post office, their hopes for the future, their morale and things of that kind,
1	feel that there are inequities as between various centres across Canada, and that the department has not taken steps quickly enough to put all their people on the same level. In the case of a department which has 50,000 employees it is impossible for any member of parliament to make an adequate analysis that will cover the entire field. One has to, as the technical term is, sample a situation; and if the conclusions are satisfactory and it is apparent that the department is doing a satisfactory job, one goes no further. If the conclusions are unsatisfactory one draws it to the attention of the Postmaster General and the house in the hope that something will be done.
In one examination I was able to make of the status of post office employees 1 found that the situation could hardly be called satisfactory. I refer to the grades held by the clerks in charge of post offices, whom we might better call postmasters because I think the term is known to us all. In order to arrive at this study I took two of Canada's major cities-I was going to say Canada's two major cities, but perhaps I should not-Montreal and Toronto. For each one of the post offices in each of these cities I inquired as to the grade of the clerk in charge, the revenue of the post office and the number of employees. One would expect that the situation would be somewhat similar in these two cities. Incidentally, I may say for the benefit of those who are not familiar with the matter that the grades go upward. In other words, grade 2 is lower than grade 3 both as to salary and status.
In Montreal we find that out of 28 postmasters 24 are grade 2. In Toronto we find that out of 17 postmasters only two are grade
2	and 14 are grade 3. That indicates rather conclusively that, for whatever reason, the great bulk of the postmasters in Montreal are grade 2 and the great bulk in Toronto are grade 3.
We find that there is no relationship between the revenue of the office and the grade of the postmaster. To take a couple of cases at random, there is one post office in Montreal with a revenue of between $500,000 and $1 million. The postmaster is a grade 2. The

Supply-Post Office
postmaster in that same class in Toronto is a grade 3. There is one situation of that kind.
In another case in Montreal there are nine post offices with a revenue of from $200,000 to $300,000 and each one has a grade 2 postmaster. In the same monetary revenue class in Toronto three of the four post offices have grade 3 postmasters. In other words there is a great discrepancy, which I would assume exists right across the country. It does seem to me that the department, which claims to be taking steps to correct that situation, is at fault in not having corrected the situation long before now.
It may be that the Postmaster General will say that the grade of the postmaster has a relationship to the number of employees, but I would point out to the house that in those post offices in Montreal with over 30 employees 75 per cent have grade 2 postmasters, and 92 per cent of similar post offices in Toronto have grade 3 postmasters. The net result leads one to the assumption that the grading of post office employees at the present time is not in line with their responsibilities, and is not on a similar basis from one city to another. I certainly feel very strongly that this is unfair and demonstrates a lack of proper organization in the department.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock I had selected one example-among quite a few which might have been brought forward-of differences in remuneration for what is substantially the same job in so far as the Post Office Department is concerned. Having given the details, I would merely say again that it is that type of situation which makes people unhappy and which causes distress within an organization.
No company organization and no government organization can operate successfully for very long if their employees do not have a high level of morale. When one reads the publication of the post office employees themselves and when one hears from time to time through the press of certain happenings across the country, one is led to wonder whether actually the morale among the staff of the post office in its entirety is as high as it should be. I rather doubt that it is. For that condition I lay the responsibility

at the door of the government because of situations such as the one I outlined to you a few moments ago.
I turn now for a few moments to the question of robberies from the post office and security within the post office generally. We have a situation which has worsened steadily over the last three years. I am prepared to say that the department had made its attempts-and I think they were attempts that were quite sincere and at times quite extensive-to deal with this situation, but to date the results that we expected have certainly not been forthcoming.
I am inclined to think-and I mentioned this before the committee-that the efforts which have been made have stemmed directly from the study made in this house a couple of years ago of the security or lack of security within the post office and of the facts which were then produced. Certainly the department since then has greatly improved its record-keeping system in respect of thefts and burglaries, and it seems to have taken some steps in other directions.
Despite that fact, we find that the incidence of break-ins with respect to the post office has increased steadily year by year. In the calendar year 1953 they were 101; in 1954 they were 171, and in 1955 they were 235. The losses-and these are for the fiscal year-in the post office in the year ended in 1954 were approximately $32,000; in the year ended in 1955 approximately $58,000, and in the year ended, in 1956 they were approximately $99,000. That is a substantial increase.
Earlier I had made reference to a comparison between our experience and that in the United States. We find that in the United States post office break-ins increased from 1953 to 1954-these are my latest figures-from 1,087 to 1,280 or by 21 per cent, while in Canada they increased from 101 to 171 or by some 70 per cent.
When we were discussing this matter in committee the minister did not like the comparison between Canada and the United States. As reported at page 682 of the proceedings of the committee on estimates he said:
What you should compare is the incidence of postal burglaries as compared to the incidence of crime and other burglaries and so on throughout this country.
And later:
If the incidence of other crime throughout the country is going down, then you would certainly be right in saying that we are the victim of more crimes than the other operations in the country. That is not the case as I understand it.
Subsequently his advisers indicated that they had no satisfactory figures by means of

which to compare their own experience with that of the situation in Canada generally. I think it is interesting that just in the last few days there has become available a government publication entitled "Statistics of Criminal and Other Offences". This shows that convictions for burglary, housebreaking and shopbreaking were 6,634 in 1953 and 7,568 in 1954. That is an increase of 14 per cent in 1954 over 1953, which is the last period for which figures are available. We know that in that same calendar year with regard to the post office the increase was approximately 70 per cent in offences. Admittedly I am comparing convictions in the one case with offences in the other. In most of these cases, however, one knows that the rate of offence and the rate of conviction remains about in ratio.
I suggest that this is a disturbing set of statistics to bring before the house. When the minister was before the committee he promised us that he would investigate the possibility of centralizing all investigation of post office thefts and burglaries under the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and that he would report to the house at this time on this matter. I hope he has made a serious study of this matter and that he can comment on it at this time.
There seems to be some indication-the department were loathe to give us details, and I must say that I understand their position-that burglar alarms are being installed in certain places across the country. That is certainly a step forward. From any evidence that I have been able to find, however, they are not being installed rapidly enough or extensively enough to deal with this situation. It would seem that the major post offices in the major cities of Canada should all be protected with a burglar alarm or some similar type of protection. After all, a net loss of $100,000 in a year is quite sufficient to pay for a good many burglar alarms. In addition, the installation of these alarms would, in many cases, ward off potential robbers not only from the post offices in which they were installed but from others as well, because people would not know where they had been installed.
There is one further point I think should be made in connection with the post office, and when I have dealt with it I shall resume my seat for the time being. I refer to their insistence upon operating a banking system in competition with the private banks of this country. In the Woods and Gordon report which analysed their operation there was a definite recommendation that this banking system be discontinued. The post office flatly refused to consider the suggestion.
Supply-Post Office
For my part I can see some justification for the department's stand that their post office banks may be needed in a limited number of small communities across the country which do not have regular banking service. But as was pointed out in the committee hearings, this same banking service in the post offices is being carried into every major city in Canada, and in many cases you have a post office bank on one corner and a commercial bank on the other. Very substantial savings to the taxpayers of Canada could be made if the operation of the post office saving bank were restricted to those very few areas where it could serve a useful purpose, and were eliminated in all those areas where it is in complete competition with the private banking system.
One word should be said, Mr. Chairman, by way of tribute to those who work in the post office, the 50,000 men and women across this country who serve that organization. We have and doubtless shall continue to have areas of strong disagreement on matters of policy. We shall no doubt disagree with the government on certain aspects of the post office operation. We shall have reservations about some of the things they may do. But from having met many of these people in various parts of Canada, I feel that under somewhat difficult and trying circumstances at times they are doing their best, that they have dedicated themselves to a life of service to the public of Canada and to making our post office as effective an operation as they can make it within the sometimes hampering restrictions imposed by government policy.

I have always believed, Mr. Chairman, in the words of that old hymn, "Count your blessings one by one". When I am counting them I always include the Post Office Department and the parliamentary assistant. My nearest neighbour for 45 years is a relative of the parliamentary assistant. He lives about nine miles from me. He is the brother of the late Lindsay Gardner who was speaker of the legislature of Nova Scotia for many years. I like to listen to him talk about the parliamentary assistant, because that is what gave me the idea of counting my blessings. He has told me and my neighbours, all the people in my district from one end to the other, that the parliamentary assistant to the minister is the greatest blessing Nova Scotia has sent to Ottawa in a century.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I come back and say that any organization or department, no matter how efficient, is bound to make mistakes and is not, on that account, free of criticism. I make it a point when I am in my constituency to talk to the post-

Supply-Post Office
masters, to the rural mail carriers, to the postmen in the cities and to anyone connected with the government service. I do not do this with the idea of looking for trouble, but to try to get the viewpoint of the employees and to learn more about the operation of the department and possibly some of those things that could be improved within the department itself.
In that connection I want to deal with a few things that were brought to my attention by the employees of the postal department in my constituency. I saw quite a number of them. First of all I found in some quarters complaints about the rules on appeals for promotional examination. The complaint was based on the ground that seniority, length of service, experience and qualifications do not, I understand, constitute grounds for appeal. I bring that to the attention of the minister because there was considerable dissatisfaction amongst a number of good employees.
Second, I found in some post offices that the local postmaster sits as chairman of the examining board for promotions in his own office. I found quite a number of employees, both those working in the post office and those carrying the mail, who complained against this. These employees complained that this makes personal preference and favouritism possible. They think the minister should be advised of this, and I believe there is some merit in it. They were complaining of the fact the local postmaster sits as chairman of the examining board that deals with promotions in the office itself.
The third complaint was one I heard on several occasions, that the observations and suggestions of post office inspectors, as well as other officials, are overruled or ignored by some postmasters with regard to the proper carrying on of staff meetings and the reorganization of mail routes, and sometimes with respect to internal arrangements. I just bring these matters to the attention of the minister because I promised these employees to do so. They are the type of employees who are not given to making frivolous complaints, so I would like him to have that situation investigated.
I want to deal for a moment or two with what I call the peculiar case of the Toronto Weekly Star which retails in Ontario for 10 cents a copy and in British Columbia for 15 cents a copy. There is a 1 cent provincial tax. The excuse given by the Toronto Weekly Star is that this cost to the purchaser there is brought about by postage rates when, as a matter of fact, I understand the postage rates to a point in Ontario and a point in British Columbia are the same, 4 cents per pound for this type of material.

There is no doubt about it, the Post Office Department loses very heavy revenue by reason of these very low rates on certain types of magazines, papers and things of that sort. I think the house agreed to this proposal in order to facilitate the distribution of papers, magazines and literature. I wonder if the Toronto Weekly Star publishers are doing their part in this respect when they charge their British Columbia subscribers 15 cents a copy when they can send it to British Columbia for exactly the same price as they can send it to a point in Ontario. I should like the minister to comment on that point.
I have been asked by quite a number of my constituents and people in southern British Columbia generally to deal with another topic. I want to make a few comments on the wildlife series of stamps. Let me say, first of all, that I am very glad to know there is a wildlife series of stamps, because I think it is an excellent theme for a stamp. I think we have been a bit unfortunate to date, if one judges from the examples I have seen. This matter has been raised in the house by the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace and one or two others.
I would not base my opinion entirely upon the statements of members in this house, because they might possibly be tinged with a political flavour. I have based my opinion on the opinions of people in British Columbia who hold very important positions. I realize the difficulty of transferring a drawing accurately to an engraving, and the difficulties of engraving certain subjects. However, I want to suggest that even Borneo produces a series of wildlife stamps which are masterpieces compared with those produced in Canada. I have some of them in my possession.
I am not blaming the artists or anyone, but possibly we could investigate some of the processes the people use in other countries where they have been successful in engraving subjects that are quite difficult. I know that in some of the Asian countries they use wildlife studies on their stamps quite frequently, and they are really works of art. I suggest that there should be some inquiry made to see whether we cannot bring our Canadian stamps up to the standard of those engraved in Borneo.
I want to illustrate that we are not just complaining members of the house. Here is a letter that was written in Ottawa about the goat stamp. We have all heard about it. I was interested in it before because there are some wild goats in my constituency-fourlegged ones-and I know what they look like because I have been out hunting. The letter reads:
Those who dislike the "goat" stamp have only to reverse it to see displayed an elder statesman,

identity undetermined. He wears a neat, if old-fashioned, derby hat, has expressive eyes, and a handsome white beard, while his sky-blue coat is marked by shoulder tabs, and lapels that might well serve as a pattern for designers seeking something new in this sartorial feature. For a greatly improved effect, use this famous stamp upside down.
That is from a prominent citizen of Ottawa. Then I have a copy of a letter from a personal friend of mine, a contractor in British Columbia, who writes me as follows:
Dear Bert:
In our local paper the Daily Colonist I read about your remarks regarding the new issue of stamps. Allow me to congratulate you. I as well as many I have spoken to here in Victoria all agree they should be withdrawn. The mountain goat looks as though it might pass out at any time. It is no more like a mountain goat than a very sleepy sheep with upright horns.
As for the caribou, it looks like something one might have after a good drunk. Talk about seeing double! In any case there appears to be seven caribou with horns and one with only one horn.
I do hope that you and the other members of the house may prevail upon the powers that be to cancel this proposed issue.
Then one other letter from the manager of one of the largest companies in British Columbia:
Dear Mr. Herridge:
I have noted with interest your comments in respect to the "wildlife" postage stamps which are coming out in the new issue.
I do not know as to whether there was any comment made in respect to one of the stamps in a previous issue-I forget what they may have commemorated but it is supposed to be, as I remember it, a mountain sheep. I am enclosing a couple of the stamps to which I refer. To my mind, this is a very poor reproduction of a mountain sheep and to me it looks more like a cross between a cow and a supreme court judge with a wig. I realize there is no point in my bringing this question up, but I was prompted to do so by the remarks which have been made in respect to the new issue.
Then a paper published in Australia that specializes in stamps and contains plenty of information about stamps of all kinds-[DOT] it is published for stamp collectors and is called Stamp News-has a leading article on page 3 entitled "Drunkard's Nightmare", with the subheading "Politician's View of Canadian Stamp", which reads as follows: By Dace Logigas
Who gives a blow to blow description of the bitter controversy which has raged around the issue of a series of wildlife stamps in Canada.
I quote briefly from it, but before doing so may I say I am sure this is much more serious than just a jocular affair in the House of Commons. Many people are concerned about this issue of stamps because they want the stamps to be worthy of the engraving art in Canada. The article reads in part:
Life these days must be a pretty grim affair for certain Canadian citizens.
Supply-Post Office
That is the minister. I continue:
They are the small but important batch of officials responsible for the issue of Canada's postage stamps. Once a happy band of individuals, praised and feted universally, they have since 1951 been a haunted, fear-ridden race, hunted looks appearing on their faces whenever the subject of stamps is mentioned.
They are in trouble again over the 1956 wildlife series and public abuse is being heaped on their unlucky heads.
But the volume of hard words directed at them in recent years has blunted their susceptibilities to such an extent that they are now said openly to wince only at the most devastating remarks of their unkind critics.
Up to 1951 all was rosy in the Canadian philatelic garden. Canada had a good record of stamp issues amongst empire countries, being among the first of the commonwealth nations to issue attractive pictorial commemoratives. Some of these it is true, were no works of art, but they did not merit any severe criticism either; and the design that occasionally fell below expectations was more than compensated by some of the really superb issues of pre-war Canada, issues such as the 1933 5-cent U.P.U. congress, 5-cent 1933 Royal William, 3-cent 1934 Cartier, 13-cent 1935 Jubilee to name but a few.
Then it goes on to deal quite critically with the musk ox stamp, the wild sheep stamp and the wild goat stamp. I mention these things to indicate even an international interest in the production of stamps in Canada. I believe our department should seek advice from some other countries so the procedures would be improved and we would be able to have stamps issued equal to those in the countries I have mentioned.
I have another little matter here, Mr. Chairman. I was very glad to note recently that the Post Office Department has a humour section, as an indication that the majority of the staff have not lost their sense of humour. I want to deal now with the cause of that humour. It is "Postmen and Pooches". A dog may be man's best friend, but it would be difficult to get the postman to agree with that sentiment, particularly a good number in my constituency who have been bitten. Post office reports indicate that 183 letter carriers have claimed compensation so far this year for bites severe enough to require medical attention. No doubt thousands of other unfortunate postmen patched themselves up without professional aid.
As far as my constituency is concerned, at the present time there are 10 cases of postmen having been bitten, but fortunately none of them seriously. However, I understand that the department has given some consideration to this, and it is an important question because it is a very serious thing for postmen delivering mail on a good many routes, and it is a concern in countries other than Canada. The department tried to rise to the occasion, Mr. Chairman, by issuing a directive to the postmen in Trail, of which I was

Supply-Post Office
given a copy. It was informing the postmen how to win friends and influence canines. This is the directive:
1.	Ignore the dog until he shows he is friendly. Never make the first advance.
2.	Don't strike at the snarling, snapping or barking dog, or he'll conclude it's all right to fight back.
3.	A vicious dog can be bluffed-just walk fast and straight past him-never turn your back and run-show unconcern.
You know, this is a directive from the Post Office Department to the postmen. There are no rules of conduct, for instance, where the vicious dog calls the postman's bluff. I mention this as an indication of the growing sense of humour within the department, and I am pleased to see it because without a sense of humour this would be a pretty unfortunate world.
However, I do suggest there are more effective ways to deal with this question. I might tell the minister frankly that the postmen did not find this directive very helpful, but the matter has been given consideration in the United States. They had a committee studying it recently. While they could not come to conclusions, after a long time and after some experiments carried out somewhat recently, they have found a fairly effective way of dealing with the dog who wants to bite the postman. What they do is give the postman a little satchel of tidbits for the dog. I do not know what it is, but it is very effective. The postman just throws one at the dog and the dog takes it and the postman drops the letter in the box and goes on scot free. I understand since they have been using those tidbits they have reduced dog bites of postmen by 90 per cent. I suggest the department should investigate this, because it may be a very cheap and effective way of dealing with this menace to postmen across this country.
My second suggestion would be that after trying this, where people insist on keeping a dog that is savage and dangerous to other people the department consider whether they would be justified in saying that no more mail would be delivered at such a house or place of business until the dog was removed.
I have got a good laugh out of the Post Office Department directly and I have enjoyed it, but it is a serious matter. I just bring the attention of the department to research and studies that have been made in the United States to see whether we could not do something along that line. I am quite sure the postmen would not mind carrying that little bag of whatnots, or whatever you like to call it, so long as it protected them from the dogs in question.

I shall take just a brief moment or two at this stage of the proceedings of the house. I understand that when a community is ready to receive mail delivery as opposed to those in the community going and getting their mail in a box, the rule of thumb, roughly speaking, is that a community must have a population of approximately
8,000	and an annual revenue, so far as the post office is concerned, of approximately $50,000.
In my constituency there are two towns that have come very close to meeting all the qualifications required. One is the town of Ingersoll and the other is the town of Till-sonburg. The latest census figures, of course, are not available because the results of the more recent census have not yet been published, but in the 1951 census the town of Ingersoll had a population of 6,524 and the town of Tillsonburg had a population of 5,330. Both these towns, particularly Tillsonburg, are growing at a very considerable rate. However, as far as the postal revenues from these towns are concerned, in 1954 Ingersoll had a postal revenue of $46,660, and in 1953 it had a revenue of $48,606. Oddly enough, the revenue appeared to be slightly higher in 1953 than it was in 1954, but I find from looking at the figures that this seems to be generally the case for one reason or another.
Tillsonburg, while having a somewhat smaller population than Ingersoll in 1951, nevertheless in 1953 had a postal revenue of $51,893 and in 1954 had a postal revenue of $50,552.
