In other words, Mr. Chairman, while the town of Tillsonburg according to the 1951 census does not quite meet the population requirements, it does meet the revenue requirements laid down by the department; and the town of Ingersoll with a slightly larger population-I imagine it would be close to 8,000 today-comes very close to meeting both the population and the revenue requirements.
I very much hope, Mr. Chairman, that the Postmaster General, his deputy and the other officers of the department will take a very close look at both Tillsonburg and Ingersoll with a view to having mail delivery service established there in the very near future. As I have pointed out, Tillsonburg already more than meets the revenue requirements and Ingersoll is very close.
There is just one other item I would like to deal with, and it relates to what I consider a very unfortunate case in the city of Woodstock. I have brought this matter to the attention of the minister and his parliamentary assistant on a previous occasion, and the results have not been very satisfactory as far as I am concerned. I might say this is the only complaint I have

had against the Post Office Department since I have been here. I would like to bring this up now in the hope that this last appeal may soften the minister's heart a bit in relation to this case. I am told that in the province of Ontario there are six or seven elderly ladies in the same position as the one whose case I am going to bring before the committee at this time. These elderly ladies are not civil servants, unfortunately, but they have held positions in post offices throughout the province where they sold stamps on a commission basis.
The lady I am going to deal with is a Miss Katherine Rose, who held such a position in the post office in Woodstock. I understand there is also one in Brantford and others in certain other places. These ladies unfortunately do not come under the civil service; consequently when they are compelled to give up their positions they have no pensions or any other type of remuneration coming to them other than the old age pension.
Miss Katherine Rose sold stamps on a concession basis in the Woodstock post office for 33 years. Last fall Miss Rose, who is approximately 80 years of age and continued to sell stamps despite her age, was discharged from the post office. I understand there were adequate reasons for discharging Miss Rose because of her age and so on; however, the one rather unfortunate aspect was that after 33 years of service she was told on September 21 that she was going to be discharged on September 30, which I think is rather short notice and somewhat abrupt, in fact one might almost say a little cold blooded.
Miss Rose, however, was fired, and now of course she has no revenue except the old age pension; because Woodstock had a population of approximately 10,000 during the period in which Miss Rose was employed, although it is a little larger now, and in a city of that size there would not be vast sales of stamps and I understand vendors receive a 2 per cent commission.
Miss Rose, as I said, is approximately 80 years of age, and according to the law of averages she probably will not live a great deal longer. I understand there are certain other ladies in the same predicament in this province, and now that we are approaching virtually a welfare state in Canada I think it is a great pity that these six or seven elderly ladies, none of whom will live very long, in all probability, could not receive some recompense from the government for their services over these many years.
It is indeed unfortunate that they are not under the civil service, but they are not; and I think it would be a very simple matter for the minister to include in his estimates or 67509-4781
Supply-Post Office
his supplementary estimates a little item reading, "Pension for so and so". We see it all through the estimates; we saw it this afternoon when we were dealing with the estimates of the Department of Justice. There is a small pension item for three ladies in those estimates and I presume it covers some unusual circumstances such as these. I am sure it will not bankrupt the country nor will it endanger the enormous surpluses of the Minister of Finance if the government should find it possible to give $600 a year to each of these six or seven ladies who served the Post Office Department. Such arrangements have been made in other departments, and I do not see why it could not be done here.
In addition to that, in our town we had another elderly lady who worked for 60 years not in the post office but as a stenographer for the province of Ontario. Because of the length of time she worked and the nature of her employment she did not receive a pension when she was obliged to retire. However, the government of the province of Ontario saw fit to give this elderly lady, who had worked for 60 years in the service of the province, a special pension under the estimates, and I cannot see why the Postmaster General could not find a way of doing it in relation to the handful of elderly ladies I have mentioned.
I know the minister may very well say, "Oh, but Miss Rose worked until she was 80 years old, and for that reason she had an income and was better off than if she had retired on a pension." Mr. Chairman, that is no answer at all. It certainly is news to me that when people are obliged to work until they are 80 years of age in order to live it is to be preferred to a pension. This lady should have retired at the age of 65 or 70 like anyone else, instead of having to work until she was 80 and able to work no more. I cannot understand why the minister is unable to find some way of softening his heart a little to help out these few elderly ladies who are scattered throughout the province of Ontario.

Mr. Chairman, I have been asked by the rural mail carriers of my own riding of Elgin to bring to the attention of the minister a petition they circulated widely among their group, which is signed by some 39 of the 50 rural carriers in the county. I have already sent a copy of the petition to the minister. It reads as follows:
We. the undersigned mail carriers of Elgin county, in view of the high cost of owning and maintaining a suitable vehicle for the purpose of delivering mail to the rural sections, feel that a minimum remuneration of $75 per contract mile per year is necessary to meet that high cost and leave a satisfactory amount for our labours.

Supply-Post Office
Therefore, we respectfully request that you bring the matter to the attention of the proper authorities and ask that our remuneration for services tendered be brought up to that minimum.
Mr. Chairman, I believe our rural carriers all across Canada perform a wonderful service in delivering the mail. They are perhaps somewhat like showmen in that the old proverb, "the show must go on" has an application for them. Come hell or high water, rain, sleet or snow, rural mail carriers feel the mail must be delivered and they see that this is done. I recall that one winter we had a severe storm which lasted for a number of weeks, and it was extremely difficult to deliver mail. I know of one particular case where for seven days in succession a carrier delivered his mail over a 24-mile route on foot through extremely deep snow.
I feel that some consideration should be given to these people. If they were in the civil service they would have already received a raise in pay. Perhaps the minister will say these people deliver mail under contract, and if they are not satisfied with the contract price all they have to do is give it up and tender on it again. That does not seem quite fair, as many of these contractors have held their contracts for long periods and they hesitate to give them up. Therefore they carry on and sometimes work actually at a loss.
There are a few suggestions I should like to pass along to the minister at this time which were passed along to me by a rural mail carrier. The first is that there should be some standardization of routes; they should be made longer. The present length of routes is based on horse and buggy days. Then it is suggested that the rural mail delivery be made a profession or occupation, not a side line. It is suggested that rates of pay be established with a certain amount of elasticity to provide for the different conditions in different districts. Contractors over 65 years of age who have had a lengthy term of service should be given a pension in keeping with their present contract prices.
I should like to endorse what the hon. member for Oxford has said about people in the post office with lengthy periods of service being entitled to pensions. When there is an amalgamation of routes the courier with seniority should be permitted to carry the new route. A pension plan should be established for the remainder, and there should be holidays with pay, sick benefits, group insurance and so forth.
Under the present system no route will sustain itself and provide the class of equipment which the public expects the courier to drive, notwithstanding the courier's own
[Mr. McBain.l
pride. This makes it necessary for him to go out and work all hours at all kinds of work, or else have some other member of the family drive the route while the contractor seeks more remunerative employment. I ask the minister and the department to give serious consideration to these suggestions. I think it is only fair to the rural mail carriers and contract mail carriers in Canada that they should be given the same consideration as the civil service recently received.

There are two matters I wish to deal with, one of which can be brought up under this item and the other one I shall bring up later. I just received a letter asking why the post office at Debec in Victoria county has been moved from the main street to another business section.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I shall endeavour to get the information before these estimates are completed.

In March of this year I put a number of questions on the order paper to which I received answers. The reason I asked those questions was the reduction in urban mail deliveries from two to one a day. Mail from the east and west hits Toronto at seven or eight o'clock in the morning, but any mail destined for Hamilton does not reach that city until after the first mail delivery has gone out. The result is that a great deal of business mail is 24 hours late, because many business firms are still on the one a day delivery. With that in mind I inquired of some of these companies as to what procedure they followed in getting their mail and I found that a number of companies have been unable to rent post office boxes at the general post office, and therefore have adopted the procedure of having the post office staff collect their mail which they pick up at the letter carrier wicket. I do not mean the general delivery wicket; as the minister knows, the letter carrier wicket is located in another part of the post office.
I have been informed that at the main post office in Montreal there are 774 post office boxes, 473 of which are rented, leaving a balance of 301 unrented. There are 2,022 companies or individuals who pick up their mail daily or perhaps several times a day at the letter carrier wicket. In Toronto there are 352 post office boxes at the main office; 350 are rented with 2 unrented; there are 1,925 companies or individuals who pick up their mail at the letter carrier wicket. In Hamilton there are 378 post office boxes in the main office, 376 of which are rented with 2 empty, and 132 companies or individuals pick up their mail at the letter carrier wicket.

In Kitchener there are 276 post office boxes, 276 being rented with none empty, and 26 companies or individuals pick up their mail at the letter carrier wicket. In St. Catharines there are 313 post office boxes, 308 of which are rented with 5 empty, and 26 companies or individuals pick up their mail at the letter carrier wicket. In Winnipeg there are 617 post office boxes, 609 of which are rented with 8 empty, and 588 companies or individuals have made arrangements to call for their mail at the letter carrier wicket. Once more I draw attention to the fact that this is not general delivery; this is a special service given to persons or companies who cannot get the service they require in the way of postal delivery.
In Regina there are 483 post office boxes, 470 of which are rented with 13 unrented, and 112 companies or individuals pick up their mail at the letter carrier wicket. In Calgary there are 400 post office boxes all of which are rented, and 354 companies or individuals pick up their mail at the letter carrier wicket. In Edmonton there are 462 post office boxes in the main post office, 461 of which are rented with 1 empty, and 221 persons or companies pick up their mail at the letter carrier wicket. In Vancouver there are 897 boxes of which 843 are rented, leaving 54 empty; 589 companies or individuals pick up their mail at the letter carrier wicket.
In some of the cities I have mentioned there are branch post offices where there are empty post office boxes, but most of these companies are within range of the downtown post office where the mail is directed first. That is where they collect the mail. It seems to me, particularly in view of the fact that the department has taken such a step to reduce mail deliveries, that some consideration should be given to these literally thousands of companies and individuals who find that in order to collect their mail and carry on business in a normal way, they are obliged not only to pick up the mail themselves at the main post office but to put the post office staff to considerable inconvenience to collect this mail and have it ready for them if and when they call to pick it up.

I was quite interested in what the member for Kootenay West had to say with regard to the various issues of postage stamps, and I shall have a little more to say about that later. On several occasions I have pointed out to the department that in this day and age, when the horse and buggy has gone and the automobile is used for the delivery of rural mail, more attention should be given to the extension of rural routes, and regulations should not be so drastic as to curtail the delivery of mail to people in the rural areas.
Supply

Post Office
There is another item that I think is rather confusing to a great number of people. Some time ago it was broadcast across the country that all first-class mail would be airborne. Such is not the case. Mail posted in many areas does not have a chance in the world of being carried by air. So it is rather misleading to many Canadian citizens who think their first-class mail is airborne. I am going to ask the minister to indicate to the house what percentage of first-class mail is actually carried by air.
The hon. member for Elgin mentioned the rural mail carrier. Probably in this day and age, when hours of work and rates of pay are very seriously considered by many industries, I think the rural mail carrier, whilst his job is let on a contract basis, is the forgotten man in the postal department.
Coming back to what the hon. member for Kootenay West had to say regarding issues of postage stamps, particularly the wildlife issues, I take some little interest in the various issues of stamps. I would suggest, among other things, that each of the provinces of Canada has a flower that is known as its provincial flower.
We have the dogwood.

I was just going to point out that the province of British Columbia has the dogwood; Alberta, the wild rose; Manitoba, the wild crocus; Saskatchewan, the red prairie lily; Ontario, the trillium; Quebec, the wild blue flag or iris; New Brunswick, the violet; Prince Edward Island, the lady's slipper; Nova Scotia, the arbutus; Newfoundland, the pitcher plant or Indian slipper. I might mention that the pitcher plant was selected for Newfoundland by the late Queen Victoria. This information is obtainable from the Canadian Geographical Journal.
The Falkland islands, as we all know very well, are very dependent upon the sea and they have a stamp issue that shows the various famous sailing vessels that called at the ports in those islands. The Falkland islands have been able to incorporate a very fine picture of our Queen in their stamps. So I suggest that when the department is considering a new issue of stamps it considers the provincial flowers that I have mentioned and, along with them, a fine portrait of the Queen. Just to show the minister what I have in mind, I am going to send over to him some samples I have here. I hope he will view them with interest.

First of all I should like to make the same remarks I made about the estimates of the transport department last week, that the figures we are discussing here

Supply-Post Office
are over a year old. We do not get the true picture of how the department is operating this year. The hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace dealt with an analysis of the figures, and I do not need to say any more about that except that there was an increase in revenue this year of $21 million. He suggested that if the double delivery postal service were restored it would probably make it come out right.
I should like to repeat what I said some two years ago, that I am much more enamoured of the technique adopted by the Postmaster General who made this a hobby, Sir William Mulock, who always provided service and increased efficiency. As the surplus mounted and mounted, he gave it back to the people who were paying for the service. In this particular case the department is working in reverse. They are anticipating there is going to be a loss, and they make the people pay for that loss. It just proves to me that the technique employed by Sir William Mulock was the right one, particularly when they follow the recommendation of the Woods-Gordon report and find that they begin to get results. This is only the first year that we are able to say they have had the benefit of the Woods-Gordon report. We shall probably have to wait till next year to get the full picture of how it is operating. I shall leave it at that for now.
The matter brought up by the hon. member for Kootenay West is an intriguing one. In regard to the postage stamps, I thought it was satire they were trying to achieve. Two years ago, I believe, I mentioned that they had brought out a new series of stamps, and they had a goose that was very effectively done. I am not criticizing the art work of the stamps, because it is very difficult to get good artistic results for a very small stamp. The original art work has to be about ten or 20 times the size of the stamp, and it is difficult to reduce it perfectly. As far as the subject matter is concerned I did not think it was humorous; I thought it was satire. When they brought in the higher postage rates I thought they were using the symbol of the goose that laid the golden eggs, because the public was the goose. It was getting the revenue from the public, who were not getting anything in return for it.
Last year they introduced another wildlife subject. I suggested that I thought it would be a very good idea if, instead of a walrus, they had taken a fish-a good slimy, slippery fish, a sucker-and probably that would be symbolic of what they were using the people

of Canada for. I should say there were a lot of suckers, because the rates were put up instead of being reduced and the surplus bounced.
This year I presumed they took my words to heart and decided to carry this lesson of symbolism to the people. Instead of giving them a fish they gave them a goat. It did not matter whether the art work was good. They got the story over, that they were using the people of Canada as the goat because they were still mulcting them for the higher rates of postage which they should not be charging.
Earlier in the year the hon. member for Peterborough brought up a matter with respect to that city, where they were quite concerned about this all-seeing eye or viewing gallery, as they call it, in the post office. Again another satirical thought occurred to me. When the Minister of Justice was discussing some of the criminal offences that were mentioned at that particular time he went down through the categories of offences of people who were becoming a nuisance, who had jail terms, who were in and out of prison and who were known to be repeaters or habitual offenders. He classified them as peeping toms if they were habitually going around schools or public places.
I suppose you would call a post office a public place. It is in the discretion of the postmaster of a particular post office whether he is going to turn on this all-seeing eye, this viewing gallery or peeping tom as I suggest you could call it now, because that is what it will be. There is going to be a problem here for the Minister of Justice in addition to the postmaster who is in charge of the post office when he turns on this all-seeing eye or peeping tom or viewing gallery, as he calls it, namely whether this could be taken to be any offence.
This gentleman is going to be a peeping Tom, and a charge could be laid against him. The first thing we know the Postmaster General may be implicated in the deal, inasmuch as he has authorized it. He is going to commit a very serious offence every time he turns this all-seeing eye or peeping tom on people who are working in the post office, particularly if there are any nice looking ladies in there and they happen to be in a compromising posture. To have this peeping tom in operation may make him liable to a fine of $500 or maybe a term in jail.
They are going to have a problem that will be very difficult to solve. I hope they are going to get the Minister of Justice and his officials to get them out of the difficulty.

I am in complete agreement with the hon. member for Elgin with regard

to the rural mail carrier. No people in Canada work more diligently and faithfully than do those people. Some time ago the postal rates were raised. I feel that these mail carriers are not getting their just benefits from that raise in rates.
At this time I have another matter which I wish to mention. We have a small problem in the post office at Seeleys Bay as to which perhaps the Postmaster General can give me the answer. During past years, in fact for as long as I can remember, the post office boxes at Seeleys Bay have been covered with glass through which post office box holders could look into the box and see whether there was any mail in it. But now that glass has been crystalized and we cannot see through it. Much inconvenience is caused to the box holders and also to the postmaster, because every time anybody goes into the post office and cannot see whether or not he has any mail in his box, the postmaster must run around and look into it.
I was just wondering whether this was a direction that came from the administrative branch of the Postmaster General or whether it was a direction that came from the divisional superintendent. Inconvenience is caused not only to the boxholders but also to the postmaster. I was wondering whether the Postmaster General could inform me whether this direction had come from the administrative branch, or whether it was from the superintendent of that particular district.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether I might be permitted at this stage to make a few remarks in answer to some of the questions that have been asked. Then possibly we could carry this first item and any specific questions could be raised on the other items in the estimates.
As is usually the case when post office estimates come before members of this house, the questions and comments cover a wide range. It is significant that this is so, because I believe every hon. member is more familiar with the everyday operations of the post office department than with those of many other departments. For that reason I welcome all the comments, suggestions and criticisms that are offered.
I do not know just how I could deal at one time with everything that has been mentioned. To start with, much has been said about the stamps of the department. The hon. member for Kootenay West, the hon. member for Middlesex East and others have referred to the various stamps issued by the department. It has been suggested by the hon. member for Middlesex East that we should possibly consider issuing stamps representing floral designs of a provincial
Supply-Post Office
character. This matter is at present under study and some designs are being looked into.
I suppose the comments which attracted most attention were those made by the hon. member for Kootenay West, when he repeated the views expressed by many others as to some of the designs in our wildlife series. In the estimates committee, as I think hon. members who sat in the committee will agree, this whole question was fairly well discussed. It was explained by the director of that particular branch of the department that we had a very intricate process of choosing designs, having them approved, referring them to artists and the national gallery and so on. But as he pointed out to the hon. member, I believe, the unfortunate fact is that goats are not good-looking animals. If we are going to represent the wildlife of Canada, we have to represent the animals as they exist. This particular design was submitted to zoologists who said it was a good goat and looked exactly like a mountain goat, and that, unattractive as it was, it was a good representation of that particular animal.
The hon. member tells me that in Borneo they have stamps representing their wildlife. I do not know whether or not the wildlife in Borneo is more attractive than that of Canada. I would hate to slander the Canadian mountain goat, but there you have the situation. As far as that is concerned, any stamp that is issued by the department and which may have a technical aspect or character is always referred to experts on that particular subject.
Of course other comments were made by the hon. member for Kootenay West. I must say that I was extremely pleased that he raised this complex question of the relationship between the letter carrier and the neighbourhood dog. As he pointed out, this is a subject which has attracted quite a bit of attention in the press lately. It is true that in the United States the matter was made the subject of a very serious study. I understand that their statistics in the last year record the fact that one out of twenty letter carriers in the United States has become the victim of some form of attack while delivering mail.
I am pleased to tell the hon. member that our record here in Canada is much better than that. I believe our ratio is something like one out of every 31 letter carriers. Whether or not this is because Canadian dogs are less aggressive or more polite than United States dogs, I do not know. It is still a serious problem. It seems that 200 out of 6,200 employees are subjected every year to this form of attack by neighbourhood dogs.

Supply-Post Office
Just how the hon. member would suggest we approach that problem, I do not know. In some years there have been campaigns to be kind to animals. I must say that the post office tries to be kind to every type of animal with which it has to deal. We sometimes wonder, however, whether the campaign should not be "to be kind to letter carriers". Perhaps there may be some way of enlisting the help of some of the finer dogs who do help the letter carrier by accompanying him along his route just because of the love they have in their hearts for the uniform of the Post Office Department.
It is a serious subject, because the owners of dogs must not forget that they are likely to lose letter carrier service to their homes if the dog prevents the letter carrier from delivering the mail. In addition, they are always liable to be charged for any workmen's compensation which may result from any injury their dog may have caused to the letter carrier. I would be very pleased if the hon. member would co-operate with me in some form of campaign to make sure that Canadian dogs are provided with a more orthodox type of dog food than the letter carriers of the Post Office Department.
I believe I can truly say that the many points that were raised by hon. members were pretty well discussed before the estimates committee. Of course that is no reason why they should not be brought before the house. Mention has been made of the fact that rural mail couriers should be paid a flat rate per mile. This was looked into by the department some years ago, and under the present act we ask for tenders for a contract. If we are to have the tendering system, we cannot fix a rate before asking for tenders. I do not think a true comparison can be made or relationship developed between the other employees of the department, who are classified civil servants, and the rural mail courier who tenders on a contract and enters into an agreement with the department to carry the mail on a particular route at a rate which he himself sets.
Under the present act, as hon. members know, any contractor may, after he has been executing his contract for two years, apply for adjustment of his rate if he feels he is not getting proper remuneration. This is done quite regularly by most rural mail contractors. Then the department can calculate the average that is paid in that particular area. If a man is receiving a rate that is below the average an adjustment is made in his contract.
The hon. member for Kootenay West mentioned the question of appeals by employees

of the department as the result of promotions. These appeals are looked after by the civil service commission. They are part of the whole civil service set-up and the department, as such, does not handle them. It is quite true that in many of these promotional examinations the postmaster in that particular district may be sitting on the examining board, but these appeals are completely outside of the hands of the department. They are done that way so that at no time can the senior employee who sat on the board have any decision on the appeal. I believe, therefore, there cannot be an injustice done.
Will the minister tell me if they are allowed to appeal to any other authority other than the board that decides on the promotion?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
They can appeal to the civil service commission directly, under the act.
The hon. member for Oxford mentioned the establishment of letter carrier service in certain localities. I think it is well understood, Mr. Chairman, that the department must have a standard which it tries to follow in connection with the establishment of new letter carrier services. Generally speaking the basis is that the locality where the post office is situated should be one where the post office has a revenue of $50,000 a year and there should be 2,500 points of call for letter carrier delivery in that locality. That is a standard but naturally, like any other formula used in a service such as the post office, it has to be flexible. So far as the revenue factor is concerned, it may vary according to circumstances. But generally speaking we find it is very difficult, unless we are sure of 2,500 points of call, to establish such a service. Each one is the subject of a special investigation, and it may be established even if all those conditions are not met. I will certainly be glad to look into the cases which the hon. member mentioned.
There were many other points brought up. The hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace mentioned various things. He suggested that possibly we were lax in getting information on other postal services outside of this country and establishing comparisons of various activities in the department with those in other countries. Well, we do keep in constant touch with the postal services of other countries and particularly with the United States and with Britain, and we do make comparisons. However, these are not always useful because bases of statistics may vary.
For instance, the hon. member mentioned the incidence of crime and the number of break-ins in postal establishments in Canada as compared with those in the United States.

Well, this is one thing on which we have been in touch with them, but we find that their statistics, like some which the hon. member quoted, were based purely on the number of arrests and convictions but not on the number of offences committed. That is the same as the figures my hon. friend gave. He did mention that the increase in break-ins of private enterprise, shops of all types, had been 14 per cent. Well, actually the increase between the last fiscal year and this year, as far as offences are concerned, was only 2-3 per cent as regards break-ins in the post office establishments, but there again it is very difficult to make any comparison because I believe the figures he gave were for convictions and not the actual number of offences committed. In other words, one is comparing two different types of statistics.
The hon. member did mention at some length what he considered was the unequal rate of pay for postal employees doing similar work in two different cities, and he referred more particularly to officers of the department in charge of postal stations in Montreal and in Toronto. These rates of pay and the grading are done by the civil service commission. A survey of the various establishments of this department and of other departments is made continuously, and the civil service commission establish the grading of the employee in his particular postal establishment.
In Toronto we have 18 postal stations; in Montreal, I believe, we have 28, which means that the volume of work in the postal stations in those two cities is not the same. The grading is made, following a survey by the civil service commission, according to the volume of work, the responsibilities and the number of employees for which the particular postal officer is responsible, and not necessarily the revenue, because it may well be that the postal station in the downtown business section of Montreal or Toronto might have a very high revenue, whereas there is actually very little volume of mail handled. That is the basis on which the civil service commission determines the salaries. But at the present time, as I mentioned, this whole situation is being surveyed, not only as between the offices in those two cities but from coast to coast.
I wonder, Mr. Chairman, whether any other comment I might make could be made on the other items as hon. members ask their questions?

Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether there is any item on which the minister would like to comment with regard to the matter I brought up relative to the two a day delivery or the one a day 67509-479
Supply-Post Office
delivery and its relation to the number of persons picking up mail at letter carriers' wickets. Does the minister propose to comment on that?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: As regards the number of business firms that pick up mail, as the hon. member has mentioned, I might point out that this is one of the services given by the Post Office Department, called the bag service. The firms pay a rate for it. They prefer calling at the post office and getting the mail addressed to their firms in one bag rather than using a box. But it usually is the case that they get such a volume of mail that one or two boxes would not be sufficient to meet their need. Therefore we provide the service at a rate which would be the rate for the maximum size of box in the post office. All their mail is sorted and put into a bag and they come and get it themselves, just as they would call for their mail in a mail box.

I daresay that is true in some instances. I cannot believe it is true in other instances, particularly in a city where all the mail boxes are already rented. For instance, in the city of Kitchener all boxes are rented. In the city of Calgary there are almost as many persons picking up their mail at the letter carrier wicket as there are holding boxes in the post office. I cannot believe that is the complete explanation. In Edmonton, Alberta, there are practically half as many people picking up mail at the letter carrier wicket as there are holding boxes.
I grant you that that may be the case in a fair percentage of instances, but I do not believe it is the case in other instances. It has been brought to my attention, and it was brought to my attention particularly at the time of the increase in postal rates and the reduction to one a day service, that a great many people wanted to pick up their mail rather than have it delivered if it meant a 24-hour delay. That condition still obtains in the city of Hamilton in a business establishment within three blocks of the general post office. The business houses are receiving their mail 24 hours late by reason of the fact that they have one a day delivery and the mail goes out the first thing in the morning. Surely the minister could rectify that situation by either making available more post boxes or have two a day delivery to business houses.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I shall be very pleased to look into that, Mr. Chairman, but I am told that as a general rule the reason this service is made use of by firms is that they prefer to have it. Now, it may be that the situation varies in different localities, but that has

Supply-Post Office
been the experience oi the department. However, I shall be glad to look into this.
I report once more that since March of this year there have been two boxes for rent in downtown Toronto and two for rent in Hamilton. You just cannot get them.

I am very glad the minister answered some of my questions and gave a sort of rule of thumb basis on which mail delivery service is supplied to communities. I am also very glad to hear that he is going to look into and consider carefully the situation in Ingersoll and Tillsonburg. However, I would like to hear if as yet there has been any melting of the minister's heart with respect to the old ladies in Ontario who have served in post offices and are deserving of small pensions for the probably two or three years which will constitute the remainder of their lives.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I can assure the hon. member, Mr. Chairman, that the minister's heart as he well knows softens very easily-
That's news.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: -but this is a question of policy, and the minister cannot allow his own personal feelings to decide the question. It is being looked into at the present time.

Did I understand the
minister correctly when he said that he could not furnish an answer to my question now but that he would do so later in writing or by a letter?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have this information now. The post office referred to by the hon. member is a revenue post office; that is, it is a post office where the annual revenue is under $3,000. The postmaster in the locality resigned. In the case of a revenue post office the postmaster has to provide the accommodation himself, and when the postmaster resigns and a new postmaster is appointed the responsibility for the accommodation is that of the new postmaster. That is the situation at the present time.
The department did not pay any rent for the former post office; is that right?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman. There was until this spring, in the case of postmasters in revenue post offices, a rental allowance which was paid to the postmaster above his salary. When the revision of salaries took place this spring the salaries of these revenue postmasters were raised, and they now include what was the equivalent of the rental allowance, so that at the present time a postmaster in a revenue post office does not

receive a rental allowance but his salary includes compensation for providing the necessary quarters.
Mr. Chairman, I have another question. Has there been a new postmaster appointed at this post office, and if so was it done under competition?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: My understanding is that he has been replaced-, Mr. Chairman.

Was it done under
competition?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I am sorry but I do not
understand.
In a revenue post office such as the one we are discussing is the appointment not made after competition, or is it purely a political appointment?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
The veterans' preference
applies.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Under the act, Mr. Chairman, the appointment is made by the Postmaster General. We have, of course, the veterans' preference, as the hon. member knows. Every legion branch in the locality is advised that this post office is going to become vacant and a notice is published in the post office, but it is not a civil service classified appointment.
That is the information I wanted.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Only when the revenue reaches $3,000 is the postmaster's appointment-
I did not catch that.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Only when the revenue of the post office reaches $3,000 does the appointment of a postmaster become a classified appointment under the civil service.

Just one more question in connection with that matter. Does the Post Office Department lay down any specifications for the space that must be provided for the revenue post office when the space is provided by the postmaster and he does not receive any more than his salary? Is he able to decide himself how much space he is going to provide for the public in the post office?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: No, the department sends an inspector into the locality and he has to give approval to the accommodation which is going to be provided by the postmaster. In fact, if the person who is to be appointed postmaster cannot provide the accommodation which we consider to be necessary, then he cannot be appointed postmaster. He has to provide it, and we check on that.

I would like to ask the Postmaster General three questions. Perhaps I can group them and save a little time. When was the last over-all adjustment made giving rural mail carriers or contract carriers an adjustment of their contracts? How was this adjustment arrived at? Is consideration now being given to a raise for them, and if so when will it come into effect?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I am sorry; may I have the third question again?
Is consideration now being given to an adjustment in the contracts and if so when will it come into effect?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member may recall that when the Post Office Act was revised during the session of 1953 a section was brought in at that time to authorize the Postmaster General to make adjustments. Up to then there was no authority for the department or for the Postmaster General to make any adjustments or give any increases. This was done during the war under an order in council passed under the Emergency Powers Act. At that time in 1953, section 33 was amended to give the Postmaster General authority to make adjustments and give increases under certain conditions which are mentioned in that particular section. Following the passing of that act in the 1953 session adjustments were made after a survey throughout the country of all rural mail contracts.
This particular section makes it necessary that a contractor must have been executing his contract for a minimum of two years before an application for an increase can be considered by the department and there is no discretion on the part of the minister or anyone in the department to deal with these matters until the contractor has been executing his contract for at least two years.
I would like the minister to answer my third question. Is consideration now being given to an adjustment for those who had been holding contracts for two years or longer?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That has now become a continuing process, Mr. Chairman. Any contractor may-and he must personally-make application after two years if he wants to have an increase in his contract. We receive them regularly and all these new contractors, as my hon. friend mentioned, after two years would write in and ask that their contracts be considered from the point of view of receiving an increase.

I have one other question. What are the necessary steps that have to be taken in order to have a letter carrier service established in a suburban area?
Supply-Post Office

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: A letter carrier service?
Yes.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Not a rural mail carrier
service?
No, a letter carrier service.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Is my hon. friend referring to a suburban area adjacent to an area already served by letter carrier?
This area is adjacent to the city of St. Thomas.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: In answer to a question by the hon. member for Oxford I outlined the standards which had to be met before a new service would be established. In the case of a suburban area adjacent to a municipality where a letter carrier service already exists, the conditions and number of calls must be such that the service can be given merely by increasing the number of letter carriers and extending the routes. Each case is considered individually, and it is difficult to say just what standards have to be met.

This matter came up just before the 1953 general election when these people petitioned to have a service. They were promised that if they would elect a Liberal government they would be taken care of. Three years have gone by and they have heard nothing morfe about it. Do they have to sign another petition before any consideration will be given to this matter?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I do not know the particulars of the case to which my hon. friend has referred, but it would not be necessary to sign a petition. If according to the views of the department-and all members may not agree-it is decided that the request for a service cannot be granted, that matter is kept under continuous review. It is looked into year after year to see whether conditions have changed so that the service may be extended.

I was interested in the reply made by the minister to the hon. member for Oxford with regard to inaugurating a letter carrier service. The minister mentioned two norms which must be met, a minimum of $50,000 revenue and 2,500 call points. The interesting part of the minister's remarks was his statement that there would be a little flexibility, and that these norms would not always necessarily be met. I should like to explore that a little further to find out just what the minister meant. If the minister will say that the application made by the town of Dauphin will be considered I shall say no more. It happens that a survey was made not long ago and we came just under

Supply-Post Office
the 2,500 mark, but we were informed that we could not have a letter carrier service. If the minister will say that the matter will be reviewed I shall have nothing more to say.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I can assure the hon. member that the case of Dauphin will be reviewed. However, it would be reviewed without any action on the part of the minister, because that is done automatically by that division of the department. As I mentioned before, when the request has been made a survey is carried out, and if it is found that the conditions cannot be met the matter is kept under continuous review and as the area develops it may be able to meet the minimum standards and the service would be established without any further request being made.
Can the minister indicate the policy followed in listing the telephone numbers of the post office in the telephone directories?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I am told that the telephone number of a post office is listed in the telephone directory only in cases where there is a letter carrier service. Otherwise the number is not listed, the reason being that where such numbers have been listed the postmaster found that he spent a good deal of his time answering telephone requests as to whether there was mail for a particular individual.
It is listed only where there is a carrier service?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It may be that there are one or two cases where it is not listed, but we are not aware of any.
I am aware of quite a few places where there is a letter carrier service and the telephone number is not listed, and I think rightly so.
What percentage of first-class mail is actually airborne?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I am informed that about 50 per cent of first class mail is for local delivery, and that approximately 60 per cent of the remainder would be carried by air mail.
That means that about 70 per cent of the people who are paying first-class postage are subsidizing the other 30 per cent who are having their mail airborne.
Can the minister give the committee any information about the demolition of the building at York and Fleet streets in Toronto?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
That question would be more appropriate for the Department of Public
[Mr. Zaplitny.l
Works, as we have nothing to do with the actual buildings we occupy.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
325. Operations-including salaries and other expenses of staff post offices, district offices, railway mail service staffs, and supplies, equipment and other items for revenue post offices, also including administration, $81,501,011.

I am pleased to learn that the department is kind to dumb animals, but I should like to ask the minister if a little more kindness could not be shown on occasion to members of the human family. I have in mind the small town postmaster who is not on pension, but who after a long term of service finds his services no longer required. I have a particular case in mind, where the post office in a small community was closed and where the postmaster had served the community for 26 years. By reason of faster train service and perhaps one or two other factors, the post office was closed and the district was turned into a rural route district service post office in a larger community. The postmaster's services were no longer required.
During the 26 years this postmaster never failed to meet the trains and dispatch and receive mail. Rain or shine, 40 below zero or summertime, he was on the job. Now, in the letter he writes to me, he says:
Small salaries, thus unpensionable, at over 65, the postmastership abruptly terminated with no appreciation or word of thanks, though I note inspectors ride up and down the province presenting ribbons or medals to longish term operators of stamp wickets, etc.
I shall not take any more time on this, but I wonder whether the minister could tell the house whether or not some provision cannot be written into the regulations respecting some form of compensation for these postmasters, even though it may be on a contributory basis. Is it not possible to bring those people into some sort of pension plan?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: If the hon. member would provide me with the name of the particular post office in the case he mentioned, I should be glad to look into it. The rule now is that a full-time postmaster whose minimum salary is $900 or more will be superannuated.
I shall bring the particular case to the minister's attention.

The
Postmaster General did not reply to a number of points I raised earlier, to one or two of which a reply might be expected. Before pointing them out to him, I should say that I thought his answer to the two points he dealt with, that is the discrepancies in staff gradings as between the two cities and the

comparison of gradings, shrugged off two rather important problems with some quick, statistical manipulation that bothered me a little.
If he examines in Hansard the details that were put there, I think he will see that the situation, particularly as regards the staff gradings in these two cities, is serious and that it covers situations in which people in substantially the same type of offices, with substantially the same number of employees and with substantially the same revenue, have different gradings. That is extremely important and should be rectified, and the people brought up to the higher grade.
Having said that, I wonder whether he would like to tell us about the research work being done in the department, with particular reference to the sorting machine and the expenditures on that to date. That was one of the questions I asked before.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot fully agree with the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace when he says that I discarded lightly his remarks as regards discrepancies in salaries of postal employees in various cities. I mentioned that a survey had been made and that the civil service commission, with a man of the department, was looking into it. Unfortunately the department itself does not set salaries.
As regards the electronic sorting machine to which my hon. friend referred in his earlier remarks today, I am sorry that I could not ask interested members of the committee, as I had undertaken to do during the committee sittings, to come and see that machine in operation. At that time I mentioned that certain components were being worked on by the contractors who are doing the electronic side of the operation and were away from our laboratories in Ottawa. I am told that not all of these components have yet been returned. However, anything we have here at the present time can be seen by any hon. member. If the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace would like to come down to see the laboratories and what we have there at the present time, and have our research staff explain to him the projected operations of that machine, I should be very glad to make arrangements at any time-tomorrow, if he so desires.
When is this million dollar monster going to get into operation, so we can see it in use?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
There is no such thing as a million dollar monster; or if there is, it exists only in the mind of the hon. gentleman from Notre Dame de Grace. It so
Supply-Post Office
happens that the Post Office Department is the only organization in Canada that carries out postal duties. Any research work that has to be done in connection with the operation of the postal service has to be done by the department. We are doing very advanced research work in electronics with a view to developing and installing machines in the larger post offices for sortation, for quicker and more efficient service. Any development work of that kind is not done simply and cheaply. We have given all the details of expenditures on that machine in the estimates committee, and my friend knows about them. We also told my hon. friend that we expected that the machine would possibly be installed in the Ottawa post office at the end of this year. I am told that the schedule might be delayed by a couple of weeks.
That would be the second delay, would it not, in the plans for installing this machine?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I do not know whether it is the second delay. I will admit that it might be the third delay. That is a situation which arises when any development work is done in that field. Surely my hon. friend, who is so familiar with all the activities of business and so on, knows that situation quite well.

I am merely trying to find out a few things about a million dollar expenditure of the Post Office Department, and I do not see why the Postmaster General is so annoyed about it at this point, as is so evident from his attitude if not from the words he has used.
He is not the only one.

The department has had some experiences with other important machines. It has spent a long time before it got them sorted out in the initial stages, when they were not satisfactory. It is doing research work which may ultimately bring us great benefit. But surely we are entitled to have information in this house without annoying the minister. If I am annoying the minister, I shall not stop but I shall apologize.
It is not only the minister who is annoyed; it is all the members of the house.

Perhaps now the minister might like to tell us whether he thinks it will be a good idea or whether he is considering as was suggested in the estimates committee, transferring

Supply-Post Office
security operations from the post office to the R.C.M.P., and their co-ordination in that Reid.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
First may I assure the hon. member for Notre Dame de Grace that he does not annoy me the least bit. I simply wanted to point out to him that the information for which he was asking had been given to him in the estimates committee, that the proceedings of the estimates committee are printed and that they are public documents.
I therefore could not see why he would not have that information.
As to the point he brought up and which we discussed at the time, namely the use of the R.C.M.P., I think at that time the hon. member had in mind that there were certain offences with regard to which the R.C.M.P. seem to take the full responsibility of investigation and police work. At that time he referred to counterfeiting and possibly to narcotics.
This matter was looked into. We made inquiries from the R.C.M.P. and from the Department of Justice. As regards break-ins and robberies in connection with individual postal establishments, we were told that the R.C.M.P. would not be justified in taking over in those provinces where there is a local police force or in those provinces where there is a provincial police force, unless they were called upon to do so. We were told that as to certain offences such as those which he mentioned, it was considered by the provincial governments which, under the constitution, have the responsibility for the administration of justice, they were of a national character, so to speak, and that investigation work could be more efficiently done by the R.C.M.P. But that is only done because such is the view of the provincial authorities which have that responsibility for the administration of justice.
In certain other cases such as revenue cases and narcotic cases the work which is done by the R.C.M.P. is part of the administration of the act itself. As my hon. friend knows, they follow the narcotics trade, so to speak, and supervise the local sale of narcotics because it is done under a federal statute. That is part of the administration of the act which the R.C.M.P. undertake. But as I mentioned earlier, in the case of these break-ins and robberies it is considered that these are offences committed in a specific locality; and if the locality has a police force or if the province has its own police force, they are the responsible people. The R.C.M.P. will of course co-operate with them, and very often they are brought in and are asked by the provincial authorities to co-operate. But it is primarily a provincial responsibility.
[Mr. Hamilton (Notre Dame de Grace).1

Mr. Chairman, over the week end there was considerable comment around Ottawa to the effect that a new postal station was going to be erected in the west end of the city. Certainly I think that news will be greeted with certain acclaim in that area and I have no doubt that those affected will be very pleased about it. On the other hand, there is another part of the city known as the Glebe. For whatever reason, my attention was drawn by telephone several times today to the fact that they had been making representations for a post office building in that area and that nothing whatsoever had been done for them. Since this is close to home,
I am wondering whether the minister might give us an explanation with regard to that matter, or whether he can say when the Glebe might expect to receive their own station.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, construction of any buildings to be used by the Post Office Department is done by the Department of Public Works, and any announcement of the construction of a new building would necessarily come from the Department of Public Works and not from this department.

Surely, Mr. Chairman, the public works department just does not go out and say, "We should like to build a post office" in this area or that area. As the minister very well knows they do it on the recommendation of the Post Office Department. I was asking him what his attitude was toward the recommendation for this post office, whether it had been recommended and if not, what expectation there was that it would be recommended.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend will realize that the Glebe is relatively close to downtown Ottawa and that the west end is about five miles away. It is quite true that these buildings are constructed by the Department of Public Works at the request of the Post Office Department. We continuously make surveys of the town, city or metropolitan area in which we are giving service. As we find that expansion is taking place which is going to extend too greatly our existing services, a new postal station is built and a new distribution centre starts from there.
That is what is taking place out in that area which, as I have already mentioned, is some five miles away from centre town, as I understand it. The need has not yet been felt as far as the area to which my hon. friend refers is concerned. This matter will be continuously reviewed. As soon as the department feels that another building will

be necessary for efficient service, the request will be made on the public works department.
Mr. Chairman, I hesitate to make this suggestion, except that I understand the Minister of Finance is arranging to have a very nice surplus this year so he can pass on adequate tax cuts next year,-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That would not be the case if you had your way. You wanted me to give it to the provinces.

As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, since the Minister of Finance has interjected, it would seem to me that if it went back in that way it would go back to the taxpayers more fairly than by anything that will be done by this government.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: No. The people want to spend their own money.

If I might be allowed to continue, I should like to say this. I made the opening reference because of my feeling in connection with this estimate. I have looked at the details on page 433. I am certainly impressed with the large groups of employees. Certainly, we cannot say that we are paying them adequately when you talk about postal clerks, mail handlers and letter carriers. I would respectfully suggest that before next year's estimates come around, the minister might seriously look over the situation as far as pay is concerned in order to see that they get an adequate living wage.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I should like to point out to the hon. member that these salaries have been adjusted since these estimates were printed.

should like to confirm my understanding of something the minister said a few moments ago. I understood him to say-and we shall use a non-controversial term-that the electronic sorting machine will be in practical operation in the post office about the middle of January, 1957.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That is what is expected at this time, yes; that it will be in actual operation in the Ottawa post office.
When does the minister expect that it will be in condition for any interested parties to inspect it?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
If my hon. friend wants to come down to the laboratory tomorrow morning I will see to it that the staff is there to
Supply-Post Office
explain to him what is there. However, I mentioned that certain components are being worked on by the contractor for the electronic device part of the machine in Toronto, and that they would not be there. Hence the whole machine would not be in operation for my hon. friend to see.
That is the point I was making. When is the pilot machine, the one that we are talking about, going to be in operation for test runs again?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It will be test run this fall at the manufacturer's laboratory. I am not an electronics engineer, but I understand that certain components of that machine can be tested and developed separately from the rest of the machine. The machine has been assembled and tried out, and certain adjustments needed to be made. The components are sent back to the manufacturers where they keep on testing and developing them. It is very difficult to say just on what date the components will be assembled this fall in Ottawa for the machine to be tested as one unit. It is expected, however, that it will be in the Ottawa post office by January 15.
May I remind the minister that my remarks still stand notwithstanding the adjustment, which we knew about.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
326. Transportation-movement of mail by land, air and water, including administration, $46,388,302.

May I ask the Postmaster General whether it has been possible to bring about any reduction in the length of time it takes to get surface mail out from the United Kingdom? From time to time I get complaints about the long delays in getting that mail across. For example, in one case it took 23 days. Has there been any improvement in that situation?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I am informed that there have been new steamers brought into service by some lines, particularly Cunard and Canadian Pacific, which will give faster surface transportation. Outside of that, however, there have been no changes.
Why is it so difficult to get the mail across in a reasonable time? Apparently the service was much faster many years ago.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
One difficulty is that there is much less shipping now than before the war. There are not as many ships or as many scheduled sailings as there used to be; that is the only difference. Furthermore, many of the ships now are slower ships than

Supply-Post Office
those big liners that used to exist before the war many of which were sunk, as my hon. friend knows.

In the first place, I should like to say a word under this item because I feel we should throw a few bouquets to some of the officials in the department if they deserve them. There have been improvements in the rural mail delivery in my constituency. I want the minister and the department to know that I feel there have been improvements. Every time I get up to say a word I am not critical of the department. There has been some improvement, but there is still room for further improvement.
There is one thing I should like to make very plain to the minister, and I am very sincere about it. I find that when these matters are taken up with the officials of the department, the superintendent and all the way through, they are handled fairly and everybody seems to be happy. However, in some cases there seem to be a lot of people who have influence with the minister, and the minute that happens I find there is not so much satisfaction. It is for that reason I should like to point out that I feel the more this department is left free to handle investigations and make recommendations, the better the service will be.
There has been improvement in several cases in my constituency. I have taken up one particular mail route with the minister because the situation is pressing, but I have had no reply. I presume he is looking into the matter. I must say that since the late postmaster general passed on, information has not been conveyed to me quite as promptly. I should like to pay my respects to the late postmaster general. I was a new member while he was postmaster general, but I always got wonderful co-operation and it was a great pleasure to work with him. The particular route to which I am referring is out of Colchester; I know the minister will recall it. I have been asked to bring this matter to the attention of the minister.
A few years ago the mail route stopped a half mile short of the last residence on this highway. I will admit frankly that I have never been able to find out why that was. I am not going into the whole story, because it is late, but the minister can find out the details from some other source if he so desires. During a period of four months when this contract was renewed the mail was carried to this last residence, and then it was stopped. This resident happens to be a widow, and now she has to walk back this half mile to get her mail. I sincerely

ask the minister to look into this, because I do not think it is fair and neither do this lady's neighbours feel it is fair that a woman should have to walk half a mile to get her mail when she lives in the same settlement as the others on that route.
In addition to that, there is a little branch off this route on which there are three boxes.
I understand there has been some relaxation of the rule concerning the mail carrier going off a short distance to service residences. I have already written about that, because I have had several letters from the person at the end of that route. She has a small family, and it is very difficult for her to go and get the mail. I hope the matter will be given consideration.
There is another thing I want to mention. There are two mail routes that might be put together if the two contracts expired at the same time. Since we now have the automobile and better roads, I believe consideration could be given to improving some of these routes by amalgamation. The roads are kept plowed in the wintertime and service could be rendered by automobile.
Those are some of the things I wanted to bring to the minister's attention. I did want him to know that we have been very well served and the service has been improved down there.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I shall be glad to give the matter consideration.
I wonder if the minister would give me a breakdown of the figure on page 436 of the estimate book, $11,135,000, the payment for mail service by air, amongst the four or five major companies involved.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: May I have that question again? What breakdown does the hon. gentleman want?

I asked for a breakdown of the payments to the four or five major companies involved in the $11,135,000 for mail service by air. If that is not possible, perhaps the minister could give us a breakdown of last year's figures.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I could give the hon. member the breakdown by various air lines, if that is what he wishes.
Yes.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
The year 1955-56 will, I think, give my hon. friend a pretty good idea. Trans-Canada received $8,419,600; and Canadian Pacific Air Lines received $1,778,500. The rest consists of various smaller lines. It is quite a lengthy list. It varies between $1,000 and $211,000. The latter figure applies

to Maritime Central Airways, which does a lot of the services in the maritimes. Eastern Provincial Airways received $150,000; Central Northern Airways Limited, $101,500; Northern Wings Limited, $53,500; Quebec Air Services, $45,000; Queen Charlotte Air Lines, $43,300; Saskatchewan Government Airways, $16,000. The remainder consists of smaller amounts. As I say, they vary between $1,000 and $10,000.
This includes the international service?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It is both domestic and international.
Is it because Trans-Canada is the only air line that is carrying mail in certain districts that the amount is so large for T.C.A. and so little for the others?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Yes. As my hon. friend knows, Trans-Canada is the only air line that handles transcontinental traffic, and similarly it is the only Canadian company that does trans-Atlantic flying, so that involves a very high volume of mail, both transcontinental and trans-Atlantic.
If all flrst-class mail that it is possible to carry by air is carried by air, why is it necessary to sell air mail stamps and why should a good many people keep on using air mail stamps?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I think the stamp to which my hon. friend refers is the 7-cent stamp. I should point out to my hon. friend that if he looks at it he will see that there is nothing on it to indicate that it is an air mail stamp. It has nothing written on it but "Postage, Canada, 7 cents". There is nothing to indicate that it is an air mail stamp. However, it does serve because all first-class matter, letters up to 8 ounces, are carried on the all-up service at 5 cents, but anything else, parcel post, and so on, will cost more, and the 7-cent stamp is used. It is also used for air mail outside of Canada. There is nothing to restrict the use of that particular 7-cent stamp to any postal facilities.

But it is understood by most people, and it has been stated in many instances, that if the person wants to be sure his letter goes by air mail, then he must put a 7-cent stamp on it. Air mail stickers for letters are still available at post offices. You do not ordinarily put an air mail sticker on parcel post.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I agree; the stickers still exist and they will be used because we must have them for air mail outside of Canada or for other postal items outside of flrst-class mail which are carried by air mail. We have
Supply-Post Office
the sticker, and the 7-cent stamp is used for that purpose. But, as I pointed out, there is nothing on that stamp to indicate that it is an airmail stamp. It is just a Canadian stamp to the value of 7 cents.

But that does not alter the fact that many people today are still paying 7 cents for an air mail sticker on the letter to be sure it goes by air. Is that necessary
or not?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It is not necessary. All firstclass matter, up to 8 ounces, will be carried by air for 5 cents, if that is the quickest way to get that letter to the addressee. If it can be carried just as fast by train, then it will go by train.
What percentage of the mail from Ottawa to Toronto goes by train?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: At the present time there would be a very high percentage, because since April 30 we have had a new train service between Montreal and Toronto which does nothing else. It was put on by the C.N.R. between Montreal and Toronto both ways and it carries nothing but mail. The Ottawa mail goes from Ottawa to Brockville by motor vehicle and is placed on that train during the night, sorted on the way down and delivered the next morning in Toronto or Montreal, depending on where it is being sent.
Is it the same from Toronto to Ottawa?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I should like to ask a question with reference to the supplementary truck service. Is it the department's policy to maintain the same service where one train has been cut off in villages in western Ontario because of the Canadian National Railways' adjustment?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: As soon as we are advised by the railway company that they intend to curtail a certain train service, or change their schedule, or perhaps bring it down from six times a week to only three times a week, we immediately get ready to set up a truck service so there will be no break in the general service.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have thought that was your purpose and policy, and I have been rather defending the government for the last six or eight months up in my district where they have had mail service coming in in the morning and going out at night so that business people could answer mail on the same day. I have had repeated requests to urge the government to continue this service, because in the past 28 months that has not been the

Supply-Post Office
situation and they are getting so hostile that I cannot keep them in very good humour toward the government unless it is changed.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I can assure the hon. gentleman that I shall look into it immediately, because if there is one thing I do not want it is that his constituency should be hostile to him.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I think it should be improved in view of a possible election next summer.
Does all the trans-Atlantic airmail from Canada go by T.C.A.?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Not necessarily, because there is now a service between Vancouver and Amsterdam which is a C.P.A. service, and there is a certain volume of mail from the western part of the country to Europe which goes by that service. The remainder does go by T.C.A.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
670. Operations-further amount required, $713,800.
Will the minister tell us what the additional amount of $141,000 for professional and special services is for?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It is an additional sum required	for this	electronic research	project.
