And how much was provided for that, Mr. Chairman, in the regular estimates for the year?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs

speechtext: That would make the total expenditure on the machine to date approximately $850,000; is that correct?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Why was it necessary to bring in this additional $140,000 late in the year, Mr. Chairman? Was it not provided for earlier? Did the planning of this machine not extend that far?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I am informed that in the planning of the main estimates at that time it was not thought that the machine would have progressed to the stage it has, nor was it thought that this additional amount would be needed quite as quickly to complete the project as will be the case.

Perhaps one of the reasons I am so interested in this, Mr. Chairman, is because of a chance remark of the deputy postmaster general which was quoted in Time magazine of April 18, 1955, when he said in part:

. . . eventually, I suppose, they may even find an electronic brain to replace me.
I hope the Postmaster General is not progressing in that direction. Could the Postmaster General give us a breakdown of the additional amount of $370,100 for the acquisition of equipment in the supplementary item?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Locks, $18,000; battery
charging equipment, $11,951; motor equipment, trucks, $20,500; mail boxes, one lot,
1,000	boxes, $63,750; one group of 500 boxes, $31,875; and scales, $4,000.
What are you going to call this machine; Walter?
Does that add up to $370,000?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: There is a contract with the research company for the supply of 20 automatic facingup machines, and part of that shipment might be delivered this year. We have provided this supplementary estimate in case the delivery does come this year.
Does it have any connection with your electronic sorting machine?

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: None whatsoever.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL REVENUE Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-
54. To provide for the requirements of the sound broadcasting service (to amount formerly authorized by chap. 32, Revised Statutes, $6,250,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall this resolution carry?

I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, but I cannot let this item pass without some further comment. When these estimates were before us on July 28, which I believe was the last time we considered them, I had not finished saying what I wanted to say because time was against me for some reason; I think perhaps I took a slow pace.
I was saying when time was called against me, Mr. Chairman, that the policy the government has followed with respect to the C.B.C. has been most contradictory; that it cannot be justified in any way by logic or reason, and that the government should take a more careful look at that policy to see if something cannot be done to make it represent the kind of policy that one would expect to find in a country that is supposed to be a free enterprise country.
I made the statement that the government had taken unto itself under its policy the right to operate broadcasting stations, but refused to allow any other government in Canada to do a similar thing no matter what their justification might be. I was quite surprised at an outburst by the minister when I was talking

about continued applications of radio station CKUA in Edmonton for a commercial licence. The minister burst in with this comment, as reported at page 6642 of Hansard for July 28, 1956:
How long was it used for political broadcasts?
I believe I said at the time, Mr. Chairman, that this statement let the cat out of the bag because for quite a long time, since 1941 in fact, the minister had held to the one answer that the reason radio station CKUA in Edmonton was not given a commercial licence so it could step up its power and be of greater service in the educational field in Alberta was that there was not room for another station in the city of Edmonton.
I drew the minister's attention to the fact that since the last application was made by the Alberta government in 1947 for a commercial licence for CKUA, the university station, two new stations had been granted licences in the city of Edmonton, and then it was that he burst in with his statement, "Well, how long was it used for political broadcasts?" indicating that what has been in the mind of the minister and his colleagues all along was the fear that granting CKUA a commercial licence would endanger the political longevity of this government or the Liberal party, because they were afraid the Alberta government would be using it for political broadcasting.
Nothing as unreasonable as that has been heard in this house for a long time. The minister knows full well that if the members of the government of Alberta wanted to use CKUA for political broadcasts they would not have applied to the C.B.C. for a commercial licence. He knows that as well as he knows he is sitting here. But he used that as an aspersion, as some form of ridicule, indicating that the reason C.B.C. did not grant CKUA a commercial licence was on the ground it would be used for political broadcasting. That indicates the level at which the minister's mind has been working in connection with this thing ever since the application was first made by the department of telephones of the government of Alberta back in 1941.
I say to the minister and the C.B.C. that their action in this case has been reprehensible and cannot be justified by any stretch of the imagination. Moreover, it indicates the truth of what I said, that the policy of the government in connection with the C.B.C. is most contradictory.
There is one other thing I wanted to mention in connection with C.B.C. activities, and I intend to deal with this by way of questions to the minister in connection with some of the programs which have been sent
Supply-C.B.C.
over C.B.C. The first question I wanted to ask the minister was whether he is aware that intensive ideological warfare is going on today and has been going on around us for quite some time in the past, conducted very largely by those who are dedicated to the task of imposing communism upon the people of the earth, those in Canada included, by force if necessary but probably and preferably by ideological and propaganda methods. I wanted to get the minister's answer on that. Is he aware of that ideological warfare in which we are engaged? If he prefers not to answer now, if he would like to wait, it is all right with me. I wish he would make a note of my questions, because I am going to pursue them and get an answer even if it takes until next week.
The second question is this. Does the minister not know that the C.B.C. radio and television services have been used in the not too distant past and doubtless are still being used from time to time by diabolically clever subversive agencies in this ideological warfare, and that government money, that is taxpayers' money, is being made available to pay the very persons who are attempting to destroy the Canadian people and take away their freedom? Is he not aware of that? If not, I shall draw to his attention some things he should know.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I can answer that. I am not aware of that. It is not my duty as liaison minister between the C.B.C. and parliament to give an opinion as to what type of programs is carried. I presume that everybody in Canada knows something more or less of the ideological warfare that is going on. That is going on all over the democratic world, in Canada as much as any place else.

I am glad to have the minister's reply to that question, but no matter how often he may say that he is not responsible, he is responsible to this house for what goes on in C.B.C. He is responsible for the application of government policy, and must keep himself informed about what is going on. Let me ask him another question which I think will help get us nearer to the point I want to make. Does the minister approve of the use of the taxpayers' money to a very substantial extent by the C.B.C. to state such a patently communist line through radio and television dramas as one entitled "We Shall Not Be Moved", which was produced over the trans-Canada network on Saturday, October 1, 1955, from 8 to 10 p.m.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I did not hear the program and cannot express any opinion about it.

That just indicates how little the minister does know about what is going

Supply-C.B.C.
on. It is about time he began to inform himself, because things are going on in the C.B.C. that the people of Canada are beginning to resent very much.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Does the hon. member think I have nothing to do but to censor the C.B.C.? The hon. member may have time to sit and look at these things on Saturday evenings, but I have not.

The minister is answerable to parliament for what goes on. The board of governors of the C.B.C. are not answerable to parliament except through the minister. The only way we can get at them is through the minister. While the minister may plead ignorance as to what is going on, let me say to him that he must be answerable to us for what goes on. Let me point out to him something about this extravaganza "We Shall Not Be Moved" about which he does not seem to know but about which he should know. Perhaps we can help him get the answer.
As I say, this was put out over the C.B.C. network on Saturday, October 1, 1955. It took two solid hours of the best time of the day and there was not even one single break to give the usual announcements.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Did you listen to it for two hours?

No, but I have a report of the facts. Let me go further. This play was built around Elizabeth Gurley Flynn, who is a Smith act criminal in jail in the United States because of her activities under that act. Does the minister not know that this was picked up by the C.B.C.? How, nobody seems to know, but I am going to try to find out during the course of my questioning. This extravaganza must have cost the taxpayers of this country a large amount of money. It attracted tremendous attention from the communist press the world over. I have in my hand a photostatic copy of page 7 of the Daily People's World, which is the communist organ of the western United States. They say in great headlines:
Joe Hill, Gurley Flynn vividly depicted in Canada radio show.
I want to read a few extracts from this communist report of what happened on Saturday, October 1 and what the C.B.C. did to advance the cause of communism. This is a special to the Daily People's World from Toronto and reads:
The Canadian Broadcasting Co. made radio history October 1 when it presented a two-hour special program "We shall not be moved" in which Elizabeth Gurley Flynn, now jailed as a Smith act victim-

Criminal is the word I used.
-is portrayed as a leading figure.
The program related in story, narration, music, chorus (including a complete rendition of "I Dreamt I Saw Joe Hill Last Night" by Paul Robeson on a recording) the frameup, trial, fight back movement, execution, and Chicago funeral of Joe Hill.
The production took over the best possible broadcasting time-eight to ten p.m. Saturday. There were no interruptions-even the usual station breaks were omitted.
Diana Maddox, Canada's leading actress, played the part of Elizabeth Gurley Flynn; another top star, Hugh McNamara, enacted Joe Hill, and a supporting cast of nearly 100 players and singers, including many of Canada's finest performers, made it brilliant and exciting. Nothing was played down, distorted or withheld out of deference to the state of Utah, the U.S. state department, nor out of fear of reaction in either country.
Then, after telling about the outstanding artists who were gathered together, more than 100 of them, to put on this extravaganza, this is what the article in this communist newspaper winds up with:
Perhaps someone has made a recording of this program as was done with the play "The Investigator" from the same network. It would be a smash hit.
Just commenting briefly on that recording of the program "The Investigator", the C.B.C. did it and made available the recordings of "The Investigator", another communist play. After it was played all over Canada, then it was made available to the communists, who were playing it all over Europe. The Canadian taxpayers' money made that available. It played right into the hands of the communists and their ideological warfare, helping the communists to mash the brains of the Canadian people with their propaganda. The worst part of it is that the people had to dig up the money out of their own pockets to pay for it.
It is time the minister looked into it to find out what it is all about. If he does not know now, let him get busy and try to find out and bring somebody to task. I say that this sort of thing, which is so welcomed by the communists the world over, is serious enough that the minister ought to track down who it was that made available the time and the facilities of the C.B.C. network to bring that drama to the Canadian people. He ought to fire him, and fire him soon; and not only that, but take steps to see that it does not happen again. What has he done? That is the question.
I was interested to note, too, about this same incident that occurred last October, that the Canadian Tribune, which is the official organ of the communist party in Canada, on October 10, soon after this extravaganza was played to the Canadian people, said in headlines, "Three Cheers for the C.B.C."

After much adulation of the C.B.C., the Tribune went on to say that it is keeping its ears open for similar programs on Canadian themes, and that those who think as it does about it should let the C.B.C. know. I suppose that if the C.B.C. got a few letters calling for more of the same kind of tripe, clever subversive propaganda against established institutions, the silly C.B.C. would say, "There is a substantial section of the Canadian public that wants it, and we are going to give it to them." .
I say you had better look inside the C.B.C. to find out those who are selling the Canadian people down the river. You are not doing it. I say to the Prime Minister and the colleagues of the minister here, who says he has no responsibility, that they ought to get someone who is going to take responsibility.
If we are going to continue to operate a government corporation and clothe it with the most extraordinary powers-powers that are so vast and so absolute that the chairman of the board of governors and his officials think they are omnipotent because they have all power, and they exercise it, believe me- then it seems to me that we have to have somebody in this parliament who is ready to stand up and say, "I have informed myself about this thing on behalf of the people; I have gone into it and have discovered that it cost X dollars. I believe that was not right and it should not have been done. We have tracked down the culprits who had infiltrated, doubtless communists themselves, into the system and had induced somebody to give them the facilities of the network."
That is the kind of thing we would have if we had a minister here who was interested and concerned. That is why I asked him, to begin with, these questions. Is he aware of the ideological warfare, the intensive warfare that is going on today? It is a question of survival, and unless we are wise to what is going on we shall not survive. Believe me, if the minister allows this sort of thing to go out over the C.B.C. the people of Canada can just as well point their finger at him and say that he is responsible for selling us down the river.
There is a substantial body of Canadian opinion that says, "We are going to retain our freedom. We are not going to compromise under any circumstances with this red stuff that is going around." The minister may not know it, but it is there, and I am stating a fact tonight.
It looks to me as if we are entitled to some intelligent answers instead of wisecracks from the minister. That sort of thing needs an answer and before I get through my questioning I want to know how much that program

cost, who it was that sanctioned it, and why it was that, after much publicity was given to it in the press late last fall, the minister did not do something about it then.
He did not even find out about it.

Those are the things we have to do. Since it is eleven o'clock I am going to give the minister a chance to get his C.B.C. people together and find out about it, so he can give us a report in the morning. In the meantime I should like to adjourn the debate.
